moderation—is almost impossible; and if abstinence be an evil (which

some have doubted), no one will deny that excess is a greater. Some

parents have entirely prohibited their children from tasting

intoxicating liquors; but a parent’s authority cannot last for ever;

children are naturally prone to hanker after forbidden things; and a

[[archetypes/child|child]], in such a case, would be likely to have a strong curiosity to

taste, and try the effect of what has been so lauded and enjoyed by

others, so strictly forbidden to himself—which curiosity would

generally be gratified on the first convenient opportunity; and the

restraint once broken, serious consequences might ensue. I don’t

pretend to be a judge of such matters, but it seems to me, that this

plan of Mrs. Graham’s, as you describe it, Mrs. Markham, extraordinary

as it may be, is not without its advantages; for here you see the [[archetypes/child|child]]

is delivered at once from [[concepts/temptation|temptation]]; he has no secret curiosity, no

hankering [[motifs/desire|desire]]; he is as [[motifs/well|well]] acquainted with the tempting liquors as

he ever wishes to be; and is thoroughly disgusted with them, without

having suffered from their effects.”



“And is that right, sir? Have I not proven to you how wrong it is—how

contrary to Scripture and to reason, to teach a [[archetypes/child|child]] to look with

contempt and disgust upon the blessings of [[concepts/providence|Providence]], instead of to

use them aright?”



“You may consider laudanum a blessing of [[concepts/providence|Providence]], sir,” replied Mr.

Lawrence, smiling; “and yet, you will allow that most of us had better

abstain from it, even in moderation; but,” added he, “I would not

[[motifs/desire|desire]] you to follow out my simile too closely—in witness whereof I

finish my glass.”



“And take another, I [[concepts/hope|hope]], Mr. Lawrence,” said my mother, pushing the

bottle towards him.



He politely declined, and pushing his chair a little away from the

table, leant back towards me—I was seated a trifle behind, on the sofa

beside Eliza Millward—and carelessly asked me if I knew Mrs. Graham.



“I have met her once or twice,” I replied.



“What do you think of her?”



“I cannot say that I like her much. She is handsome—or rather I should

say distinguished and interesting—in her appearance, but by no means

amiable—a woman liable to take strong prejudices, I should fancy, and

stick to them through thick and thin, twisting everything into

conformity with her own preconceived opinions—too hard, too sharp, too

bitter for my taste.”



He made no reply, but looked down and bit his lip, and shortly after

[[motifs/rose|rose]] and sauntered up to Miss Wilson, as much repelled by me, I fancy,

as attracted by her. I scarcely noticed it at the [[motifs/time|time]], but afterwards

I was led to recall this and other trifling facts, of a similar [[concepts/nature|nature]],

to my remembrance, when—but I must not anticipate.



We wound up the evening with dancing—our worthy pastor thinking it no

scandal to be present on the occasion, though one of the village

musicians was engaged to direct our evolutions with his violin. But

Mary Millward obstinately refused to join us; and so did [[characters/richard|Richard]]

Wilson, though my mother earnestly entreated him to do so, and even

offered to be his partner.



We managed very [[motifs/well|well]] without them, however. With a single set of

quadrilles, and several country dances, we carried it on to a pretty

late hour; and at length, having called upon our musician to strike up

a waltz, I was just about to whirl Eliza round in that delightful

[[motifs/dance|dance]], accompanied by Lawrence and Jane Wilson, and Fergus and [[motifs/rose|Rose]],

when Mr. Millward interposed with:—“No, no; I don’t allow that! Come,

it’s [[motifs/time|time]] to be going now.”



“Oh, no, papa!” pleaded Eliza.



“High [[motifs/time|time]], my girl—high [[motifs/time|time]]! Moderation in all things, remember!

That’s the plan—‘Let your moderation be known unto all men!’”



But in [[concepts/revenge|revenge]] I followed Eliza into the dimly-lighted passage, where,

under pretence of helping her on with her shawl, I [[concepts/fear|fear]] I must plead

guilty to snatching a kiss behind her father’s back, while he was

enveloping his throat and chin in the folds of a mighty comforter. But

alas! in turning round, there was my mother close beside me. The

consequence was, that no sooner were the guests departed, than I was

doomed to a very serious remonstrance, which unpleasantly checked the

galloping course of my spirits, and made a disagreeable close to the

evening.



“My dear Gilbert,” said she, “I wish you wouldn’t do so! You know how

deeply I have your advantage at heart, how I [[motifs/love|love]] you and prize you

above everything else in the world, and how much I long to see you [[motifs/well|well]]

settled in life—and how bitterly it would grieve me to see you married

to that girl—or any other in the neighbourhood. What you _see_ in her I

don’t know. It isn’t only the want of money that I think about—nothing

of the kind—but there’s neither [[concepts/beauty|beauty]], nor cleverness, nor goodness,

nor anything else that’s desirable. If you knew your own value, as I

do, you wouldn’t dream of it. Do wait awhile and see! If you bind

yourself to her, you’ll repent it all your lifetime when you look round

and see how many better there are. Take my word for it, you will.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], mother, do be quiet!—I hate to be lectured!—I’m not going to

marry yet, I tell you; but—dear me! mayn’t I enjoy myself at _all?_”



“Yes, my dear boy, but not in that way. Indeed, you shouldn’t do such

things. You would be wronging the girl, if she were what she ought to

be; but I assure you she is as artful a little hussy as anybody need

wish to see; and you’ll get entangled in her snares before you know

where you are. And if you _do_ marry her, Gilbert, you’ll break my

heart—so there’s an end of it.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], don’t cry about it, mother,” said I, for the [[motifs/tears|tears]] were gushing

from her eyes; “there, let that kiss efface the one I gave Eliza; don’t

abuse her any more, and set your mind at rest; for I’ll promise

never—that is, I’ll promise to think twice before I take any important

step you seriously disapprove of.”



So saying, I lighted my candle, and went to bed, considerably quenched

in spirit.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Sotto i suoi piedi.



Successivamente entrò più nel dettaglio dell’argomento e ne fornì una spiegazione approfondita.

La follia e l’impietà di un simile comportamento… Mia madre lo ascoltò attentamente.

La più profonda reverenza; persino la signora Wilson si degnò di riposare…

Per un momento rimase in silenzio, ascoltando attentamente mentre lei, con aria soddisfatta.

Bevve il suo gin mescolato con un po' d’acqua. Il signor Lawrence sedeva, appoggiando il gomito sul tavolo.

Mentre giocava distrattamente con il suo bicchiere di vino semivuoto, sorrideva in segreto.

Per sé stesso.



“Ma non le sembra, signor Millward…”, suggerì quando finalmente…

Il gentiluomo fece una pausa nel suo discorso: “quando un [[archetypes/child|>bambino]] possa essere naturalmente, ”

Propenso all’ubriachezza… a causa dei difetti dei genitori o degli antenati…

“Occorrono alcune precauzioni in questo caso…” (Ora era generalmente riconosciuto che…)

Si credeva che il padre del signor Lawrence avesse accelerato la sua fine…

(L’ubriachezza.)



“Alcune precauzioni, forse sì; ma la moderazione, signore, è una cosa… e…”

“Abstinenza… un’altra scelta.”



“Ma ho sentito dire che, per alcune persone, la moderazione… cioè…”

Moderazione… è quasi impossibile; e se l’astinenza fosse un male (il che…)

(#Alcuni ne hanno dubitato, ma nessuno può negare che l’eccesso sia davvero un problema grave.) Alcuni…

I genitori hanno completamente vietato ai loro figli di assaggiare…

Alcolici inebrianti… ma l’autorità di un genitore non può durare per sempre.

I bambini sono naturalmente inclini ad anelare alle cose proibite… e così via.

In tal caso, un [[archetypes/child|bambino]] probabilmente avrebbe una grande curiosità di.

Assaggia e prova l’effetto di ciò che è stato così lodato e apprezzato da tutti…

“Altri… una curiosità che a lui stesso era severamente vietata.”

Di solito si è soddisfatti alla prima opportunità disponibile… e così via.

“Una volta rotta la restrizione, potrebbero seguirne conseguenze gravi… Io no.”

Pretendi di essere un giudice in queste questioni, ma a mio parere…

Il piano straordinario della signora Graham, secondo quanto lo descrivete voi, signora Markham

Come può essere, non è privo di vantaggi; perché qui si vede il [[archetypes/child|>bambino]].

Viene subito liberato dalla [[concepts/temptation|tentazione]]; non ha alcuna curiosità nascosta, nessun.

Con un forte desiderio, conosceva quei liquori allettanti altrettanto bene quanto.

Mai desidera diventare uno di loro; e ne è profondamente disgustato.

“Avendo sofferto delle loro conseguenze.”



“E davvero è così, signore? Non vi ho forse dimostrato quanto sia sbagliato…?”

Contrariamente alla Scrittura e alla ragione, insegnare a un [[archetypes/child|>bambino]] a guardare in quel modo.

Disprezzo e disgusto verso le benedizioni della [[concepts/providence|Provvidenza]], invece di riconoscerle.

“Usarli nel modo giusto?”



“Potete considerare il laudano una benedizione della [[concepts/providence|Provvidenza]], signore,” rispose il signor.

Lawrence sorride: “Eppure, dovete ammettere che la maggior parte di noi farebbe meglio…”

“Evitatelo del tutto, anche in piccole dosi; ma,” aggiunse, “io non lo farei.”

Desidero che tu non segua troppo fedelmente il mio esempio; a dimostrazione di ciò.

"Finisci il mio bicchiere."



“E ne prenda un altro, spero, signor Lawrence,” disse mia madre, spingendo il.

La bottiglia gli volò verso di lui.



Rifiutò educatamente e spostò leggermente la sedia lontano…

“Si appoggiò alla tavola e si rivolse verso di me; io ero seduto un po’ più indietro, sul divano.”

Accanto a Eliza Millward, mi chiese distrattamente se conoscessi la signora Graham.



“L’ho incontrata un paio di volte,” risposi.



“Che ne pensi di lei?”



“Non posso dire di apprezzarla molto… È attraente, ma forse dovrei dire…”

Distinta e interessante nell’aspetto… ma in nessun altro modo

Amabile… una donna che, immagino, tende ad assumere pregiudizi forti…

Restare al loro fianco nei momenti buoni e in quelli difficili, trasformando tutto in…

Conformità alle proprie opinioni preconcette… troppo difficile, troppo radicale, troppo…

“Non è abbastanza amaro per i miei gusti…”



Non rispose nulla, ma abbassò lo sguardo e morse il labbro; poco dopo…

La [[motifs/rose|rosa]], e si avvicinò lentamente a Miss Wilson; immagino che lei fosse profondamente disgustata da me.

Attratto da lei. A quel [[motifs/time|momento]] quasi non me ne accorsi, ma in seguito sì.

Questo e altri piccoli fatti, di simile [[concepts/nature|natura]], mi sono tornati in mente.

Per quanto ne ricordo, quando, ma non dovrei anticipare gli eventi.



Abbiamo concluso la serata ballando… il nostro stimato pastore non la pensava così.

Scandalo essere presenti all’occasione, anche se si è uno dei villaggi…

I musicisti furono chiamati a guidare le nostre “evoluzioni” con il loro violino… Ma

Mary Millward si rifiutò ostinatamente di unirsi a noi; lo stesso fece anche [[characters/richard|Richard]].

Wilson, nonostante mia madre lo pregasse con insistenza di farlo…

Si offrì di essere sua compagna.



Tuttavia, ce la siamo cavata molto [[motifs/well|bene]] senza di loro. Con un solo insieme di.

“Quadrille e diversi balli campestri… continuammo così fino a tarda notte.”

Ora tarda… E finalmente, dopo aver chiesto al nostro musicista di iniziare a suonare…

“Una valzer… Stavo proprio per far girare Eliza su quella deliziosa pista…”

La [[motifs/dance|danza]], accompagnata da Lawrence e Jane Wilson, nonché da Fergus e [[motifs/rose|Rose]].

Quando il signor Millward intervenne dicendo: “No, no; non lo permetto! Vieni…”

È ora di andarsene.



“Oh, no, papà!” supplicò Eliza.



“Buona [[motifs/time|serata]], mia ragazza, buona [[motifs/time|serata]]! Ricorda sempre di moderare in tutto.”

“Ecco il piano: ‘Fate conoscere a tutti la vostra moderazione!’”



Ma per vendetta, seguii Eliza nel corridoio poco illuminato, dove.

Sotto il pretesto di aiutarla a indossare il suo scialle, temo di dovermi scusare.

Colpevole di averle rubato un bacio di nascosto, mentre suo padre non guardava...

Avvolto dalle pieghe di un enorme piumone che gli copre la gola e il mento… Ma

Ahimè… voltandomi, mia madre era lì accanto a me.

La conseguenza fu che, non appena gli ospiti se ne furono andati, io…

Destinato a una severa rimprovera, il quale ostacolò in modo sgradevole…

Il rapido declino del mio umore… e una conclusione sgradevole

sera.



“Mio caro Gilbert,” disse lei, “vorrei che non lo facessi… Lo sai bene come…”

Con tutto il mio cuore penso a te in modo positivo; quanto ti amo e quanto ti apprezzo.

Più di qualsiasi altra cosa al mondo, quanto desidero vederti [[motifs/well|in buona salute]]!

"Ben sistemato nella vita… e quanto mi addolorerebbe vedere te sposato."

“Per quella ragazza… o per qualsiasi altra nel quartiere. Quello che tu _vedi_ in lei…”

Non lo so… Non è solo la mancanza di denaro a cui penso… Niente.

Di quel tipo, ma non c’è né [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]], né intelligenza, né bontà.

“Né nulla altro che possa essere desiderabile… Se solo conoscessi il tuo vero valore, come faccio io…”

Titolo:  
Non te lo sogneresti nemmeno… Aspetta un attimo e vedrai! Se solo riuscissi a…

Ti pentirai per tutta la vita se ti dedichi completamente a lei…

“E vedrai quante altre possibilità migliori esistono… Fidati di me, ne troverai molte.”



“Beh, mamma, per favore stai zitta! Odio che mi si dia la lezione. Non ho intenzione di, ”

“Sposati pure, vi dico… ma, per l’amor del cielo, non posso forse divertirmi un po’?”



“Sì, caro ragazzo mio, ma non in quel modo. Davvero, non dovresti comportarti così.”

"Cose… Saresti ingiusto con quella ragazza, se lei fosse davvero ciò che dovrebbe essere."

Mai come mai… ma vi assicuro che è una piccola civetta davvero astuta, quanto ne abbiano bisogno tutti.

Desideri vederla… ma prima ancora che te ne accorga, finirai intrappolato nelle sue trappole.

Dove ti trovi… E se davvero la sposi, Gilbert, mi spezzerai il cuore.

“Cuore… ecco dunque la sua fine.”



“Beh, non piangere per questo, mamma”, dissi, perché le [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] scorrevano a fiotti.

Dai suoi occhi; “Ecco, lascia che questo bacio cancelli quello che ho dato a Eliza… Non farlo.”

“Se la maltrattate ancora una volta, potete stare tranquilli: ve lo prometto.”

Mai… cioè, prometto di pensarci bene prima di intraprendere qualsiasi decisione importante.

“Una mossa che tu disapprovi seriamente.”



Così dicendo, accesi la mia candela e andai a letto, piuttosto soddisfatto.

In spirito.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_05" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 5" data-chapter="Chapter 05" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/artist,archetype/child,archetype/fool,motif/desire,motif/fire,motif/flowers,motif/garden,motif/grave,motif/hill,motif/night,motif/road,motif/rose,motif/spring,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,motif/winter,concept/beauty,concept/fear,concept/freedom,form/sketch,setting/london,character/arthur,character/bottom"></span>


CHAPTER V





It was about the close of the month, that, yielding at length to the

urgent importunities of [[motifs/rose|Rose]], I accompanied her in a visit to Wildfell

Hall. To our surprise, we were ushered into a room where the first

object that met the eye was a painter’s easel, with a table beside it

covered with rolls of canvas, bottles of oil and varnish, palette,

brushes, paints, &c. Leaning against the wall were several sketches in

various stages of progression, and a few finished paintings—mostly of

landscapes and figures.



“I must make you welcome to my studio,” said Mrs. Graham; “there is no

[[motifs/fire|fire]] in the sitting-room to-day, and it is rather too cold to show you

into a place with an empty grate.”



And disengaging a couple of chairs from the artistical lumber that

usurped them, she bid us be seated, and resumed her place beside the

easel—not facing it exactly, but now and then glancing at the picture

upon it while she conversed, and giving it an occasional touch with her

brush, as if she found it impossible to wean her attention entirely

from her occupation to fix it upon her guests. It was a view of

Wildfell Hall, as seen at early morning from the field below, rising in

dark relief against a sky of clear silvery blue, with a few red streaks

on the horizon, faithfully drawn and coloured, and very elegantly and

artistically handled.



“I see your heart is in your work, Mrs. Graham,” observed I: “I must

beg you to go on with it; for if you suffer our presence to interrupt

you, we shall be constrained to regard ourselves as unwelcome

intruders.”



“Oh, no!” replied she, throwing her brush on to the table, as if

startled into politeness. “I am not so beset with visitors but that I

can readily spare a few minutes to the few that do favour me with their

company.”



“You have almost completed your painting,” said I, approaching to

observe it more closely, and surveying it with a greater degree of

admiration and delight than I cared to express. “A few more touches in

the foreground will finish it, I should think. But why have you called

it Fernley Manor, Cumberland, instead of Wildfell Hall, ——shire?” I

asked, alluding to the name she had traced in small characters at the

[[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the canvas.



But immediately I was sensible of having committed an act of

impertinence in so doing; for she coloured and hesitated; but after a

moment’s pause, with a kind of desperate frankness, she replied:—



“Because I have friends—acquaintances at least—in the world, from whom

I [[motifs/desire|desire]] my present abode to be concealed; and as they might see the

picture, and might possibly recognise the style in spite of the false

initials I have put in the corner, I take the precaution to give a

false name to the place also, in order to put them on a wrong scent, if

they should attempt to trace me out by it.”



“Then you don’t intend to keep the picture?” said I, anxious to say

anything to change the subject.



“No; I cannot afford to paint for my own amusement.”



“Mamma sends all her pictures to [[settings/london|London]],” said [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]; “and somebody

sells them for her there, and sends us the money.”



In looking round upon the other pieces, I remarked a pretty [[forms/sketch|sketch]] of

Lindenhope from the top of the [[motifs/hill|hill]]; another view of the old hall

basking in the sunny haze of a quiet [[motifs/summer|summer]] afternoon; and a simple but

striking little picture of a [[archetypes/child|child]] brooding, with looks of silent but

deep and sorrowful regret, over a handful of withered [[motifs/flowers|flowers]], with

glimpses of dark low hills and autumnal fields behind it, and a dull

beclouded sky above.



“You see there is a sad dearth of subjects,” observed the fair [[archetypes/artist|artist]].

“I took the old hall once on a moonlight [[motifs/night|night]], and I suppose I must

take it again on a snowy [[motifs/winter|winter]]’s day, and then again on a dark cloudy

evening; for I really have nothing else to paint. I have been told that

you have a fine view of the sea somewhere in the neighbourhood. Is it

true?—and is it within walking distance?”



“Yes, if you don’t object to walking four miles—or nearly so—little

short of eight miles, there and back—and over a somewhat rough,

fatiguing [[motifs/road|road]].”



“In what direction does it lie?”



I described the situation as [[motifs/well|well]] as I could, and was entering upon an

explanation of the various roads, lanes, and fields to be traversed in

order to reach it, the goings straight on, and turnings to the right

and the left, when she checked me with,—



“Oh, stop! don’t tell me now: I shall forget every word of your

directions before I require them. I shall not think about going till

next [[motifs/spring|spring]]; and then, perhaps, I may trouble you. At present we have

the [[motifs/winter|winter]] before us, and—”



She suddenly paused, with a suppressed exclamation, started up from her

seat, and saying, “Excuse me one moment,” hurried from the room, and

shut the door behind her.



Curious to see what had startled her so, I looked towards the

[[motifs/window|window]]—for her eyes had been carelessly fixed upon it the moment

before—and just beheld the skirts of a man’s coat vanishing behind a

large holly-bush that stood between the [[motifs/window|window]] and the porch.



“It’s mamma’s friend,” said [[characters/arthur|Arthur]].



[[motifs/rose|Rose]] and I looked at each other.



“I don’t know what to make of her at all,” whispered [[motifs/rose|Rose]].



The [[archetypes/child|child]] looked at her in [[motifs/grave|grave]] surprise. She straightway began to

talk to him on indifferent matters, while I amused myself with looking

at the pictures. There was one in an obscure corner that I had not

before observed. It was a little [[archetypes/child|child]], seated on the grass with its

lap full of [[motifs/flowers|flowers]]. The tiny features and large blue eyes, smiling

through a shock of light brown curls, shaken over the forehead as it

bent above its treasure, bore sufficient resemblance to those of the

young gentleman before me to proclaim it a portrait of [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Graham in

his early infancy.



In taking this up to bring it to the light, I discovered another behind

it, with its face to the wall. I ventured to take that up too. It was

the portrait of a gentleman in the full prime of youthful

manhood—handsome enough, and not badly executed; but if done by the

same hand as the others, it was evidently some years before; for there

was far more careful minuteness of detail, and less of that freshness

of colouring and [[concepts/freedom|freedom]] of handling that delighted and surprised me in

them. Nevertheless, I surveyed it with considerable interest. There was

a certain individuality in the features and expression that stamped it,

at once, a successful likeness. The bright blue eyes regarded the

spectator with a kind of lurking drollery—you almost expected to see

them wink; the lips—a little too voluptuously full—seemed ready to

break into a smile; the warmly-tinted cheeks were embellished with a

luxuriant growth of reddish whiskers; while the bright chestnut hair,

clustering in abundant, wavy curls, trespassed too much upon the

forehead, and seemed to intimate that the owner thereof was prouder of

his [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] than his intellect—as, perhaps, he had reason to be; and yet

he looked no [[archetypes/fool|fool]].



I had not had the portrait in my hands two minutes before the fair

[[archetypes/artist|artist]] returned.



“Only some one come about the pictures,” said she, in apology for her

abrupt departure: “I told him to wait.”



“I [[concepts/fear|fear]] it will be considered an act of impertinence,” I said “to

presume to look at a picture that the [[archetypes/artist|artist]] has turned to the wall;

but may I ask—”



“It _is_ an act of very great impertinence, sir; and therefore I beg

you will ask nothing about it, for your curiosity will not be

gratified,” replied she, attempting to cover the tartness of her rebuke

with a smile; but I could see, by her flushed cheek and kindling eye,

that she was seriously annoyed.



“I was only going to ask if you had painted it yourself,” said I,

sulkily resigning the picture into her hands; for without a grain of

ceremony she took it from me; and quickly restoring it to the dark

corner, with its face to the wall, placed the other against it as

before, and then turned to me and laughed.



But I was in no humour for jesting. I carelessly turned to the [[motifs/window|window]],

and stood looking out upon the desolate [[motifs/garden|garden]], leaving her to talk to

[[motifs/rose|Rose]] for a minute or two; and then, telling my sister it was [[motifs/time|time]] to

go, shook hands with the little gentleman, coolly bowed to the lady,

and moved towards the door. But, having bid adieu to [[motifs/rose|Rose]], Mrs. Graham

presented her hand to me, saying, with a soft voice, and by no means a

disagreeable smile,—“Let not the sun go down upon your wrath, Mr.

Markham. I’m sorry I offended you by my abruptness.”



When a lady condescends to apologise, there is no keeping one’s anger,

of course; so we parted good friends for once; and _this_ [[motifs/time|time]] I

squeezed her hand with a cordial, not a spiteful pressure.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO V





Titolo:  
Verso la fine del mese, alla fine cedette…

A causa delle insistenti suppliche di [[motifs/rose|Rose]], l'accompagnai in una visita a Wildfell.

Hall… A nostra sorpresa, fummo introdotti in una stanza dove…

L’oggetto che colpì immediatamente lo sguardo era un cavalletto da pittore, con un tavolo accanto ad esso.

Coperto di rotoli di tela, bottiglie di olio e vernice, paletta…

Pennelli, colori e altro… Appoggiati al muro c’erano diversi schizzi

Diverse fasi di sviluppo e alcune opere d’arte completate… per lo più raffiguranti…

Paesaggi e figure.



“Devo farvi accomodare nel mio studio,” disse la signora Graham; “non c’è…

Oggi c'è stato un [[motifs/fire|incendio]] nel soggiorno; fa davvero troppo freddo per mostrarvelo.

“In un posto con una grata vuota.”



Liberando un paio di sedie da quei mobili “artistici”…

Ne ha preso il posto; ci ha invitati a sederci e poi si è rimessa al suo posto accanto a…

Cavalletto: non proprio rivolto verso di esso, ma di tanto in tanto lanciando uno sguardo al dipinto

Mentre parlava, lo teneva in mano e di tanto in tanto lo accarezzava con esso.

“Brush… come se trovasse impossibile distogliere del tutto la sua attenzione.”

Dalla sua occupazione fino al momento in cui la applicava ai suoi ospiti… Era una visione del tutto particolare.

Wildfell Hall, vista all’alba dal campo sottostante, si erge maestosa…

**Contrasto scuro su un cielo di limpido blu argenteo, con alcune strisce rosse**

Sul orizzonte, dipinto e colorato con fedeltà, e in modo davvero elegante…

Rappresentato in modo artistico.



“Vedo che dedica tutto se stessa al proprio lavoro, signora Graham… Devo dire che è davvero encomiabile.”

"Per favore, continuate; perché se permettete che la nostra presenza vi interrompa..."

Noi saremo costretti a considerarci indesiderati

“Gli intrusi”.



“Oh, no!”, rispose lei, gettando la penna sul tavolo, come se…

“Spaventato, sono diventato cortese… Non ho così tanti visitatori da non riuscire a gestirli…”

“Non esita certo a dedicare qualche minuto a coloro che mi dimostrano la loro simpatia…”

"Compagnia."



“Hai quasi completato il tuo dipinto”, dissi avvicinandomi.

Osservalo più da vicino e esaminalo con maggiore attenzione.

“Un’ammirazione e una gioia tali che non sapevo nemmeno come esprimerle… ‘Solo qualche altro tocco ancora…’”

Titolo:  
“La parte in primo piano dovrebbe bastare, penso… Ma perché mi hai chiamato?”

“Fernley Manor, nel Cumberland… invece di Wildfell Hall… nella contea di…”

Chiesto, alludendo al nome che aveva tracciato in caratteri piccoli…

[[characters/bottom|parte inferiore]] della tela.



Ma immediatamente mi resi conto di aver commesso un atto…

L’imprudenza di farlo; poiché arrossì e esitò, ma dopo…

“Un momento di pausa… con una sorta di disperata franchezza, lei rispose:”



Titolo:  
“Perché ho amici… almeno conoscenti… nel mondo, da cui…”

Desidero che la mia attuale dimora venga nascosta; e poiché potrebbero vederla.

Immagine, e forse sarebbe in grado di riconoscere lo stile nonostante le differenze apparenti

Titolo:  
“Le iniziali che ho messo nell’angolo… Prendo la precauzione di fornire…”

Falso nome anche per quel luogo… al fine di farli prendere una strada sbagliata.

“Dovrebbero provare a rintracciarmi attraverso di esso.”



“Allora non intendi tenere il quadro?” dissi, ansioso di sapere.

Qualsiasi cosa pur di cambiare argomento.



“No; non posso permettermi di dipingere solo per divertimento personale.”



“Mamma manda tutte le sue foto a [[settings/london|Londra]],” disse [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]; “e qualcuno, ”

“Li vende lì e ci manda i soldi.”



Guardando gli altri pezzi intorno a me, notai un bellissimo [[forms/sketch|schizzo]] di.

Lindenhope, dalla cima della [[motifs/hill|collina]]; un altro punto di vista sulla vecchia sala.

Godersi la nebbiolina soleggiata di una tranquilla pomeriggia estiva. E nient’altro, se non semplicità.

Un’immagine incantevole di un [[archetypes/child|bambino]] assorto nei suoi pensieri, con uno sguardo silenzioso ma.

Un profondo e doloroso rimorso, per un pugno di fiori appassiti.

Barlumi di basse colline scure e campi autunnali al loro fondo… e una luce opaca.

Il cielo sopra era coperto da nuvole scure.



“Vedete, c’è davvero una grave carenza di soggetti”, osservò la bella [[archetypes/artist|artista]].

“Una volta, in una notte di luna piena, entrai nella vecchia sala. Immagino che debba farlo.”

Prova di nuovo in una giornata nevosa d’inverno, e poi ancora una volta in una notte buia e nuvolosa.

“Serata… perché davvero non ho più nulla da dipingere. Mi è stato detto…”

Da qualche parte nelle vicinanze, si ha una splendida vista sul mare… Non è vero?

“Davvero? E si trova a distanza di cammino?”



“Sì, purché non vi dispiaccia camminare per quattro miglia… o quasi.”

A meno di otto miglia, andata e ritorno… e su un terreno piuttosto accidentato.

“Strada estenuante.”



“In quale direzione si trova?”



Ho descritto la situazione nel miglior modo possibile e stavo per iniziare.

Spiegazione dei vari sentieri, corsie e campi da attraversare

Per raggiungerlo, bisogna proseguire dritti e poi svoltare a destra.

“E a sinistra, quando mi guardò…”



“Oh, basta! Non dirmelo ora… Altrimenti dimenticherò ogni singola parola che dirai.”

Istruzioni prima di procedere… Non penserò nemmeno ad andare fino a quando non le avrò ricevute.

La prossima [[motifs/spring|primavera]]; e poi, forse, potrò disturbarvi di nuovo. Al momento abbiamo.

L’inverno che ci aspetta davanti a noi, e, “



Si fermò all’improvviso, emettendo un’esclamazione soffocata, poi si alzò in piedi…

“Scusate un attimo”, disse, poi uscì di fretta dalla stanza.

Chiuse la porta dietro di lei.



Curioso di sapere cosa l’avesse spaventata a tal punto, guardai nella direzione…

La [[motifs/window|finestra]], perché i suoi occhi erano stati fissati su di essa per un attimo.

Dietro l’orlo del mantello

Un grande cespuglio di alloro che si trovava tra la [[motifs/window|finestra]] e il portico.



“È l’amica di mamma,” disse [[characters/arthur|Arthur]].



[[motifs/rose|Rose]] ed io ci guardammo l’una con l’altra.



“Non so proprio cosa pensare di lei,” sussurrò [[motifs/rose|Rose]].



Il [[archetypes/child|>bambino]] la guardò con un [[motifs/grave|grande]] stupore. Lei immediatamente iniziò a.

Parlare con lui di argomenti banali, mentre io mi divertivo a osservare…

“Alle immagini… C’era una in un angolo nascosto che non avevo ancora notato.”

Prima non era mai stato osservato. Era un piccolo [[archetypes/child|>bambino]], seduto sull’erba con.

Un grembo pieno di [[motifs/flowers|>fiori]]. Quei piccoli tratti del viso e quegli grandi occhi blu, sorridono.

Tra una cascata di riccioli castano chiari, ondeggianti sulla fronte…

Curvo sopra il proprio tesoro…

Il giovane gentiluomo davanti a me ha dichiarato che si trattava di un ritratto di [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] Graham.

Nei primi mesi della sua infanzia.



Scoprendo questo e portandolo alla luce, ne ho scoperto un altro nascosto dietro

Con la faccia contro il muro… Ho osato prendere in considerazione anche quella possibilità.

Il ritratto di un gentiluomo nel pieno della sua giovinezza

Titolo:  
“Maturità maschile… abbastanza attraente, e realizzato con discreta cura; ma se eseguito da…”

Lo stesso autore degli altri… evidentemente alcuni anni prima; perché lì…

Una maggiore attenzione ai dettagli, ma meno di quella freschezza originale…

Per i colori utilizzati e per la libertà di espressione che ne derivava, tutto ciò mi ha deliziato e sorpreso.

Li esaminai con notevole interesse… C’erano…

Una certa individualità nei tratti e nell’espressione che la rendeva unica.

In un istante, una somiglianza perfetta… Gli occhi blu brillanti lo fissavano.

Spettatore con una sorta di ironia nascosta… Si sarebbe quasi aspettato di vederlo apparire.

Il loro sorriso; le labbra, leggermente troppo piene e sensuali, sembravano pronte…

Si illumina in un sorriso; le guance, dal colore caldo e naturale, sembrano ancora più belle…

**Crescita rigogliosa di baffi rossastri; mentre i capelli castani brillanti…**

"Clustering in Abundant, Wavy Curls: Trespassing Too Much Upon..."

Fronte, e sembrava indicare che il suo proprietario ne fosse particolarmente orgoglioso…

La sua [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] era più evidente del suo intelletto. Forse aveva ragione di pensarla così; eppure.

Non sembrava affatto uno [[archetypes/fool|idiota]].



Non avevo ancora tenuto il ritratto tra le mani da due minuti che la fiera era già iniziata

L’[[archetypes/artist|artista]] è tornato.



“Solo qualcuno dovrebbe venire a vedere queste foto…”, disse lei, scusandosi per…

Partenza improvvisa: “Gli avevo detto di aspettare”.



“Temo che venga considerato un atto di impertinenza,” dissi, “farlo, ”

Si presume che stia guardando un dipinto che l’[[archetypes/artist|artista]] ha appoggiato al muro.

“Ma posso chiedere…”



“È un atto di grande impertinenza, signore; perciò le chiedo…”

Non chiederai mai nulla al riguardo, perché la tua curiosità non verrà soddisfatta…

“Soddisfatta”, rispose lei, cercando di mascherare l’asprezza della sua rimprovera.

Con un sorriso… ma potevo vedere, dal suo viso arrossito e dai suoi occhi luminosi, che…

Che fosse seriamente infastidita.



“Volevo solo chiederti se l’avevi dipinto tu stesso”, dissi.

Con riluttanza, lasciò che le mettessero la foto in mano; perché non c’era nemmeno un briciolo…

Cerimonia in cui me lo prese e poi lo restituì rapidamente nell’oscurità

In angolo, con la faccia rivolta al muro, posizionò l’altro contro di esso…

Prima, poi si girò verso di me e rise.



Ma non ero affatto nello umore di scherzare. Senza pensarci troppo, mi voltai verso la [[motifs/window|finestra]].

E rimase lì, a guardare quel desolato [[motifs/garden|giardino]], lasciandola parlare da sola.

La [[motifs/rose|rosa]] rimase lì per un minuto o due; poi, dissi alla mia sorella che era arrivato il [[motifs/time|momento]].

“Vai, stringi la mano al giovane signore e fai un inchino cortese alla signora.”

E si diresse verso la porta. Ma, dopo aver detto addio a [[motifs/rose|Rose]], la signora Graham.

Mi tese la mano e disse, con voce dolce… e in nessun modo…

Un sorriso sgradevole, “Non lasciate che il sole tramonti sul vostro sdegno, signore.”

“Markham… Mi dispiace di averla offesa con la mia bruschezza.”



Quando una signora si degrada a chiedere scusa, non c’è modo di trattenere la rabbia

Certo; così ci separammo come buoni amici, per una volta. E _questa_ volta io.

Le strinse la mano con una pressione cordiale, non malvagia.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_06--part_01" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 6 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 06" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/rose,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/friendship,character/arthur"></span>


CHAPTER VI





During the next four months I did not enter Mrs. Graham’s house, nor

she mine; but still the ladies continued to talk about her, and still

our acquaintance continued, though slowly, to advance. As for their

talk, I paid but little attention to that (when it related to the fair

hermit, I mean), and the only information I derived from it was, that

one fine frosty day she had ventured to take her little boy as far as

the vicarage, and that, unfortunately, nobody was at [[motifs/home|home]] but Miss

Millward; nevertheless, she had sat a long [[motifs/time|time]], and, by all accounts,

they had found a good deal to say to each other, and parted with a

mutual [[motifs/desire|desire]] to meet again. But Mary liked children, and fond mammas

like those who can duly appreciate their treasures.



But sometimes I saw her myself, not only when she came to church, but

when she was out on the hills with her son, whether taking a long,

purpose-like walk, or—on special fine days—leisurely rambling over the

moor or the bleak pasture-lands, surrounding the old hall, herself with

a book in her hand, her son gambolling about her; and, on any of these

occasions, when I caught sight of her in my solitary walks or rides, or

while following my agricultural pursuits, I generally contrived to meet

or overtake her, for I rather liked to see Mrs. Graham, and to talk to

her, and I decidedly liked to talk to her little companion, whom, when

once the ice of his shyness was fairly broken, I found to be a very

amiable, intelligent, and entertaining little fellow; and we soon

became excellent friends—how much to the gratification of his mamma I

cannot undertake to say. I suspected at first that she was desirous of

throwing cold [[motifs/water|water]] on this growing intimacy—to quench, as it were, the

kindling flame of our [[concepts/friendship|friendship]]—but discovering, at length, in spite

of her prejudice against me, that I was perfectly harmless, and even

[[motifs/well|well]]-intentioned, and that, between myself and my dog, her son derived

a great deal of pleasure from the acquaintance that he would not

otherwise have known, she ceased to object, and even welcomed my coming

with a smile.



As for [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], he would shout his welcome from afar, and run to meet me

fifty yards from his mother’s side. If I happened to be on horseback he

was sure to get a canter or a gallop; or, if there was one of the

draught horses within an available distance, he was treated to a steady

ride upon that, which served his turn almost as [[motifs/well|well]]; but his mother

would always follow and trudge beside him—not so much, I believe, to

ensure his safe conduct, as to see that I instilled no objectionable

notions into his infant mind, for she was ever on the watch, and never

would allow him to be taken out of her sight. What pleased her best of

all was to see him romping and racing with Sancho, while I walked by

her side—not, I [[concepts/fear|fear]], for [[motifs/love|love]] of my company (though I sometimes

deluded myself with that idea), so much as for the delight she took in

seeing her son thus happily engaged in the enjoyment of those active

sports so invigorating to his tender frame, yet so seldom exercised for

want of playmates suited to his years: and, perhaps, her pleasure was

sweetened not a little by the fact of my being with _her_ instead of

with _him_, and therefore incapable of doing him any injury directly or

indirectly, designedly or otherwise, small thanks to her for that same.



But sometimes, I believe, she really had some little gratification in

conversing with me; and one bright February morning, during twenty

minutes’ stroll along the moor, she laid aside her usual asperity and

reserve, and fairly entered into conversation with me, discoursing with

so much eloquence and depth of thought and feeling on a subject happily

coinciding with my own ideas, and looking so beautiful withal, that I

went [[motifs/home|home]] enchanted; and on the way (morally) started to find myself

thinking that, after all, it would, perhaps, be better to spend one’s

days with such a woman than with Eliza Millward; and then I

(figuratively) blushed for my inconstancy.



On entering the parlour I found Eliza there with [[motifs/rose|Rose]], and no one else.

The surprise was not altogether so agreeable as it ought to have been.

We chatted together a long [[motifs/time|time]], but I found her rather frivolous, and

even a little insipid, compared with the more mature and earnest Mrs.

Graham. Alas, for human constancy!



“However,” thought I, “I ought not to marry Eliza, since my mother so

strongly objects to it, and I ought not to delude the girl with the

idea that I intended to do so. Now, if this mood continue, I shall have

less difficulty in emancipating my affections from her soft yet

unrelenting sway; and, though Mrs. Graham might be equally

objectionable, I may be permitted, like the doctors, to cure a greater

evil by a less, for I shall not fall seriously in [[motifs/love|love]] with the young

widow, I think, nor she with me—that’s certain—but if I find a little

pleasure in her society I may surely be allowed to seek it; and if the

star of her divinity be bright enough to dim the lustre of Eliza’s, so

much the better, but I scarcely can think it.”



And thereafter I seldom suffered a fine day to pass without paying a

visit to Wildfell about the [[motifs/time|time]] my new acquaintance usually left her

hermitage; but so frequently was I baulked in my expectations of

another interview, so changeable was she in her times of coming forth

and in her places of resort, so transient were the occasional glimpses

I was able to obtain, that I felt half inclined to think she took as

much pains to avoid my company as I to seek hers; but this was too

disagreeable a supposition to be entertained a moment after it could

conveniently be dismissed.

the rolling of the meadow-land, and the repairing of a hedge in the

CAPITOLO VI





Nel corso dei successivi quattro mesi non entrai nella casa della signora Graham, né.

“Lei è mia… ma comunque le signore continuarono a parlare di lei.”

La nostra conoscenza continuò ad avanzare, sebbene lentamente… Per quanto riguarda loro…

“Parlare… Ho prestato poca attenzione a quelle cose (soprattutto quando riguardavano la fiera)”.

“Eretico… intendo dire”, e l’unica informazione che ne ho tratto è stata quella…

Un bel giorno gelido, lei decise di portare suo figlio con sé fino a…

La canonica, e, purtroppo, nessuno era in [[motifs/home|>casa]] tranne la signorina.

Millward; tuttavia, era rimasta seduta per un lungo [[motifs/time|tempo]], e secondo tutti.

Avevano molto da dirsi e si separarono con…

Un reciproco [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di rivedersi. Ma Mary amava i bambini e le mamme premurose.

Come coloro che sanno apprezzare davvero i loro tesori.



Ma a volte la vedevo io stesso, non solo quando veniva in chiesa, ma…

Quando era fuori in collina con suo figlio, che fosse per una lunga passeggiata…

Passeggiate con uno scopo preciso… o, nei giorni particolarmente belli, semplici escursioni rilassate…

La brughiera desolata o i campi sterili che circondano la vecchia sala…

Con un libro in mano e suo figlio che gioca intorno a lei… In qualsiasi di queste scene.

Occasionalmente, quando la intravedevo durante le mie solitarie passeggiate o cavalcate…

Durante le mie attività agricole, cercavo sempre di incontrare…

O forse superarla… perché mi piaceva davvero incontrare la signora Graham e chiacchierare con lei.

Lei… e a me piaceva davvero parlare con la sua piccola compagna.

Una volta superata la sua timidezza, scoprii che era davvero una persona molto…

Un giovane simpatico, intelligente e divertente… e presto…

Diventarono ottimi amici… quanto questo fu motivo di grande soddisfazione per sua madre!

Non posso affermarlo con certezza. All’inizio sospettavo che lei desiderasse…

Versare acqua fredda su questa intimità che cresceva, per spegnerla, in qualche modo.

Accendendo la fiamma della nostra [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], ma scoprendo, alla fine, nonostante tutto.

A causa del suo pregiudizio nei miei confronti, lei riteneva che io fossi completamente innocuo… e persino di più.

Aveva buone intenzioni, e grazie a lei, mio cane e suo figlio poterono trarne beneficio.

Molta soddisfazione derivava dall’averlo conosciuto…

Altrimenti avrebbe saputo… Così smise di opporsi e anzi accolse con favore il mio arrivo.

Con un sorriso.



Per quanto riguarda [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], lui gridava il suo benvenuto da lontano e poi correva ad incontrarmi.

Cinquanta metri dal fianco di sua madre… Se per caso fossi stato a cavallo…

Sicuramente avrebbe accelerato al trotto o al galoppo… se solo ci fosse stato qualcuno…

Cavalli da tiro entro una distanza raggiungibile… gli vennero offerti per uso continuo.

Si basò su ciò che gli era stato utile, quasi in modo perfetto; ma sua madre.

Sempre lo avrebbe seguito e camminato al suo fianco… non tanto, credo, per…

Assicurarsi che possa viaggiare in sicurezza, per verificare che non abbia introdotto nulla di inappropriato…

Concetti nella sua giovane mente… poiché lei era sempre all’erta, e mai lasciava che quelle idee si perdessero.

Ciò che le dava maggiore soddisfazione era il fatto che questo gli permettesse di allontanarsi dai suoi occhi.

“Tutto ciò che si poteva vedere era lui che correva e giocava con Sancho, mentre io passavo accanto…”

Il suo lato, no, non temo nulla, per amore della mia compagnia (anche se a volte, )

Mi sono illuso con quell’idea… tanto quanto per il piacere che lei ne traeva.

Vedendo suo figlio così felicemente immerso nel godimento di quelle attività…

Sport che rinvigoriscono il suo corpo ancora fragile… eppure praticati così di rado…

Mancanza di compagni di gioco adatti alla sua età; e forse, anche il suo piacere derivava da questo…

Il fatto che fossi con lei, invece di… rendeva la situazione un po’ più piacevole.

Con lui… e quindi incapace di fargli del male in modo diretto o indiretto.

Indirettamente, intenzionalmente o in qualche altro modo, le diede comunque un piccolo ringraziamento per quello stesso gesto.



Ma a volte, credo, provasse davvero una certa soddisfazione…

“Conversando con me… e una mattina luminosa di febbraio, durante le venti…”

Una passeggiata di pochi minuti lungo la brughiera… Lasciò da parte la sua solita asprezza e…

Titolo:  
Si è tenuto a distanza, ma ha iniziato una conversazione con me, parlando con…

Tanta eloquenza, profondità di pensiero e sentimento su un argomento così importante…

Che coincida perfettamente con le mie idee… e che sia anche così bella…

Tornò a casa incantato; e lungo la strada iniziò, a livello morale, a riconoscere se stesso.

“Pensando che, dopotutto, forse fosse meglio spendere le proprie risorse…”

Giorni trascorsi con una donna come Eliza Millward… e poi…

(Per metafora) arrossì per la mia incostanza.



Entrando nel salotto, trovai Eliza lì con [[motifs/rose|Rose]], e nessun altro.

La sorpresa non fu affatto così piacevole come avrebbe dovuto essere.

Abbiamo chiacchierato a lungo, ma ho trovato che fosse piuttosto frivola.

Anche se un po’ insapore, rispetto alla più matura e seria signora.

Graham. Ahimè, quanto sia difficile mantenere la costanza umana.



“Comunque,” pensai, “non dovrei sposare Eliza, visto che mia madre la considera così…”

Si oppone fermamente, e non dovrei ingannare la ragazza con…

L’idea che avevo in mente di realizzare… Ora, se questo umore dovesse continuare, riuscirò a farlo.

Meno difficoltà nell’ liberare i miei sentimenti da quella dolcezza… ma anche…

Un'influenza inclemente… E sebbene la signora Graham potesse essere altrettanto…

“Obiezioneabile… Forse mi sarà permesso, come ai medici, di curare qualcosa di ancora più grande.”

Il male, anche se minore, perché non dovrei innamorarmi seriamente di quel giovane.

“Vedova… penso di no; nemmeno lei con me… è certo… ma se riesco a trovare qualcosa…”

Godettermi la sua compagnia… senza dubbio mi è permesso farlo; e se…

Che la stella della sua divinità sia abbastanza luminosa da offuscare lo splendore di quello di Eliza…

Molto meglio, ma fatico a crederci.



E da allora, raramente trascorreva una bella giornata senza che io…

La visita a Wildfell avvenne più o meno nel momento in cui la mia nuova conoscente di solito se ne andava.

“Eremo… ma troppo spesso le mie aspettative venivano deluse.”

Un altro colloquio… Quanto fosse imprevedibile nel suo modo di comportarsi nei momenti in cui si esprimeva…

E nei luoghi dove si recava per il riposo, quelle fugaci visioni erano davvero effimere…

Riuscii ad ottenere… e quasi pensai che lei l’avesse preso come…

“Molti sforzi da parte di entrambi per evitare la compagnia dell’altro… ma questo era davvero troppo.”

Una supposizione sgradevole da prendere in considerazione nemmeno per un istante…

Poter essere facilmente scartato.



Un pomeriggio tranquillo e sereno di marzo, mentre supervisionavo…

Il movimento ondulante dei prati, e la riparazione di un recinto nel.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_06--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 6 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 06" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/hill,motif/home,motif/horse,motif/love,motif/moon,motif/nakedness,motif/time,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/winter,concept/beauty,form/sketch,character/arthur"></span>


valley, I saw Mrs. Graham down by the brook, with a [[forms/sketch|sketch]]-book in her

hand, absorbed in the exercise of her favourite art, while [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] was

putting on the [[motifs/time|time]] with constructing dams and breakwaters in the

shallow, stony stream. I was rather in want of amusement, and so rare

an opportunity was not to be neglected; so, leaving both meadow and

hedge, I quickly repaired to the spot, but not before Sancho, who,

immediately upon perceiving his young friend, scoured at full gallop

the intervening space, and pounced upon him with an impetuous mirth

that precipitated the [[archetypes/child|child]] almost into the middle of the beck; but,

happily, the stones preserved him from any serious wetting, while their

smoothness prevented his being too much hurt to laugh at the untoward

event.



Mrs. Graham was studying the distinctive characters of the different

varieties of trees in their [[motifs/winter|winter]] [[motifs/nakedness|nakedness]], and copying, with a

spirited, though delicate touch, their various ramifications. She did

not talk much, but I stood and watched the progress of her pencil: it

was a pleasure to behold it so dexterously guided by those fair and

graceful fingers. But ere long their dexterity became impaired, they

began to hesitate, to tremble slightly, and make false strokes, and

then suddenly came to a pause, while their owner laughingly raised her

face to mine, and told me that her [[forms/sketch|sketch]] did not profit by my

superintendence.



“Then,” said I, “I’ll talk to [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] till you’ve done.”



“I should like to have a ride, Mr. Markham, if mamma will let me,” said

the [[archetypes/child|child]].



“What on, my boy?”



“I think there’s a [[motifs/horse|horse]] in that field,” replied he, pointing to where

the strong black mare was pulling the roller.



“No, no, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]; it’s too far,” objected his mother.



But I promised to bring him safe back after a turn or two up and down

the meadow; and when she looked at his eager face she smiled and let

him go. It was the first [[motifs/time|time]] she had even allowed me to take him so

much as half a field’s length from her side.



[Illustration]



Enthroned upon his monstrous steed, and solemnly proceeding up and down

the wide, steep field, he looked the very incarnation of quiet, gleeful

satisfaction and delight. The rolling, however, was soon completed; but

when I dismounted the gallant horseman, and restored him to his mother,

she seemed rather displeased at my keeping him so long. She had shut up

her [[forms/sketch|sketch]]-book, and been, probably, for some minutes impatiently

waiting his return.



It was now high [[motifs/time|time]] to go [[motifs/home|home]], she said, and would have bid me

good-evening, but I was not going to leave her yet: I accompanied her

half-way up the [[motifs/hill|hill]]. She became more sociable, and I was beginning to

be very happy; but, on coming within sight of the grim old hall, she

stood still, and turned towards me while she spoke, as if expecting I

should go no further, that the conversation would end here, and I

should now take leave and depart—as, indeed, it was [[motifs/time|time]] to do, for

“the clear, cold eve” was fast “declining,” the sun had set, and the

gibbous [[motifs/moon|moon]] was visibly brightening in the pale grey sky; but a

feeling almost of compassion riveted me to the spot. It seemed hard to

leave her to such a lonely, comfortless [[motifs/home|home]]. I looked up at it. Silent

and grim it frowned before us. A faint, red light was gleaming from the

lower windows of one wing, but all the other windows were in darkness,

and many exhibited their black, cavernous gulfs, entirely destitute of

glazing or framework.



“Do you not find it a desolate place to live in?” said I, after a

moment of silent contemplation.



“I do, sometimes,” replied she. “On [[motifs/winter|winter]] evenings, when [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] is in

bed, and I am sitting there alone, hearing the bleak [[motifs/wind|wind]] moaning round

me and howling through the ruinous old chambers, no books or

occupations can repress the dismal thoughts and apprehensions that come

crowding in—but it is folly to give way to such weakness, I know. If

Rachel is satisfied with such a life, why should not I?—Indeed, I

cannot be too thankful for such an asylum, while it is left me.”



The closing sentence was uttered in an under-tone, as if spoken rather

to herself than to me. She then bid me good-evening and withdrew.



I had not proceeded many steps on my way homewards when I perceived Mr.

Lawrence, on his pretty grey pony, coming up the rugged lane that

crossed over the [[motifs/hill|hill]]-top. I went a little out of my way to speak to

him; for we had not met for some [[motifs/time|time]].



“Was that Mrs. Graham you were speaking to just now?” said he, after

the first few words of greeting had passed between us.



“Yes.”



“Humph! I thought so.” He looked contemplatively at his [[motifs/horse|horse]]’s mane,

as if he had some serious cause of dissatisfaction with it, or

something else.



“[[motifs/well|Well]]! what then?”



“Oh, nothing!” replied he. “Only I thought you disliked her,” he

quietly added, curling his classic lip with a slightly sarcastic smile.



“Suppose I did; mayn’t a man change his mind on further acquaintance?”



“Yes, of course,” returned he, nicely reducing an entanglement in the

pony’s redundant hoary mane. Then suddenly turning to me, and fixing

his shy, hazel eyes upon me with a steady penetrating gaze, he added,

“Then you _have_ changed your mind?”

expected he would, the first start of surprise, at the audacious

question, was followed by a tittering laugh, as if he was highly amused

at the idea.



“_I_ in [[motifs/love|love]] with her!” repeated he. “What makes you dream of such a

thing?”



“From the interest you take in the progress of my acquaintance with the

lady, and the changes of my opinion concerning her, I thought you might

He laughed again. “Jealous! no. But I thought you were going to marry

Eliza Millward.”



“You thought wrong, then; I am not going to marry either one or the

other—that I know of—”



“Then I think you’d better let them alone.”



“Are you going to marry Jane Wilson?”



He coloured, and played with the mane again, but answered—“No, I think

not.”



“Then you had better let her alone.”



“She won’t let me alone,” he might have said; but he only looked silly

and said nothing for the space of half a minute, and then made another

attempt to turn the conversation; and this [[motifs/time|time]] I let it pass; for he

had borne enough: another word on the subject would have been like the

last atom that breaks the camel’s back.



I was too late for tea; but my mother had kindly kept the teapot and

muffin warm upon the hobs, and, though she scolded me a little, readily

admitted my excuses; and when I complained of the flavour of the

overdrawn tea, she poured the remainder into the slop-basin, and bade

[[motifs/rose|Rose]] put some fresh into the pot, and reboil the kettle, which offices

were performed with great commotion, and certain remarkable comments.



“[[motifs/well|Well]]!—if it had been me now, I should have had no tea at all—if it had

been Fergus, even, he would have to put up with such as there was, and

been told to be thankful, for it was far too good for him; but _you_—we

can’t do too much for you. It’s always so—if there’s anything

particularly nice at table, mamma winks and nods at me to abstain from

it, and if I don’t attend to that, she whispers, ‘Don’t eat so much of

that, [[motifs/rose|Rose]]; Gilbert will like it for his supper.’—_I’m_ nothing at all.

In the parlour, it’s ‘Come, [[motifs/rose|Rose]], put away your things, and let’s have

the room nice and tidy against they come in; and keep up a good [[motifs/fire|fire]];

Gilbert likes a cheerful [[motifs/fire|fire]].’ In the kitchen—‘Make that pie a large

one, [[motifs/rose|Rose]]; I daresay the boys’ll be hungry; and don’t put so much

pepper in, they’ll not like it, I’m sure’—or, ‘[[motifs/rose|Rose]], don’t put so many

spices in the pudding, Gilbert likes it plain,’—or, ‘Mind you put

plenty of currants in the cake, Fergus liked plenty.’ If I say, ‘[[motifs/well|Well]],

Mamma, _I_ don’t,’ I’m told I ought not to think of myself. ‘You know,

[[motifs/rose|Rose]], in all household matters, we have only two things to consider,

first, what’s proper to be done; and, secondly, what’s most agreeable

to the gentlemen of the house—anything will do for the ladies.’”



“And very good doctrine too,” said my mother. “Gilbert thinks so, I’m

sure.”



“Very convenient doctrine, for us, at all events,” said I; “but if you

would really study my pleasure, mother, you must consider your own

comfort and convenience a little more than you do—as for [[motifs/rose|Rose]], I have

no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] she’ll take care of herself; and whenever she does make a

sacrifice or perform a remarkable act of devotedness, she’ll take good

care to let me know the extent of it. But for _you_, I might sink into

the grossest condition of [[concepts/self|self]]-indulgence and carelessness about the

wants of others, from the mere habit of being constantly cared for

myself, and having all my wants anticipated or immediately supplied,

while left in total ignorance of what is done for me,—if [[motifs/rose|Rose]] did not

enlighten me now and then; and I should receive all your kindness as a

matter of course, and never know how much I owe you.”



“Ah! and you never _will_ know, Gilbert, till you’re married. Then,

when you’ve got some trifling, [[concepts/self|self]]-conceited girl like Eliza Millward,

careless of everything but her own immediate pleasure and advantage, or

some misguided, obstinate woman, like Mrs. Graham, ignorant of her

principal duties, and clever only in what concerns her least to

know—then you’ll find the difference.”



“It will do me good, mother; I was not sent into the world merely to

exercise the good capacities and good feelings of others—was I?—but to

exert my own towards them; and when I marry, I shall expect to find

more pleasure in making my wife happy and comfortable, than in being

made so by her: I would rather give than receive.”



“Oh! that’s all nonsense, my dear. It’s mere boy’s talk that! You’ll

soon tire of petting and humouring your wife, be she ever so charming,

and _then_ comes the trial.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], then, we must bear one another’s burdens.”



“Then you must fall each into your proper place. You’ll do your

business, and she, if she’s worthy of you, will do hers; but it’s your

business to please yourself, and hers to please you. I’m sure your

poor, dear father was as good a husband as ever lived, and after the

first six months or so were over, I should as soon have expected him to

fly, as to put himself out of his way to pleasure me. He always said I

was a good wife, and did my duty; and he always did his—bless him!—he

was steady and punctual, seldom found fault without a reason, always

did justice to my good dinners, and hardly ever spoiled my cookery by

delay—and that’s as much as any woman can expect of any man.”



Is it so, Halford? Is that the extent of _your_ domestic virtues; and

does your happy wife exact no more?
