CAPITOLO XXIV





25 marzo.—[[characters/arthur|Arthur]] si sta stancando. Non di me, spero, ma delle.

Una vita oziosa e tranquilla. E nessuno [[concepts/wonder|stupore]], perché ha così poche fonti di.

Divertimento: non legge mai nulla se non giornali e notizie sportive.

Riviste… e quando mi vede impegnata a leggere un libro, non mi lascia fare.

Aspetta che io lo chiuda… Con il bel tempo, di solito riesce a farlo.

Nel corso del tempo è andato piuttosto bene, ma nei giorni di pioggia, ne abbiamo avuti molti.

Molto spesso ultimamente, è davvero doloroso assistere alla sua noia… Faccio tutto ciò che posso…

Non riesco a divertirlo, ma è impossibile far sì che si interessi a nulla.

Titolo: Di cosa mi piace parlare di più, mentre lui preferisce…

Parlare di cose che non mi interessano… o addirittura che mi infastidiscono…

Questi gli piacciono soprattutto: il suo passatempo preferito è infatti sedersi…

O si sdraia accanto a me sul divano e mi racconta storie del suo passato…

Amori che finiscono sempre con la rovina di una ragazza ingenua e fiduciosa…

Inganni su un marito ingenuo; e quando esprimo il mio orrore…

Indignato, attribuisce tutto alla [[concepts/jealousy|invidia]] e ride fino a.

Le [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] scorrono lungo le sue guance. Io un tempo mi lasciavo travolgere dalle passioni o, mi scioglievo completamente.

All’inizio erano [[motifs/tears|lacrime]], ma vedendo che la sua gioia aumentava in proporzione.

"#La mia rabbia e agitazione… Da allora ho cercato di reprimerle."

Prova sentimenti e riceve le sue rivelazioni nel [[motifs/silence|silenzio]] di un calmo disprezzo.

“Ma comunque legge nella mia espressione quella lotta interiore e la interpreta male…”

L'amarezza dell’[[motifs/soul|'anima]] per la propria inadeguatezza si trasformava nei tormenti di chi è ferito.

[[concepts/jealousy|invidia]]; e quando si è sufficientemente distratto con quella, o.

Teme che la mia disapprovazione possa diventare troppo grave per il suo benessere, quindi cerca di…

“Per baciarmi e consolarmi fino a farmi sorridere di nuovo… Mai prima d’ora i suoi carezzi erano stati così…”

“Che benvenuto poco gradito… Questo è doppio egoismo, dimostrato proprio verso di me.”

E anche alle vittime del suo precedente [[motifs/love|amore]]. Ci sono momenti in cui, con un.

Un breve dolore, un lampo di disperazione selvaggia. Mi chiedo: “[[characters/helen|Helen]], cosa hai fatto?”

“L’hai fatto davvero?” Ma rimprovero quella voce interiore che continua a pormi domande e scaccio via quelle intrusioni fastidiose.

Pensieri che mi assalgono… perché se fosse dieci volte più sensuale…

Impenetrabile a pensieri buoni e nobili, so bene di non avere alcun diritto a.

Non mi lamento. E non mi lamenterò mai. Lo amo ancora, e lo amerò sempre.

E non mi pento, né mi pentirò mai, di aver legato il mio destino al suo.



4 aprile – Abbiamo avuto una vera e propria lite. I dettagli sono…

segue: [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] mi aveva raccontato, in diversi momenti, tutta la storia di.

La sua relazione con Lady F..., di cui prima non avrei mai creduto. Era…

“Una certa consolazione, tuttavia, è scoprire che in questo caso la signora…”

Era più colpevole di lui, perché all’[[motifs/time|epoca]] era molto giovane, e lei.

A quanto pare, aveva effettivamente fatto i primi passi avanti, se ciò che diceva era vero…

La odiavo per questo, perché sembrava che fosse stata lei la principale responsabile di…

La sua corruzione… e quando iniziò a parlare di lei… l’altra.

“Giorno… Gli pregai di non menzionarla, perché odiavo semplicemente il suono del suo nome.”

del suo nome.



“Non perché la amassi, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], intendo, ma perché ti ha fatto del male.”

Una donna spregevole che ingannò suo marito

“Di chi dovresti vergognarti anche solo di menzionare il nome.”



Ma la difese sostenendo che avesse un vecchio marito devoto e affettuoso…

Era impossibile [[motifs/love|amare]].



“Allora perché lo ha sposato?” dissi io.



“Per i suoi soldi,” fu la risposta.



“Allora quello è stato un altro crimine. E la sua solenne promessa di [[motifs/love|amare]] e [[concepts/honour|onorare]], ”

“C’era un altro ancora, il che aumentava soltanto l’enormità di quello precedente.”



“Siete troppo severi con quella povera signora,” rise lui. “Ma non importa…”

[[characters/helen|Helen]], ora non mi interessa più; in realtà, nessuna di loro mi è mai piaciuta nemmeno la metà.

Proprio come io faccio per te, non c’è motivo che tu abbia paura di essere abbandonato come loro.



“Se mi avessi detto queste cose prima, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], non avrei mai, ”

“Se ti venisse data l’opportunità…”



“Non lo faresti anche tu, mio caro?”



"Certamente no!"



Rise, incredulo.



“Vorrei tanto riuscire a convincervene ora!” esclamai, alzandomi in piedi.

Accanto a lui. E per la prima [[motifs/time|volta]] nella mia vita, e spero che sia anche l’ultima, io.

Avrei voluto non essermi sposata con lui.



“[[characters/helen|Helen]],” disse lui, con maggiore serietà, “sai che se ora ti credessi, ”

Dovrei essere molto arrabbiato… ma grazie al cielo non lo sono. Anche se tu sei lì…

Con quel tuo viso pallido e quegli occhi scintillanti, mi guardi come se fossi qualcosa di molto…

"Tigress… conosco quel cuore che porti dentro di te, forse anche meglio di quanto tu stessa lo conosca."

“Lo sai bene tu stesso.”



Senza dire una parola, lasciai la stanza e mi chiusi dentro la mia camera.

Stanza… Dopo circa mezz’ora arrivò alla porta e, prima di tutto, provò…

Prese il manico e poi bussò.



“Non mi lascerai entrare, [[characters/helen|Helen]]?” disse lui. “No; mi hai offeso,” risposi io.

Rispose: “E non voglio più vedere il tuo viso né sentire la tua voce.”

“Fino all’alba.”



Si fermò per un momento, come se fosse rimasto sbalordito o incerto su come rispondere a una domanda del genere.

Discorso… e poi si girò e se ne andò. Era passata soltanto un’ora da allora.

Cena: Sapevo che gli sarebbe sembrato molto noioso stare seduto da solo per tutta la sera.

E questo attenuò considerevolmente il mio risentimento, anche se non riuscì a far sì che io…

Non cedere mai. Ero decisa a fargli capire che il mio cuore non era suo schiavo.

E avrei potuto vivere senza di lui, se avessi voluto… E così mi sedetti e scrissi.

Lettera lunga alla mia zia… in cui, ovviamente, non le dico nulla di tutto questo. Presto.

Dopo le dieci di [[motifs/clock|ore]], lo sentii tornare su, ma passò davanti alla mia porta e.

Andò direttamente nel suo bagno privato e si chiuse lì dentro

di notte.



Ero piuttosto ansioso di vedere come avrebbe reagito al mio arrivo la mattina seguente…

Non poco deluso nel vederlo entrare in sala da pranzo con…

Un sorriso negligente.



“Sei ancora arrabbiata, [[characters/helen|Helen]]?”, disse avvicinandosi come per salutarmi.

Mi voltai freddamente verso il tavolo e iniziai a versare il caffè.

Notando che era piuttosto in ritardo.



Emise un fischio sommesso e si avviò verso la [[motifs/window|finestra]], dove.

Titolo:  
È rimasto fermo per alcuni minuti, ammirando quella piacevole vista…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_24--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 24 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 24" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/grave,motif/horse,motif/night,motif/rose,motif/silence,motif/sleep,motif/tears,motif/time,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/revenge,concept/self,setting/london,character/arthur,character/helen"></span>


grey clouds, streaming rain, soaking lawn, and dripping leafless trees,

and muttering execrations on the weather, and then sat down to

breakfast. While taking his coffee he muttered it was “d—d cold.”



“You should not have left it so long,” said I.



He made no answer, and the meal was concluded in [[motifs/silence|silence]]. It was a

relief to both when the letter-bag was brought in. It contained upon

examination a newspaper and one or two letters for him, and a couple of

letters for me, which he tossed across the table without a remark. One

was from my brother, the other from Milicent Hargrave, who is now in

[[settings/london|London]] with her mother. His, I think, were business letters, and

apparently not much to his mind, for he crushed them into his pocket

with some muttered expletives that I should have reproved him for at

any other [[motifs/time|time]]. The paper he set before him, and pretended to be deeply

absorbed in its contents during the remainder of breakfast, and a

considerable [[motifs/time|time]] after.



The reading and answering of my letters, and the direction of household

concerns, afforded me ample employment for the morning: after lunch I

got my drawing, and from dinner till bed-[[motifs/time|time]] I read. Meanwhile, poor

[[characters/arthur|Arthur]] was sadly at a loss for something to amuse him or to occupy his

[[motifs/time|time]]. He wanted to appear as busy and as unconcerned as I did. Had the

weather at all permitted, he would doubtless have ordered his [[motifs/horse|horse]] and

set off to some distant region, no matter where, immediately after

breakfast, and not returned till [[motifs/night|night]]: had there been a lady anywhere

within reach, of any age between fifteen and forty-five, he would have

sought [[concepts/revenge|revenge]] and found employment in getting up, or trying to get up,

a desperate flirtation with her; but being, to my private satisfaction,

entirely cut off from both these sources of diversion, his sufferings

were truly deplorable. When he had done yawning over his paper and

scribbling short answers to his shorter letters, he spent the remainder

of the morning and the whole of the afternoon in fidgeting about from

room to room, watching the clouds, cursing the rain, alternately

petting and teasing and abusing his dogs, sometimes lounging on the

sofa with a book that he could not force himself to read, and very

often fixedly gazing at me when he thought I did not perceive it, with

the vain [[concepts/hope|hope]] of detecting some traces of [[motifs/tears|tears]], or some tokens of

remorseful anguish in my face. But I managed to preserve an undisturbed

though [[motifs/grave|grave]] serenity throughout the day. I was not really angry: I

felt for him all the [[motifs/time|time]], and longed to be reconciled; but I

determined he should make the first advances, or at least show some

signs of an humble and contrite spirit first; for, if I began, it would

only minister to his [[concepts/self|self]]-conceit, increase his arrogance, and quite

destroy the lesson I wanted to give him.



He made a long stay in the dining-room after dinner, and, I [[concepts/fear|fear]], took

an unusual quantity of wine, but not enough to loosen his tongue: for

when he came in and found me quietly occupied with my book, too busy to

lift my head on his entrance, he merely murmured an expression of

suppressed disapprobation, and, shutting the door with a bang, went and

stretched himself at full length on the sofa, and composed himself to

[[motifs/sleep|sleep]]. But his favourite cocker, Dash, that had been lying at my feet,

took the liberty of jumping upon him and beginning to lick his face. He

struck it off with a smart blow, and the poor dog squeaked and ran

cowering back to me. When he woke up, about half an hour after, he

called it to him again, but Dash only looked sheepish and wagged the

tip of his tail. He called again more sharply, but Dash only clung the

closer to me, and licked my hand, as if imploring protection. Enraged

at this, his master snatched up a heavy book and hurled it at his head.

The poor dog set up a piteous outcry, and ran to the door. I let him

out, and then quietly took up the book.



“Give that book to me,” said [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], in no very courteous tone. I gave

it to him.



“Why did you let the dog out?” he asked; “you knew I wanted him.”



“By what token?” I replied; “by your throwing the book at him? but

perhaps it was intended for me?”



“No; but I see you’ve got a taste of it,” said he, looking at my hand,

that had also been struck, and was rather severely grazed.



I returned to my reading, and he endeavoured to occupy himself in the

same manner; but in a little while, after several portentous yawns, he

pronounced _his_ book to be “cursed trash,” and threw it on the table.

Then followed eight or ten minutes of [[motifs/silence|silence]], during the greater part

of which, I believe, he was staring at me. At last his patience was

tired out.



“What _is_ that book, [[characters/helen|Helen]]?” he exclaimed.



I told him.



“Is it interesting?”



“Yes, very.”



I went on reading, or pretending to read, at least—I cannot say there

was much communication between my eyes and my brain; for, while the

former ran over the pages, the latter was earnestly wondering when

[[characters/arthur|Arthur]] would speak next, and what he would say, and what I should

answer. But he did not speak again till I [[motifs/rose|rose]] to make the tea, and

then it was only to say he should not take any. He continued lounging

on the sofa, and alternately closing his eyes and looking at his watch

and at me, till bed-[[motifs/time|time]], when I [[motifs/rose|rose]], and took my candle and retired.



“[[characters/helen|Helen]]!” cried he, the moment I had left the room. I turned back, and

stood awaiting his commands.



“What do you want, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?” I said at length.



“Nothing,” replied he. “Go!”



I went, but hearing him mutter something as I was closing the door, I

turned again. It sounded very like “confounded slut,” but I was quite

willing it should be something else.



“Were you speaking, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?” I asked.

Con un colpo deciso lo eliminò, e il povero cane emise un grido acuto prima di scappare via

Ritirandosi verso di me, tremante… Quando si svegliò, circa mezz’ora dopo, era ancora lì.

La coda di Dash… Lo chiamò di nuovo più forte, ma Dash si attaccò solo ancora di più.

Gliel’ho detto.

Continuai a leggere, o almeno fingevo di leggere… Non posso dire con certezza…

Risposta. Ma non parlò più fino a quando non mi alzai per preparare il tè.

Seduto sul divano, chiudeva gli occhi e poi li riapriva di continuo, guardando l’orologio.

Erano in attesa dei suoi ordini.

“Stavi parlando, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?”, chiesi.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_24--part_03" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 24 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 24" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/fire,motif/horse,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/memory,motif/rose,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,setting/london,character/arthur,character/helen,character/richard"></span>


“No,” was the answer, and I shut the door and departed. I saw nothing

more of him till the following morning at breakfast, when he came down

a full hour after the usual [[motifs/time|time]].



“You’re very late,” was my morning’s salutation.



“You needn’t have waited for me,” was his; and he walked up to the

[[motifs/window|window]] again. It was just such weather as yesterday.



“Oh, this confounded rain!” he muttered. But, after studiously

regarding it for a minute or two, a bright idea, seemed to strike him,

for he suddenly exclaimed, “But I know what I’ll do!” and then returned

and took his seat at the table. The letter-bag was already there,

waiting to be opened. He unlocked it and examined the contents, but

said nothing about them.



“Is there anything for me?” I asked.



“No.”



He opened the newspaper and began to read.



“You’d better take your coffee,” suggested I; “it will be cold again.”



“You may go,” said he, “if you’ve done; I don’t want you.”



I [[motifs/rose|rose]] and withdrew to the next room, wondering if we were to have

another such miserable day as yesterday, and wishing intensely for an

end of these mutually inflicted torments. Shortly after I heard him

ring the bell and give some orders about his wardrobe that sounded as

if he meditated a long [[motifs/journey|journey]]. He then sent for the coachman, and I

heard something about the carriage and the horses, and [[settings/london|London]], and

seven o’[[motifs/clock|clock]] to-morrow morning, that startled and disturbed me not a

little.



“I must not let him go to [[settings/london|London]], whatever comes of it,” said I to

myself; “he will run into all kinds of mischief, and I shall be the

cause of it. But the question is, How am I to alter his purpose? [[motifs/well|Well]],

I will wait awhile, and see if he mentions it.”



I waited most anxiously, from hour to hour; but not a word was spoken,

on that or any other subject, to me. He whistled and talked to his

dogs, and wandered from room to room, much the same as on the previous

day. At last I began to think I must introduce the subject myself, and

was pondering how to bring it about, when John unwittingly came to my

relief with the following message from the coachman:



“Please, sir, [[characters/richard|Richard]] says one of the horses has got a very bad cold,

and he thinks, sir, if you could make it convenient to go the day after

to-morrow, instead of to-morrow, he could physic it to-day, so as—”



“Confound his impudence!” interjected the master.



“Please, sir, he says it would be a deal better if you could,”

persisted John, “for he hopes there’ll be a change in the weather

shortly, and he says it’s not _likely_, when a [[motifs/horse|horse]] is so bad with a

cold, and physicked and all—”



“Devil take the [[motifs/horse|horse]]!” cried the gentleman. “[[motifs/well|Well]], tell him I’ll think

about it,” he added, after a moment’s reflection. He cast a searching

glance at me, as the servant withdrew, expecting to see some token of

deep astonishment and alarm; but, being previously prepared, I

preserved an aspect of stoical indifference. His countenance fell as he

met my steady gaze, and he turned away in very obvious disappointment,

and walked up to the [[motifs/fire|fire]]-place, where he stood in an attitude of

undisguised dejection, leaning against the chimney-piece with his

forehead sunk upon his arm.



“Where do you want to go, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?” said I.



“To [[settings/london|London]],” replied he, gravely.



“What for?” I asked.



“Because I cannot be happy here.”



“Why not?”



“Because my wife doesn’t [[motifs/love|love]] me.”



“She would [[motifs/love|love]] you with all her heart, if you deserved it.”



“What must I do to deserve it?”



This seemed humble and earnest enough; and I was so much affected,

between sorrow and joy, that I was obliged to pause a few seconds

before I could steady my voice to reply.



“If she gives you her heart,” said I, “you must take it, thankfully,

and use it [[motifs/well|well]], and not pull it in pieces, and laugh in her face,

because she cannot snatch it away.”



He now turned round, and stood facing me, with his back to the [[motifs/fire|fire]].

“Come, then, [[characters/helen|Helen]], are you going to be a good girl?” said he.



This sounded rather too arrogant, and the smile that accompanied it did

not please me. I therefore hesitated to reply. Perhaps my former answer

had implied too much: he had heard my voice falter, and might have seen

me brush away a tear.



“Are you going to forgive me, [[characters/helen|Helen]]?” he resumed, more humbly.



“Are _you_ penitent?” I replied, stepping up to him and smiling in his

face.



“Heart-broken!” he answered, with a rueful countenance, yet with a

merry smile just lurking within his eyes and about the corners of his

mouth; but this could not repulse me, and I flew into his arms. He

fervently embraced me, and though I shed a torrent of [[motifs/tears|tears]], I think I

never was happier in my life than at that moment.



“Then you won’t go to [[settings/london|London]], [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?” I said, when the first transport

of [[motifs/tears|tears]] and kisses had subsided.



“No, [[motifs/love|love]],—unless you will go with me.”



“I will, gladly,” I answered, “if you think the change will amuse you,

and if you will put off the [[motifs/journey|journey]] till next week.”



He readily consented, but said there was no need of much preparation,

as he should not be for staying long, for he did not wish me to be

Londonized, and to lose my country freshness and originality by too

much intercourse with the ladies of the world. I thought this folly;

but I did not wish to contradict him now: I merely said that I was of

very domestic habits, as he [[motifs/well|well]] knew, and had no particular wish to

mingle with the world.



So we are to go to [[settings/london|London]] on Monday, the day after to-morrow. It is now

four days since the termination of our quarrel, and I am sure it has

done us both good: it has made me like [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] a great deal better, and

made him behave a great deal better to me. He has never once attempted

to annoy me since, by the most distant allusion to Lady F——, or any of

those disagreeable reminiscences of his former life. I wish I could

blot them from my [[motifs/memory|memory]], or else get him to regard such matters in the

same light as I do. [[motifs/well|Well]]! it is something, however, to have made him

see that they are not fit subjects for a conjugal jest. He may see

further some [[motifs/time|time]]. I will put no limits to my hopes; and, in spite of

my aunt’s forebodings and my own unspoken fears, I trust we shall be

happy yet.

“No,” fu la risposta; così chiusi la porta e me ne andai. Non vidi nulla.

“Lo rivedemmo solo la mattina seguente, a colazione, quando scese di sotto.”

Un’ora intera dopo l’orario abituale.



“Sei molto in ritardo”, fu il mio saluto mattutino.



“Non dovevi aspettarmi,” disse lui, e si avvicinò.

Di nuovo la [[motifs/window|finestra]]. Era proprio lo stesso tempo di ieri.



“Ah, questa maledetta pioggia…”, mormorò. Ma poi, dopo averci pensato attentamente…

Dopo averci pensato per un minuto o due, gli sembrò di avere un’idea geniale.

“Perché all’improvviso esclamò: ‘Ma so cosa farò!’, e poi se ne andò.”

Si sedette al tavolo e vide che la borsa della posta era già lì.

In attesa di essere aperto. Lo aprì e esaminò il contenuto, ma…

Non disse nulla a loro riguardo.



“C’è qualcosa per me?” chiesi.



“No.”



Aprì il giornale e iniziò a leggere.



“Faresti meglio a prendere il tuo caffè”, suggerii; “si raffredderà di nuovo”.



“Puoi andare,” disse lui, “se hai finito; non ti voglio più qui.”



Le [[motifs/rose|rose]] furono raccolte e portate nella stanza accanto; ci chiedevamo se saremmo mai riusciti a.

Un altro giorno miserabile come ieri… e il desiderio di qualcosa di diverso diventa ancora più forte.

Fine di queste sofferenze reciproche… Poco dopo averlo sentito…

“Suonare la campanella e dare alcune istruzioni riguardo al suo guardaroba…”

Se avesse riflettuto a lungo su un possibile [[motifs/journey|viaggio]], avrebbe poi chiamato il cocchiere, e io.

Ho sentito parlare di una carrozza, dei cavalli, e anche di [[settings/london|Londra]], ma.

Alle sette di domani mattina. Quello non mi ha affatto spaventato né disturbato.

Piccolo.



“Non devo lasciarlo andare a [[settings/london|Londra]], a qualunque costo,” dissi.

“Mi ritroverò nei guai, e sarò io ad esserne responsabile…”

La causa di tutto ciò. Ma la domanda è: come posso modificare il suo scopo? [[motifs/well|Beh]],

“Aspetterò un po’ e vedrò se ne parla.”



Aspettavo con ansia crescente, ora dopo ora… ma non fu detto una parola.

Su quell’argomento o su qualsiasi altro, con me… Sibilava e parlava con se stesso.

Cani, che vagavano da una stanza all’altra, proprio come la volta precedente.

Finalmente iniziai a pensare che dovesse essere io ad affrontare l’argomento.

Stavo riflettendo su come realizzarlo, quando John, senza saperlo, mi venne in aiuto…

Un po’ di sollievo con il seguente messaggio dal cocchiere



“Per favore, signore, [[characters/richard|Richard]] dice che uno dei cavalli ha preso un raffreddore molto grave.”

E lui pensa: “Signore, se potesse essere possibile andare il giorno dopo…”

Domani, invece di domani, avrebbe potuto risolvere la questione oggi stesso, così da…



“Confonda la sua sfrontatezza!” intervenne il maestro.



“Per favore, signore: dice che sarebbe molto meglio se potesse farlo.”

“Insiste John”, disse, “perché spera che il tempo cambierà”.

In breve, e dice che non è _probabile_, quando un [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] è in così cattive condizioni.

“Freddo… e malato… e tutto il resto…”



“Che il diavolo prenda quel [[motifs/horse|cavallo]]!” gridò il gentiluomo. “Beh, digli che ci penserò, ”

“Su questo argomento…”, aggiunse dopo un momento di riflessione. Lanciò uno sguardo attento e indagatore.

“Guardami un attimo, mentre il servitore si allontana… Aspettavo di vedere qualche segno…”

Profondo stupore e allarme… ma essendo stato preparato in anticipo, io…

Mantenne un aspetto di indifferenza stoica… Il suo volto si rabbuiò mentre…

Mi fissò con uno sguardo deciso, ma poi distolse lo sguardo, chiaramente deluso.

E si avvicinò al luogo dove ardeva il [[motifs/fire|fuoco]], rimanendo lì in una certa posizione.

Un disperazione senza veli, appoggiato al camino…

La fronte gli si appoggiò sul braccio.



“Dove vuoi andare, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?”, dissi io.



“Verso [[settings/london|Londra]],” rispose lui, con serietà.



“Perché?” chiesi.



“Perché qui non posso essere felice.”



Perché no?



“Perché mia moglie non mi [[motifs/love|ama]].”



“Lei ti amerebbe con tutto il cuore, se lo meritassi.”



“Cosa devo fare per meritarlo?”



“Sembrava abbastanza umile e sincero… E ne fui profondamente commosso.”

Tra dolore e gioia, fui costretto a fermarmi per qualche secondo.

Prima che riuscissi a calmare la voce per rispondere.



“Se ti dona il suo cuore”, dissi, “devi accettarlo, con gratitudine.”

E usarlo bene, senza strapparlo a pezzi, e ridere in suo viso.

“Perché non può strapparglielo via.”



Ora si girò e si mise di fronte a me, con le spalle rivolte verso il [[motifs/fire|fuoco]].

“Allora, [[characters/helen|Helen]], diventerai una brava ragazza?” le chiese.



Un sorriso troppo arrogante…

Non mi piace affatto… Per questo ho esitato a rispondere. Forse la mia precedente risposta…

Aveva insinuato troppo: aveva sentito il mio respiro tremare e forse anche visto…

Mi scaccio una lacrima via con la mano.



“Mi perdonerai, [[characters/helen|Helen]]?”, riprese lui, con maggiore umiltà.



“Sei pentito?” risposi avvicinandomi a lui e sorridendogli.

faccia.



“Con il cuore spezzato!”, rispose, con un’espressione piena di rimpianto.

Un sorriso felice che si nasconde nei suoi occhi e agli angoli della sua bocca

Bocca… ma questo non riuscì a respingermi, e mi gettai tra le sue braccia. Lui…

Mi abbracciò con fervore, e anche se versai un fiume di [[motifs/tears|lacrime]], credo che.

Nella mia vita non sono mai stato più felice di quel momento.



“Allora non andrai a [[settings/london|Londra]], [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]?” dissi quando arrivò il primo convoglio.

Le lacrime e i baci erano ormai svaniti.



“No, [[motifs/love|amore]], a meno che tu non venga con me.”



“Con piacere lo farò,” risposi, “se pensate che questo cambiamento vi diverta.”

E se volete rimandare il[[motifs/journey|viaggio]] alla prossima settimana.



Accettò volentieri, ma disse che non era necessaria molta preparazione.

Non avrebbe dovuto trattenersi a lungo, poiché non voleva che io lo facessi.

“Londinizzata… e così perdendo la freschezza e l’originalità della mia terra natale.”

“Molti rapporti con le donne del mondo… Pensavo che fosse una follia.”

Ma in quel momento non volevo contraddirlo; ho semplicemente detto di essere d’accordo con lui.

Abitudini molto domestiche, come lui stesso [[motifs/well|ben]] sapeva, e non aveva alcun desiderio particolare di cambiare.

Mescolarsi con il mondo.



Quindi andremo a [[settings/london|Londra]] lunedì, il giorno dopo domani. Ora è.

Quattro giorni dopo la fine della nostra lite… e sono sicuro che ora…

Ci è stato utile a entrambi: mi ha fatto apprezzare molto di più [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], e.

Lo ha fatto comportarsi molto meglio con me… Non ha mai più tentato nulla del genere.

“Per infastidirmi… visto che anche solo menzionare Lady F—, o chiunque altro…”

Quei sgradevoli ricordi della sua vita passata… Vorrei poterli dimenticare.

cancellali dalla mia [[motifs/memory|memoria]], altrimenti fai sì che lui consideri queste cose in un altro modo.

La stessa luce che ho io. Beh! Comunque, è qualcosa avergli dato questa possibilità.

“Assicurarsi che non siano soggetti adatti a scherzi coniugali… Lui può farlo.”

Dopo ancora un po’ di [[motifs/time|tempo]]. Non porrò limiti alle mie speranze; e, nonostante.

"#Le premonizioni di mia zia e le mie paure inespressi… Spero che tutto vada per il meglio."

Felice, ancora una volta.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_25--part_01" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 25 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 25" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/longing,concept/pride,concept/truth,setting/london,character/arthur,character/helen"></span>


CHAPTER XXV





On the eighth of April we went to [[settings/london|London]], on the eighth of May I

returned, in obedience to [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]’s wish; very much against my own,

because I left him behind. If he had come with me, I should have been

very glad to get [[motifs/home|home]] again, for he led me such a round of restless

dissipation while there, that, in that short space of [[motifs/time|time]], I was quite

tired out. He seemed bent upon displaying me to his friends and

acquaintances in particular, and the public in general, on every

possible occasion, and to the greatest possible advantage. It was

something to feel that he considered me a worthy object of [[concepts/pride|pride]]; but I

paid dear for the gratification: for, in the first place, to please him

I had to violate my cherished predilections, my almost rooted

principles in favour of a plain, dark, sober style of dress—I must

sparkle in costly jewels and deck myself out like a painted butterfly,

just as I had, long since, determined I would never do—and this was no

trifling sacrifice; in the second place, I was continually straining to

satisfy his sanguine expectations and do [[concepts/honour|honour]] to his choice by my

general conduct and deportment, and fearing to disappoint him by some

awkward misdemeanour, or some trait of inexperienced ignorance about

the customs of society, especially when I acted the part of hostess,

which I was not unfrequently called upon to do; and, in the third

place, as I intimated before, I was wearied of the throng and bustle,

the restless hurry and ceaseless change of a life so alien to all my

previous habits. At last, he suddenly discovered that the [[settings/london|London]] air

did not agree with me, and I was languishing for my country [[motifs/home|home]], and

must immediately return to Grassdale.



I laughingly assured him that the case was not so urgent as he appeared

to think it, but I was quite willing to go [[motifs/home|home]] if he was. He replied

that he should be obliged to remain a week or two longer, as he had

business that required his presence.



[Illustration]



“Then I will stay with you,” said I.



“But I can’t do with you, [[characters/helen|Helen]],” was his answer: “as long as you stay

I shall attend to you and neglect my business.”



“But I won’t let you,” I returned; “now that I know you have business

to attend to, I shall insist upon your attending to it, and letting me

alone; and, to tell the [[concepts/truth|truth]], I shall be glad of a little rest. I can

take my rides and walks in the Park as usual; and your business cannot

occupy all your [[motifs/time|time]]: I shall see you at meal-times, and in the

evenings at least, and that will be better than being leagues away and

never seeing you at all.”



“But, my [[motifs/love|love]], I cannot let you stay. How can I settle my affairs when

I know that you are here, neglected—?”



“I shall not feel myself neglected: while you are doing your duty,

[[characters/arthur|Arthur]], I shall never complain of neglect. If you had told me before,

that you had anything to do, it would have been half done before this;

and now you must make up for lost [[motifs/time|time]] by redoubled exertions. Tell me

what it is; and I will be your taskmaster, instead of being a

hindrance.”



“No, no,” persisted the impracticable creature; “you _must_ go [[motifs/home|home]],

[[characters/helen|Helen]]; I must have the satisfaction of knowing that you are safe and

[[motifs/well|well]], though far away. Your bright eyes are faded, and that tender,

delicate bloom has quite deserted your cheek.”



“That is only with too much gaiety and fatigue.”



“It is not, I tell you; it is the [[settings/london|London]] air: you are pining for the

fresh breezes of your country [[motifs/home|home]], and you shall feel them before you

are two days older. And remember your situation, dearest [[characters/helen|Helen]]; on your

health, you know, depends the health, if not the life, of our future

[[concepts/hope|hope]].”



“Then you really wish to get rid of me?”



“Positively, I do; and I will take you down myself to Grassdale, and

then return. I shall not be absent above a week or fortnight at most.”



“But if I must go, I will go alone: if you must stay, it is needless to

waste your [[motifs/time|time]] in the [[motifs/journey|journey]] there and back.”



But he did not like the idea of sending me alone.



“Why, what helpless creature do you take me for,” I replied, “that you

cannot trust me to go a hundred miles in our own carriage, with our own

footman and a maid to attend me? If you come with me I shall assuredly

keep you. But tell me, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], what _is_ this tiresome business; and

why did you never mention it before?”



“It is only a little business with my lawyer,” said he; and he told me

something about a piece of property he wanted to sell, in order to pay

off a part of the incumbrances on his estate; but either the account

was a little confused, or I was rather dull of comprehension, for I

could not clearly understand how that should keep him in town a

fortnight after me. Still less can I now comprehend how it should keep

him a month, for it is nearly that [[motifs/time|time]] since I left him, and no signs

of his return as yet. In every letter he promises to be with me in a

few days, and every [[motifs/time|time]] deceives me, or deceives himself. His excuses

are vague and insufficient. I cannot [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] that he has got among his

former companions again. Oh, why did I leave him! I wish—I do intensely

wish he would return!



June 29th.—No [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] yet; and for many days I have been looking and

[[concepts/longing|longing]] in vain for a letter. His letters, when they come, are kind, if

fair words and endearing epithets can give them a claim to the

title—but very short, and full of trivial excuses and promises that I

cannot trust; and yet how anxiously I look forward to them! how eagerly

I open and devour one of those little, hastily-scribbled returns for

the three or four long letters, hitherto unanswered, he has had from

me!



Oh, it is cruel to leave me so long alone! He knows I have no one but
