CAPITOLO XXXVIII





20 dicembre 1826 – Il quinto anniversario del mio giorno di nozze… e io

“Fiducia… l’ultima cosa che spenderò sotto questo tetto. La mia decisione è presa.”

Il mio piano è stato elaborato e già parzialmente messo in atto. La mia [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]].

Non mi incolpa, ma mentre il momento giusto arriva, permettimi di ingannare qualcuno…

In queste lunghe serate invernali, ho avuto il tempo di esporre i motivi che mi soddisfacevano.

Un passatempo noioso, ma che sembra una occupazione utile…

E poiché essere inseguiti rappresenta per me un compito, mi si adatterà meglio di qualcosa di più leggero.



In settembre, la tranquilla Grassdale tornò a vivere grazie a un gruppo di signore che organizzarono una festa.

E gentiluomini (così detti), composti dagli stessi individui di quelli…

Invitati l’anno prima scorso, insieme ad altri due o tre.

Tra questi c’erano la signora Hargrave e sua figlia minore… Gli uomini.

Lady Lowborough fu invitata per il piacere e la comodità di…

Il padrone di casa… Le altre signore, suppongo, per motivi di apparenza…

Per tenermi sotto controllo e far sì che mi comportassi con discrezione e cortesia.

Ma le signore rimasero solo tre settimane; i gentiluomini, invece, due…

Eccezioni: per periodi superiori a due mesi… poiché il loro ospitale anfitrione non ne aveva voglia.

Dovere separarsi da loro e rimanere solo con il proprio intelligenza brillante.

Una coscienza senza macchie, e sua moglie, amata e amorevole.



Il giorno dell’arrivo di Lady Lowborough, la seguii nella sua stanza

Camera, e le dissi chiaramente che, se avessi trovato motivo di credere…

Continuò comunque a mantenere quel legame criminale con il signor Huntingdon…

Dovrei ritenere mio assoluto dovere informare suo marito di…

Circostanza… o almeno suscitare i suoi sospetti, per quanto doloroso possa essere.

Essere, anche a costo di conseguenze terribili… All’inizio ne fu sorpresa.

La dichiarazione, così inaspettata eppure così decisa e calma

“Risposta fredda e calma: ‘Deliverato… ma dopo un momento di ripresa, rispose con freddezza che, se lo avessi visto…”

Se nel suo comportamento ci fosse qualcosa di realmente riprovevole o sospetto, lei…

"Permettetemi liberamente di raccontare tutto al suo signore. Sono disposto a farlo."

Soddisfatto di questo, la lasciai; e certamente non vidi nulla.

Da quel momento in poi, il suo comportamento divenne particolarmente riprovevole o sospetto.

Verso la sua ospite… Ma poi dovevo occuparmi degli altri ospiti.

Non li osservai con attenzione. Perché, a dire la [[concepts/truth|verità]], avevo paura di farlo.

Non si nota nulla tra loro. Non lo consideravo più una questione che mi riguardasse in alcun modo.

Mio. E se fosse stato mio dovere illuminare [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]], allora lo avrei fatto.

Un dovere doloroso, temevo che mi venisse chiesto di compierlo.



Ma i miei timori finirono in un modo che non mi aspettavo.

Una sera, circa quindici giorni dopo l’arrivo degli ospiti, io…

Ritiratosi in biblioteca per godersi qualche minuto di riposo dallo stress forzato

Allegria e discorsi noiosi… dopo un periodo così lungo…

“Seclusion… indeed dreary, come so often I found it to be; yet even then, I couldn’t always…”

Titolo:  
Sembrerebbe che stia ferendo i miei sentimenti e stimolando le mie emozioni in modo negativo…

"#Parla, sorridi, ascolta e comportati come una padrona di casa attenta… o anche di più."

Amico allegro: Mi ero appena rifugiato nell’arcata…

La [[motifs/window|finestra]], che dava sul lato ovest, mostrava le colline ormai immerse nell’oscurità.

La [[motifs/rose|rosa]], con i suoi contorni netti e definiti contro la chiara luce ambrata del tramonto, quella.

Gradualmente si fusero e scomparvero nel blu puro e pallido del cielo sopra di noi

Cielo, dove una stella luminosa brillava, come se promettesse: “Quando…”

Quando quella luce morente scomparirà, il mondo non rimarrà nel buio…

Coloro che confidano in Dio, i cui cuori non sono offuscati dalle nebbie…

“L’incredulità e il peccato non sono mai del tutto privi di conforto…”, quando udii qualcuno parlare in fretta.

Il passo si avvicinava, e [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] entrò. Questa stanza era ancora sua.

Il suo rifugio preferito… Chiuse la porta con una violenza insolita e poi…

Il suo cappello, gettato via senza curarsi di dove fosse caduto… Che cosa poteva esserci che non andasse?

Il suo viso era pallidissimo; i suoi occhi erano fissi sul terreno.

I denti erano serrati; la fronte brillava per il sudore dell’agonia.

Era evidente che finalmente aveva capito i propri errori!



Senza accorgersi della mia presenza, iniziò a camminare avanti e indietro nella stanza, in uno stato di…

Agitazione frenetica: stringeva le mani con forza e emetteva gemiti sommessi.

Frasi incoerenti e senza senso… Feci un gesto per fargli capire che…

Non era solo; ma era troppo assorto nei suoi pensieri per accorgersene. Forse, mentre.

Aveva le spalle rivolte verso di me; avrei potuto attraversare la stanza e allontanarmi in silenzio.

Non fu notato. Ho provato a farlo, ma poi mi ha visto. Lui.

Si fermò per un momento, poi si asciugò la fronte sudata.

E, avvicinandosi a me con una sorta di compostezza innaturale, disse…

Un tono profondo, quasi sepolcrale… “Signora Huntingdon, devo lasciarla.”

“Domani.”



“Domani!”, ripetei. “Non chiedo il motivo.”



“Quindi lo sai già, e puoi essere così calmo!”, disse, osservandomi attentamente.

Profondo stupore, non privo di una certa riluttanza…

Amarezza, così come mi sembrava.



“Da molto tempo sono a conoscenza di, ” Mi fermai per un attimo nel [[motifs/time|tempo]] e aggiunsi: “della mia, ”

“Con il carattere di mio marito, niente può sorprendermi.”



“Ma questo… da quanto tempo ne eri a conoscenza?” chiese, con tono deciso.

“La sua mano stretta sul tavolo accanto a lui, mentre mi guardava con attenzione…”

Fissamente negli occhi.



Mi sentivo come un criminale.



“Non molto presto,” risposi.



“Lo sapevi!” esclamò con amara veemenza, “e non me l’hai detto.”

“Me! Mi hai aiutato a essere ingannato…”



“Mio signore, non ho affatto contribuito a ingannarvi.”



“Allora perché non me l’hai detto?”



“Perché sapevo che ti avrebbe fatto male… Speravo che lei tornasse.”

Il suo dovere… e allora non ci sarebbe bisogno di ferire i tuoi sentimenti con…

Tale…



“Dio mio! Da quanto tempo va avanti tutto questo? Quanto tempo è passato, signora, ”

“Huntingdon? Ditemi… DEVO saperlo!” esclamò, con intensità e paura.

fretta.



“Circa due anni, credo.”



“Mio Dio! Mi ha ingannato per tutto questo [[motifs/time|tempo]], ” Si allontanò, disgustato.

“Un gemito soffocato di dolore… e poi camminare avanti e indietro nella stanza, in preda a un attacco di…”

Nuova agitazione… Il mio cuore batteva forte; ma cercai comunque di consolarlo.

Anche se non sapevo come procedere.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_38--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 38 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 38" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/marriage,motif/nature,motif/pain,motif/rose,motif/time,motif/window,concept/courage,concept/fear,concept/nature,character/lord_lowborough"></span>


“She is a wicked woman,” I said. “She has basely deceived and betrayed

you. She is as little worthy of your regret as she was of your

affection. Let her injure you no further; abstract yourself from her,

and stand alone.”



“And you, Madam,” said he sternly, arresting himself, and turning round

upon me, “you have injured me too by this ungenerous concealment!”



There was a sudden revulsion in my feelings. Something [[motifs/rose|rose]] within me,

and urged me to resent this harsh return for my heartfelt sympathy, and

defend myself with answering severity. Happily, I did not yield to the

impulse. I saw his anguish as, suddenly smiting his forehead, he turned

abruptly to the [[motifs/window|window]], and, looking upward at the placid sky, murmured

passionately, “O God, that I might die!”—and felt that to add one drop

of bitterness to that already overflowing cup would be ungenerous

indeed. And yet I [[concepts/fear|fear]] there was more coldness than gentleness in the

quiet tone of my reply:—“I might offer many excuses that some would

admit to be valid, but I will not attempt to enumerate them—”



“I know them,” said he hastily: “you would say that it was no business

of yours: that I ought to have taken care of myself; that if my own

blindness has led me into this pit of hell, I have no right to blame

another for giving me credit for a larger amount of sagacity than I

possessed—”



“I confess I was wrong,” continued I, without regarding this bitter

interruption; “but whether want of [[concepts/courage|courage]] or mistaken kindness was the

cause of my error, I think you blame me too severely. I told Lady

Lowborough two weeks ago, the very hour she came, that I should

certainly think it my duty to inform you if she continued to deceive

you: she gave me full liberty to do so if I should see anything

reprehensible or suspicious in her conduct; I have seen nothing; and I

trusted she had altered her course.”



He continued gazing from the [[motifs/window|window]] while I spoke, and did not answer,

but, stung by the recollections my words awakened, stamped his foot

upon the floor, ground his teeth, and corrugated his brow, like one

under the influence of acute physical [[motifs/pain|pain]].



“It was wrong, it was wrong!” he muttered at length. “Nothing can

excuse it; nothing can atone for it,—for nothing can recall those years

of cursed credulity; nothing obliterate them!—nothing, nothing!” he

repeated in a whisper, whose despairing bitterness precluded all

resentment.



“When I put the case to myself, I own it _was_ wrong,” I answered; “but

I can only now regret that I did not see it in this light before, and

that, as you say, nothing can recall the past.”



Something in my voice or in the spirit of this answer seemed to alter

his mood. Turning towards me, and attentively surveying my face by the

dim light, he said, in a milder tone than he had yet employed,—“You,

too, have suffered, I suppose.”



“I suffered much, at first.”



“When was that?”



“Two years ago; and two years hence you will be as calm as I am now,

and far, far happier, I trust, for you are a man, and free to act as

you please.”



Something like a smile, but a _very_ bitter one, crossed his face for a

moment.



“You have not been happy, lately?” he said, with a kind of effort to

regain composure, and a determination to waive the further discussion

of his own calamity.



“Happy?” I repeated, almost provoked at such a question. “Could I be

so, with such a husband?”



“I have noticed a change in your appearance since the first years of

your [[motifs/marriage|marriage]],” pursued he: “I observed it to—to that infernal demon,”

he muttered between his teeth; “and he said it was your own sour temper

that was eating away your bloom: it was making you old and ugly before

your [[motifs/time|time]], and had already made his fireside as comfortless as a

convent cell. You smile, Mrs. Huntingdon; nothing moves you. I wish my

[[concepts/nature|nature]] were as calm as yours.”



“My [[concepts/nature|nature]] was not originally calm,” said I. “I have learned to appear

so by dint of hard lessons and many repeated efforts.”



At this juncture Mr. Hattersley burst into the room.



“Hallo, Lowborough!” he began—“Oh! I beg your pardon,” he exclaimed on

seeing me. “I didn’t know it was a _tête-à-tête_. Cheer up, man,” he

continued, giving [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] a thump on the back, which caused the

latter to recoil from him with looks of ineffable disgust and

irritation. “Come, I want to speak with you a bit.”



“Speak, then.”



“But I’m not sure it would be quite agreeable to the lady what I have

to say.”



“Then it would not be agreeable to me,” said his lordship, turning to

leave the room.



“Yes, it would,” cried the other, following him into the hall. “If

you’ve the heart of a man, it would be the very ticket for you. It’s

just this, my lad,” he continued, rather lowering his voice, but not

enough to prevent me from hearing every word he said, though the

half-closed door stood between us. “I think you’re an ill-used man—nay,

now, don’t flare up; I don’t want to offend you: it’s only my rough way

of talking. I must speak right out, you _know_, or else not at all; and

I’m come—stop now! let me explain—I’m come to offer you my services,

for though Huntingdon is my friend, he’s a devilish scamp, as we all

know, and I’ll be _your_ friend for the nonce. I know what it is you

want, to make matters straight: it’s just to exchange a shot with him,

and then you’ll feel yourself all right again; and if an accident

happens—why, that’ll be all right too, I daresay, to a desperate fellow

like you. Come now, give me your hand, and don’t look so black upon it.

Name [[motifs/time|time]] and place, and I’ll manage the rest.”



“That,” answered the more low, deliberate voice of [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]], “is

just the remedy my own heart, or the devil within it, suggested—to meet

him, and _not to sever without blood_. Whether I or he should fall, or

both, it would be an _inexpressible_ relief to me, if—”

“È una donna malvagia”, dissi. “Ha ingannato e tradito in modo spregevole”.

Lei non merita affatto il tuo rimpianto, proprio come allora…

Distacco affettivo. Lascia che non ti faccia più del male; allontanati da lei.

e rimanere solo.”



“E lei, signora,” disse lui con severità, poi si fermò e si girò.

“Su di me… ‘Mi avete anche ferito con questo comportamento ingiusto e meschino!’”



All'improvviso i miei sentimenti subirono un cambiamento radicale. Qualcosa dentro di me si risvegliò.

E mi esortò a provare rancore per questa dura reazione alla mia sincera solidarietà…

“Mi difesi rispondendo con durezza… Fortunatamente, non cedetti.”

Impulso… Vidi la sua angoscia quando, all’improvviso, si colpì la fronte e si girò.

“La cecità mi ha trascinato in questo abisso d’inferno… Non ho alcun diritto di biasimare nessuno.”

Un altro che mi attribuisce una saggezza maggiore di quella che realmente possiedo…

Interruzione; “ma se fosse per mancanza di [[concepts/courage|coraggio]] o per una gentilezza errata, ”

“A causa del mio errore, penso che mi stiate rimproverando troppo severamente… Ho detto alla signora…”

Due settimane fa a Lowborough, nell’esatto istante in cui lei arrivò…

Credo certamente di dovervi informare nel caso in cui continui a ingannarvi.

Tu: Mi ha dato totale libertà di farlo, se mai avessi visto qualcosa…

“Nessun comportamento riprovevole o sospetto da parte sua; non ho notato nulla del genere…”

“Credeva che avesse cambiato rotta…”



Continuò a guardare fuori dalla [[motifs/window|finestra]] mentre parlavo, senza rispondere.

Ma, ferito dai ricordi che le mie parole avevano risvegliato, batté il piede a terra.

Con i denti stretti e la fronte corrugata… come se…

sotto l’effetto di un acuto dolore fisico.



“Era sbagliato, era davvero sbagliato!“ mormorò infine. “Niente può…”

Scusami… nulla può compensare per questo… perché nulla può riportare indietro quegli anni.

“Di una credulità maledetta… Niente può cancellarle! Nessuno cosa, assolutamente nulla…”

Ripetuto sottovoce, con una amarezza disperata che impediva qualsiasi altra reazione…

Rancore.



“Riflettendoci bene, devo ammettere che avevo torto”, risposi; “ma…”

Ora solo mi pento di non averlo visto sotto questa luce prima…

“Come dici tu, nulla può richiamare indietro il passato.”



Qualcosa nella mia voce… o nello spirito di questa risposta, sembrò cambiare tutto.

Il suo umore… Si voltò verso di me e osservò attentamente il mio viso.

“Luce fioca,” disse, con un tono più dolce di quanto avesse mai usato prima, “tu…”

“Anch’io, immagino, abbia sofferto…”



“All’inizio ho sofferto molto.”



“Quando è stato?”



“Due anni fa… e tra due anni sarai altrettanto calmo quanto lo sono io ora.”

E molto, molto più felice, ne sono certo… perché sei un uomo e libero di agire come desideri.

“Per favore…”



Qualcosa di simile a un sorriso, ma _molto_ amaro, gli apparve sul viso per un istante.

Momento.



“Non sei stato felice ultimamente, vero?”, disse, con un certo sforzo…

Riacquistare la compostezza e la determinazione di rinunciare a ulteriori discussioni

A causa della propria stessa calamità.



“Felice?”, ripetei, quasi provocato da una domanda del genere. “Come potrei non esserlo…”

“Eh… con un marito del genere…”



Un cambiamento nel tuo aspetto dai primi anni…

“Il tuo [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]]”, continuò, “l’ho visto, con quel demone infernale.”

Mormorò tra i denti: “E disse che era colpa del tuo cattivo carattere”.

Quello che stava consumando la tua giovinezza e la tua bellezza… ti faceva invecchiare e diventare brutta prima del tempo.

Nel tuo [[motifs/time|tempo]], aveva già reso il suo angolo accanto al fuoco altrettanto scomodo quanto.

Cella monastica… Sorridete, signora Huntingdon; nulla sembra scuotervi… Vorrei che anche io potessi essere così…

La [[concepts/nature|natura]] era altrettanto calma della tua.



“La mia [[concepts/nature|natura]] originariamente non era tranquilla,” dissi. “Ho imparato a sembrarlo.”

“Solo attraverso lezioni dure e molti sforzi ripetuti…”



In questo momento, il signor Hattersley irruppe nella stanza.



“Salve, Lowborough!” esordì – “Oh! Mi scusi,” esclamò subito dopo.

“Non sapevo che fosse un ‘tête-à-tête’… Rilassati, amico.”

Continuò, dando un pugno sulla schiena a [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]], il che lo fece cadere.

“Coloro che lo vedevano si allontanavano da lui con espressioni di disgusto indescrivibile…”

“Vieni, voglio parlarti un attimo.”



"Dì pure allora."



“Ma non sono sicuro che alla signora piaccia davvero ciò che ho proposto…”

“Per dirlo in altre parole…”



“Allora non mi sarebbe gradito”, disse il suo signore, rivolgendosi…

Uscite dalla stanza.



“Sì, lo farebbe,” esclamò l’altro, seguendolo nel corridoio. “Se…”

Hai il cuore di un uomo… Questo sarebbe davvero l’elemento perfetto per te.

“Proprio questo, ragazzo mio,” continuò, abbassando un po’ la voce, ma non…

A sufficienza per impedirmi di sentire ogni parola che diceva…

Una porta semi-chiusa ci separava. “Penso che tu sia un uomo maltrattato… anzi,

Ora, non arrabbiarti… Non voglio offenderti: è solo il mio modo un po’ brusco di esprimermi.

Parlare apertamente. Devo dire ciò che penso, lo sai bene… altrimenti non dirò nulla affatto.

“Sono arrivato… fermatevi ora! Lasciate che vi spieghi: sono qui per offrirvi i miei servizi.”

“Perché anche se Huntingdon è mio amico, è davvero un diavolo di birichino… come tutti noi.”

“Conosco… e per il momento sarò tuo amico. So cosa sei.”

Per chiarire le cose: voglio semplicemente scambiare un colpo con lui.

E poi ti sentirai di nuovo bene… E se dovesse accadere un incidente…

Accade… perché, suppongo che anche questo vada bene per un uomo disperato.

Come te. Dai, dammi la tua mano, e non guardarla in quel modo, come se fosse qualcosa di brutto.

Indica il nome, l’ora e il luogo; il resto lo gestirò io.



“Quello,” rispose la voce più bassa e ponderata di [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]], “è, ”

Esattamente quella cura che il mio cuore, o il diavolo che vi abita, mi suggeriva… per affrontare la situazione.

“Lui… e che non ci sia separazione senza sangue. Che io o lui cadiamo…”

“Entrambi… Sarebbe un vero sollievo per me se…”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_38--part_03" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 38 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 38" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/fool,archetype/villain,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/love,motif/night,motif/well,motif/window,concept/faith,concept/temptation,character/arthur,character/bottom,character/lord_lowborough"></span>


“Just so! [[motifs/well|Well]] then,—”



“No!” exclaimed his lordship, with deep, determined emphasis. “Though I

hate him from my heart, and should rejoice at any calamity that could

befall him, I’ll leave him to God; and though I abhor my own life, I’ll

leave that, too, to Him that gave it.”



“But you see, in this case,” pleaded Hattersley—



“I’ll not hear you!” exclaimed his companion, hastily turning away.

“Not another word! I’ve enough to do against the fiend within me.”



“Then you’re a white-livered [[archetypes/fool|fool]], and I wash my hands of you,”

grumbled the tempter, as he swung himself round and departed.



“Right, right, [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]],” cried I, darting out and clasping his

burning hand, as he was moving away to the stairs. “I begin to think

the world is not worthy of you!” Not understanding this sudden

ebullition, he turned upon me with a stare of gloomy, bewildered

amazement, that made me ashamed of the impulse to which I had yielded;

but soon a more humanised expression dawned upon his countenance, and

before I could withdraw my hand, he pressed it kindly, while a gleam of

genuine feeling flashed from his eyes as he murmured, “God help us

both!”



“Amen!” responded I; and we parted.



I returned to the drawing-room, where, doubtless, my presence would be

expected by most, desired by one or two. In the ante-room was Mr.

Hattersley, railing against [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]]’s poltroonery before a

select audience, viz. Mr. Huntingdon, who was lounging against the

table, exulting in his own treacherous villainy, and laughing his

victim to scorn, and Mr. Grimsby, standing by, quietly rubbing his

hands and chuckling with fiendish satisfaction.



In the drawing-room I found Lady Lowborough, evidently in no very

enviable state of mind, and struggling hard to conceal her discomposure

by an overstrained affectation of unusual cheerfulness and vivacity,

very uncalled-for under the circumstances, for she had herself given

the company to understand that her husband had received unpleasant

intelligence from [[motifs/home|home]], which necessitated his immediate departure, and

that he had suffered it so to bother his mind that it had brought on a

bilious headache, owing to which, and the preparations he judged

necessary to hasten his departure, she believed they would not have the

pleasure of seeing him to-[[motifs/night|night]]. However, she asserted, it was only a

business concern, and so she did not intend it should trouble _her._

She was just saying this as I entered, and she darted upon me such a

glance of hardihood and defiance as at once astonished and revolted me.



“But I _am_ troubled,” continued she, “and vexed too, for I think it my

duty to accompany his lordship, and of course I am very sorry to part

with all my kind friends so unexpectedly and so soon.”



“And yet, Annabella,” said Esther, who was sitting beside her, “I never

saw you in better spirits in my life.”



“Precisely so, my [[motifs/love|love]]: because I wish to make the best of your

society, since it appears this is to be the last [[motifs/night|night]] I am to enjoy it

till heaven knows when; and I wish to leave a good impression on you

all,”—she glanced round, and seeing her aunt’s eye fixed upon her,

rather too scrutinizingly, as she probably thought, she started up and

continued: “To which end I’ll give you a song—shall I, aunt? shall I,

Mrs. Huntingdon? shall I ladies and gentlemen all? Very [[motifs/well|well]]. I’ll do

my best to amuse you.”



She and [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] occupied the apartments next to mine. I know

not how _she_ passed the [[motifs/night|night]], but I lay awake the greater part of it

listening to his heavy step pacing monotonously up and down his

dressing-room, which was nearest my chamber. Once I heard him pause and

throw something out of the [[motifs/window|window]] with a passionate ejaculation; and in

the morning, after they were gone, a keen-bladed clasp-knife was found

on the grass-plot below; a razor, likewise, was snapped in two and

thrust deep into the cinders of the grate, but partially corroded by

the decaying embers. So strong had been the [[concepts/temptation|temptation]] to end his

miserable life, so determined his resolution to resist it.



My heart bled for him as I lay listening to that ceaseless tread.

Hitherto I had thought too much of myself, too little of him: now I

forgot my own afflictions, and thought only of his; of the ardent

affection so miserably wasted, the fond [[concepts/faith|faith]] so cruelly betrayed,

the—no, I will not attempt to enumerate his wrongs—but I hated his wife

and my husband more intensely than ever, and not for my sake, but for

his.



They departed early in the morning, before any one else was down,

except myself, and just as I was leaving my room [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] was

descending to take his place in the carriage, where his lady was

already ensconced; and [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] (or Mr. Huntingdon, as I prefer calling

him, for the other is my [[archetypes/child|child]]’s name) had the gratuitous insolence to

come out in his dressing-gown to bid his “friend” good-by.



“What, going already, Lowborough!” said he. “[[motifs/well|Well]], good-morning.” He

smilingly offered his hand.



I think the other would have knocked him down, had he not instinctively

started back before that bony fist quivering with rage and clenched

till the knuckles gleamed white and glistening through the skin.

Looking upon him with a countenance livid with furious hate, Lord

Lowborough muttered between his closed teeth a deadly execration he

would not have uttered had he been calm enough to choose his words, and

departed.



“I call that an unchristian spirit now,” said the [[archetypes/villain|villain]]. “But I’d

never give up an old friend for the sake of a wife. You may have mine

if you like, and I call that handsome; I can do no more than offer

restitution, can I?”



But Lowborough had gained the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the stairs, and was now

crossing the hall; and Mr. Huntingdon, leaning over the banisters,

called out, “Give my [[motifs/love|love]] to Annabella! and I wish you both a happy

[[motifs/journey|journey]],” and withdrew, laughing, to his chamber.



He subsequently expressed himself rather glad she was gone. “She was so

deuced imperious and exacting,” said he. “Now I shall be my own man

again, and feel rather more at my ease.”

“Giusto, giusto, [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]],” gridai, uscendo di corsa e abbracciandolo.

Mani che si muovevano e risate emesse con una soddisfazione malvagia.



Nella sala da pranzo trovai Lady Lowborough, chiaramente non molto…

Uno stato d’animo invidiabile… ma che richiede grandi sforzi per nascondere il proprio disagio.

Con un’eccessiva affettazione di allegria e vivacità forzata…

“Assolutamente inutile, date le circostanze… visto che era stata lei stessa ad averlo fatto.”

Mal di testa acuto, a causa del quale… e delle preparazioni che ritenne necessarie

Un’impresa commerciale… quindi non intendeva che rappresentasse un problema per lei.

Un’occhiata piena di coraggio e sfida, che allo stesso tempo mi sorprese e mi indignò.

Dovera di accompagnare Sua Signoria… e naturalmente mi dispiace molto dovermi separare

La società, poiché sembra che questa sia l’ultima [[motifs/night|notte]] in cui potrò godermela.

Fino a quando solo il cielo lo sa… E desidero lasciarti una buona impressione.

“Tutti…”, disse, guardandosi intorno e vedendo che lo sguardo di sua zia era fisso su di lei.

Con un’attenzione forse eccessiva, come probabilmente pensava lei, si alzò e…

Signora Huntingdon. Dovremmo tutti procedere, signore e signori? Molto bene. Lo farò.

Lei e [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] abitavano gli appartamenti accanto ai miei. Lo so.

Mio cuore sanguinava per lui mentre ascoltavo quel passo incessante.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_39--part_01" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 39 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 39" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/artist,archetype/child,archetype/fool,motif/cross,motif/dawn,motif/death,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/rose,motif/time,concept/despair,concept/poverty,histref/new_england,character/arthur,character/nurse"></span>


CHAPTER XXXIX





My greatest source of uneasiness, in this [[motifs/time|time]] of trial, was my son,

whom his father and his father’s friends delighted to encourage in all

the embryo vices a little [[archetypes/child|child]] can show, and to instruct in all the

evil habits he could acquire—in a word, to “make a man of him” was one

of their staple amusements; and I need say no more to justify my alarm

on his account, and my determination to deliver him at any hazard from

the hands of such instructors. I first attempted to keep him always

with me, or in the nursery, and gave Rachel particular injunctions

never to let him come down to dessert as long as these “gentlemen”

stayed; but it was no use: these orders were immediately countermanded

and overruled by his father; he was not going to have the little fellow

moped to [[motifs/death|death]] between an old [[characters/nurse|nurse]] and a cursed [[archetypes/fool|fool]] of a mother. So

the little fellow came down every evening in spite of his [[motifs/cross|cross]] mamma,

and learned to tipple wine like papa, to swear like Mr. Hattersley, and

to have his own way like a man, and sent mamma to the devil when she

tried to prevent him. To see such things done with the roguish naïveté

of that pretty little [[archetypes/child|child]], and hear such things spoken by that small

infantile voice, was as peculiarly piquant and irresistibly droll to

them as it was inexpressibly distressing and painful to me; and when he

had set the table in a roar he would look round delightedly upon them

all, and add his shrill laugh to theirs. But if that beaming blue eye

rested on me, its light would vanish for a moment, and he would say, in

some concern, “Mamma, why don’t _you_ laugh? Make her laugh, papa—she

never will.”



Hence was I obliged to stay among these human brutes, watching an

opportunity to get my [[archetypes/child|child]] away from them instead of leaving them

immediately after the removal of the cloth, as I should always

otherwise have done. He was never willing to go, and I frequently had

to carry him away by force, for which he thought me very cruel and

unjust; and sometimes his father would insist upon my letting him

remain; and then I would leave him to his kind friends, and retire to

indulge my bitterness and [[concepts/despair|despair]] alone, or to rack my brains for a

remedy to this great evil.



But here again I must do Mr. Hargrave the justice to acknowledge that I

never saw _him_ laugh at the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s misdemeanours, nor heard him utter

a word of encouragement to his aspirations after manly accomplishments.

But when anything very extraordinary was said or done by the infant

profligate, I noticed, at times, a peculiar expression in his face that

I could neither interpret nor define: a slight twitching about the

muscles of the mouth; a sudden flash in the eye, as he darted a sudden

glance at the [[archetypes/child|child]] and then at me: and then I could fancy there arose

a gleam of hard, keen, sombre satisfaction in his countenance at the

look of impotent wrath and anguish he was too certain to behold in

mine. But on one occasion, when [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] had been behaving particularly

ill, and Mr. Huntingdon and his guests had been particularly provoking

and insulting to me in their encouragement of him, and I particularly

anxious to get him out of the room, and on the very point of demeaning

myself by a burst of uncontrollable passion—Mr. Hargrave suddenly [[motifs/rose|rose]]

from his seat with an aspect of stern determination, lifted the [[archetypes/child|child]]

from his father’s knee, where he was sitting half-tipsy, cocking his

head and laughing at me, and execrating me with words he little knew

the meaning of, handed him out of the room, and, setting him down in

the hall, held the door open for me, gravely bowed as I withdrew, and

closed it after me. I heard high words exchanged between him and his

already half-inebriated host as I departed, leading away my bewildered

and disconcerted boy.



But this should not continue: my [[archetypes/child|child]] must not be abandoned to this

corruption: better far that he should live in [[concepts/poverty|poverty]] and obscurity,

with a fugitive mother, than in luxury and affluence with such a

father. These guests might not be with us long, but they would return

again: and he, the most injurious of the whole, his [[archetypes/child|child]]’s worst

enemy, would still remain. I could endure it for myself, but for my son

it must be borne no longer: the world’s opinion and the feelings of my

friends must be alike unheeded here, at least—alike unable to deter me

from my duty. But where should I find an asylum, and how obtain

subsistence for us both? Oh, I would take my precious charge at early

[[motifs/dawn|dawn]], take the coach to M——, flee to the port of ——, [[motifs/cross|cross]] the

Atlantic, and seek a quiet, humble [[motifs/home|home]] in [[historical-references/new-england|New England]], where I would

support myself and him by the labour of my hands. The palette and the

easel, my darling playmates once, must be my sober toil-fellows now.

But was I sufficiently skilful as an [[archetypes/artist|artist]] to obtain my livelihood in

a strange land, without friends and without recommendation? No; I must

wait a little; I must labour hard to improve my talent, and to produce

something worth while as a specimen of my powers, something to speak

favourably for me, whether as an actual painter or a teacher. Brilliant

success, of course, I did not look for, but some degree of security

from positive failure was indispensable: I must not take my son to

starve. And then I must have money for the [[motifs/journey|journey]], the passage, and

some little to support us in our retreat in case I should be

unsuccessful at first: and not too little either: for who could tell

how long I might have to struggle with the indifference or neglect of

others, or my own inexperience or inability to suit their tastes?



What should I do then? Apply to my brother and explain my circumstances

and my resolves to him? No, no: even if I told him _all_ my grievances,

Un ospite già mezzo ubriaco quando me ne andai, portando via il mio sbalordito…

e il ragazzo confuso.



Ma questo non può continuare: mio [[archetypes/child|bambino]] non deve essere abbandonato in questa situazione.

Corruzione: è meglio che viva nella [[concepts/poverty|povertà]] e nell’oscurità.

Con una madre fuggitiva, piuttosto che nella lussuria e nell’abbondanza con una persona del genere…

Padre… Questi ospiti potrebbero non rimanere con noi a lungo, ma torneranno.

Ancora una volta: ed egli, il più dannoso di tutti, il peggiore per il proprio [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

Nemico… che comunque resterebbe. Potrei sopportarlo per me stesso, ma per mio figlio… no.

“Non può essere più tollerato: l’opinione del mondo e i sentimenti di…”

Amici devono essere simili… Almeno qui, nessuno dei loro tentativi riesce a fermarmi.

Dalla mia responsabilità… Ma dove posso trovare un rifugio, e come ottenerlo?

“Una sussistenza per entrambi… Oh, prenderei volentieri in carico la mia preziosa responsabilità fin da subito.”

All’[[motifs/dawn|'alba]], prendi il treno per M———, fuggi al porto di ————, poi [[motifs/cross|attraversa]].

L’Atlantico, e cercare una casa tranquilla, umile, nella [[historical-references/new-england|Nuova Inghilterra]], dove potrei.

"#Guadagnarmi da vivere io e lui con il lavoro delle mie mani. La tavolozza e…"

Il cavalletto, un tempo i miei cari compagni di gioco, ora deve diventare i miei fedeli compagni nel duro lavoro quotidiano.

Ma ero abbastanza abile come [[archetypes/artist|artista]] per guadagnarmi da vivere con questo lavoro?

Una terra strana, senza amici e senza referenze… No; devo procedere lo stesso.

Aspetta un attimo… Devo lavorare sodo per migliorare il mio talento e riuscire a produrre qualcosa di significativo.

Qualcosa che valga la pena come esempio delle mie capacità… qualcosa che possa parlare per me.

A mio favore, sia come pittore che come insegnante… Davvero ottimo.

Il successo, ovviamente, non era quello che cercavo, ma piuttosto un certo grado di sicurezza.

Dalla sconfitta positiva… era indispensabile: Non devo portare mio figlio con me

Morire di fame. E poi devo avere abbastanza soldi per il [[motifs/journey|Viaggio]], per il biglietto del traghetto, e.

Un piccolo aiuto per sostenerci durante il nostro ritiro, nel caso io dovessi…

Inizialmente senza successo… e non di poco: chi avrebbe potuto dirlo?

Per quanto tempo dovrò lottare contro l’indifferenza o l’ignoranza altrui…

Gli altri, o forse la mia stessa inesperienza o incapacità di soddisfare i loro gusti?



Che cosa dovrei fare allora? Chiedere aiuto a mio fratello e spiegargli la mia situazione.

E le mie risoluzioni nei suoi confronti? No, no: anche se gli raccontassi _tutte_ le mie lamentele…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_39--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 39 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 39" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/villain,motif/home,motif/marriage,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/madness,concept/wonder,character/arthur,character/lord_lowborough"></span>


which I should be very reluctant to do, he would be certain to

disapprove of the step: it would seem like [[concepts/madness|madness]] to him, as it would

to my uncle and aunt, or to Milicent. No; I must have patience and

gather a hoard of my own. Rachel should be my only confidante—I thought

I could persuade her into the scheme; and she should help me, first, to

find out a picture-dealer in some distant town; then, through her

means, I would privately sell what pictures I had on hand that would do

for such a purpose, and some of those I should thereafter paint.

Besides this, I would contrive to dispose of my jewels, not the family

jewels, but the few I brought with me from [[motifs/home|home]], and those my uncle

gave me on my [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]. A few months’ arduous toil might [[motifs/well|well]] be borne

by me with such an end in view; and in the interim my son could not be

much more injured than he was already.



Having formed this resolution, I immediately set to work to accomplish

it, I might possibly have been induced to wax cool upon it afterwards,

or perhaps to keep weighing the pros and cons in my mind till the

latter overbalanced the former, and I was driven to relinquish the

project altogether, or delay the execution of it to an indefinite

period, had not something occurred to confirm me in that determination,

to which I still adhere, which I still think I did [[motifs/well|well]] to form, and

shall do better to execute.



Since [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]]’s departure I had regarded the library as

entirely my own, a secure retreat at all hours of the day. None of our

gentlemen had the smallest pretensions to a literary taste, except Mr.

Hargrave; and he, at present, was quite contented with the newspapers

and periodicals of the day. And if, by any chance, he should look in

here, I felt assured he would soon depart on seeing me, for, instead of

becoming less cool and distant towards me, he had become decidedly more

so since the departure of his mother and sisters, which was just what I

wished. Here, then, I set up my easel, and here I worked at my canvas

from daylight till dusk, with very little intermission, saving when

pure necessity, or my duties to little [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], called me away: for I

still thought proper to devote some portion of every day exclusively to

his instruction and amusement. But, contrary to my expectation, on the

third morning, while I was thus employed, Mr. Hargrave _did_ look in,

and did _not_ immediately withdraw on seeing me. He apologized for his

intrusion, and said he was only come for a book; but when he had got

it, he condescended to cast a glance over my picture. Being a man of

taste, he had something to say on this subject as [[motifs/well|well]] as another, and

having modestly commented on it, without much encouragement from me, he

proceeded to expatiate on the art in general. Receiving no

encouragement in that either, he dropped it, but did not depart.



“You don’t give us much of your company, Mrs. Huntingdon,” observed he,

after a brief pause, during which I went on coolly mixing and tempering

my colours; “and I cannot [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at it, for you must be heartily sick

of us all. I myself am so thoroughly ashamed of my companions, and so

weary of their irrational conversation and pursuits—now that there is

no one to humanize them and keep them in check, since you have justly

abandoned us to our own devices—that I think I shall presently withdraw

from amongst them, probably within this week; and I cannot suppose you

will regret my departure.”



He paused. I did not answer.



“Probably,” he added, with a smile, “your only regret on the subject

will be that I do not take all my companions along with me. I flatter

myself, at times, that though among them I am not of them; but it is

natural that you should be glad to get rid of me. I may regret this,

but I cannot blame you for it.”



“I shall not rejoice at _your_ departure, for you _can_ conduct

yourself like a gentleman,” said I, thinking it but right to make some

acknowledgment for his good behaviour; “but I must confess I shall

rejoice to bid adieu to the rest, inhospitable as it may appear.”



“No one can blame you for such an avowal,” replied he gravely: “not

even the gentlemen themselves, I imagine. I’ll just tell you,” he

continued, as if actuated by a sudden resolution, “what was said last

[[motifs/night|night]] in the dining-room, after you left us: perhaps you will not mind

it, as you’re so _very_ philosophical on certain points,” he added with

a slight sneer. “They were talking about [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] and his

delectable lady, the cause of whose sudden departure is no secret

amongst them; and her character is so [[motifs/well|well]] known to them all, that,

nearly related to me as she is, I could not attempt to defend it. Curse

me!” he muttered, _par parenthése_, “if I don’t have vengeance for

this! If the [[archetypes/villain|villain]] must disgrace the family, must he blazon it abroad

to every low-bred knave of his acquaintance? I beg your pardon, Mrs.

Huntingdon. [[motifs/well|Well]], they were talking of these things, and some of them

remarked that, as she was separated from her husband, he might see her

again when he pleased.”



“‘Thank you,’ said he; ‘I’ve had enough of her for the present: I’ll

not trouble to see her, unless she comes to me.’



“‘Then what do you mean to do, Huntingdon, when we’re gone?’ said Ralph

Hattersley. ‘Do you mean to turn from the error of your ways, and be a

good husband, a good father, and so forth; as I do, when I get shut of

you and all these rollicking devils you call your friends? I think it’s

[[motifs/time|time]]; and your wife is fifty times too good for you, you _know_—’



“And he added some praise of you, which you would not thank me for

repeating, nor him for uttering; proclaiming it aloud, as he did,

without delicacy or discrimination, in an audience where it seemed

profanation to utter your name: himself utterly incapable of

understanding or appreciating your real excellences. Huntingdon,

“Per mio zio e mia zia… o forse per Milicent? No, devo avere pazienza.”

Raccogliere una mia riserva personale… Rachel dovrebbe essere la mia unica confidente… Pensavo così.

Scoprire una donna che vende quadri in una città lontana… e poi, attraverso di lei…

In altre parole, venderei privatamente le foto che ho a disposizione quelle che potrebbero essere interessanti…

Per tale scopo, e ce ne sono alcuni che in seguito dovrò dipingere.

Oltre a questo, cercherei di disfarmi dei miei gioielli… non quelli di famiglia.

Gemme, ma solo quelle poche che ho portato con me da [[motifs/home|casa]], e quelle di mio zio.

Me l'ha dato il giorno del mio [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]]. Qualche mese di duro lavoro potrebbe benissimo essere sopportato.

Con tale scopo in mente… e nel frattempo, mio figlio non poteva essere…

Molto più ferito di quanto non lo fosse già.



Una volta presa questa decisione, mi misi immediatamente all’opera per realizzarla.

Potrei anche essere stato indotto a cambiare idea in seguito…

O forse per continuare a valutare i pro e i contro nella mia mente…

In seguito, il secondo fattore prevalse sul primo, e fui costretto ad arrendermi.

Abbandonare completamente il progetto, o rinviarne l’esecuzione a data indefinita

Period… Non era accaduto nulla che potesse confermare quella mia determinazione.

A cui ancora attengo, per il quale penso ancora di aver fatto bene a crearlo.

Sarà meglio eseguire.



Dall’uscita di [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]], consideravo la biblioteca come.

Un rifugio tutto mio, sicuro in qualsiasi momento della giornata… Nessuno di noi…

Gli uomini non avevano la minima pretesa di possedere un gusto letterario, tranne il signor.

Hargrave; e al momento, era piuttosto soddisfatto dei giornali.

Titoli e pubblicazioni periodiche dell’epoca. E se, per qualche motivo, dovesse darci un’occhiata…

Qui, ero sicura che se mi avesse vista se ne sarebbe andato subito… perché, invece…

Diventando sempre meno freddo e distante con me, era diventato decisamente più…

Dopo la partenza di sua madre e delle sue sorelle… proprio così.

“Lo desideravo ardentemente… Così, piazzai il mio cavalletto e iniziai a lavorare sulla mia tela.”

Da giorno a notte, con pochissime pause, tranne quando…

Per pura necessità, o a causa dei miei doveri verso il piccolo [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], fui costretto ad andarmene; perché io.

Ancora ritengo opportuno dedicare una parte di ogni giorno esclusivamente a…

Per il suo insegnamento e divertimento… Ma, contrariamente alle mie aspettative, su…

Terza mattina, mentre ero impegnato in queste attività, il signor Hargrave venne davvero a trovarmi.

E non si ritirò immediatamente non appena mi vide… Si scusò per il suo comportamento.

"Intruzione… e disse di essere venuto solo per prendere un libro; ma una volta che l’ebbe preso…”

“Lui, con aria di superiorità, decise di dare un’occhiata al mio ritratto… Essendo un uomo…”

In materia di gusto, aveva qualcosa da dire sia su questo argomento che su altri.

Avendo espresso commenti modesti al riguardo, senza ricevere molto incoraggiamento da parte mia, lui…

Proseguì spiegando in dettaglio l’arte in generale… senza ricevere alcuna risposta.

Un incoraggiamento nel senso che, o bien l’aveva lasciato cadere, o bien non se n’era andato.



“Non ci racconta molto di sé, signora Huntingdon”, osservò lui.

Dopo una breve pausa, durante la quale continuai tranquillamente a mescolare e amalgamare…

I miei colori. E non posso meravigliarmene, perché devi essere davvero molto malato.

Di tutti noi… Anch’io provo un profondo imbarazzo per i miei compagni… E così anche loro.

Cansati delle loro conversazioni irrazionali e delle loro attività insensate… ora che finalmente c’è…

"Nessuno per umanizzarli e tenerli sotto controllo, poiché hai agito con giustizia..."

Ci ha abbandonati a noi stessi… Credo che tra poco mi ritirerò.

Titolo:  
Tra di loro, probabilmente entro questa settimana… E non posso immaginare che tu…

“Mi pentirò della mia partenza.”



Si fermò. Non risposi.



“Probabilmente”, aggiunse sorridendo, “l’unico rimpianto che avrai al riguardo…”

Non porterò tutti i miei compagni con me… Mi lusingo così.

A volte penso a me stesso come a qualcuno che, nonostante sia tra loro, in realtà non fa parte di loro…

“Natural che tu sia felice di liberarti di me… Forse me ne pentirò.”

“Ma non posso biasimarti per questo.”



"#Non gioirò della tua partenza, perché tu sei in grado di gestire..."

“Comportati da gentiluomo”, dissi, ritenendo che fosse giusto farlo.

Ringraziamento per il suo buon comportamento; “ma devo ammettere che…”

“Rallegrati di poter dire addio al resto, per quanto possa sembrare inospitale…”



“Nessuno può biasimarti per una tale dichiarazione”, rispose seriamente: “no”.

“Anche i signori stessi, immagino… Vi dirò semplicemente…”

“Continuò, come se fosse spinta da una improvvisa determinazione: ‘Quello che è stato detto l’altro ieri…’”

[[motifs/night|Di notte]], in sala da pranzo, dopo che ci avete lasciati, forse non vi dispiacerà.

“Beh, visto che sei davvero molto filosofico su certi argomenti…”, aggiunse.

Un leggero sorriso beffardo. “Stavano parlando di [[characters/lord-lowborough|Lord Lowborough]] e della sua, ”

Signora deliziosa… la causa della sua improvvisa partenza non è certo un segreto.

Tra loro; inoltre, il suo carattere è così ben conosciuto da tutti loro, che.

Non posso nemmeno provare a difenderlo… Maledizione.

“Mio Dio!”, mormorò, _a titolo di parentesi_, “se non mi vendico…”

Proprio questo! Se il [[archetypes/villain|villano]] vuole disonorare la famiglia, non dovrebbe forse farlo sapere in giro?

A ogni individuo spregevole che conoscesse? Mi scusi, signora.

Huntingdon. Beh, stavano parlando di queste cose, e alcuni di loro.

Osservò che, essendo separata dal marito, lui potrebbe vederla.

“Di nuovo, quando ne aveva voglia.”



“Grazie,” disse; “Per il momento ne ho abbastanza di lei: me ne andrò…”

“Non è difficile vederla, a meno che non venga da me.”



“E allora, cosa intendi fare, Huntingdon, quando noi non ci saremo più?” chiese Ralph.

Hattersley. “Intendi davvero abbandonare la strada sbagliata e cambiare vita?”

Buon marito, buon padre, e così via… proprio come faccio io, quando vengo lasciato da solo.

“Tu e tutti questi ‘diavoli’ che chiami amici… Penso che sia…”

Il tempo. E tua moglie è cinquanta volte migliore di te, lo sai bene.



“E ha aggiunto anche qualche complimento su di te… per cui probabilmente non mi ringrazieresti.”

“Ripetendolo ad alta voce, proprio come fece lui…”

Senza alcuna delicatezza o discriminazione, di fronte a un pubblico che sembrava…

Profanazione del tuo nome: lui stesso totalmente incapace di…

Comprendere o apprezzare le tue vere eccellenze. Huntingdon



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_39--part_03" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 39 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 39" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="topos/double,archetype/child,archetype/shadow,archetype/villain,motif/blood,motif/love,motif/well,motif/window,concept/conscience,concept/doubt,concept/wonder,character/helen,character/nurse"></span>


meanwhile, sat quietly drinking his wine,—or looking smilingly into his

glass and offering no interruption or reply, till Hattersley shouted

out,—‘Do you hear me, man?’



“‘Yes, go on,’ said he.



“‘Nay, I’ve done,’ replied the other: ‘I only want to know if you

intend to take my advice.’



“‘What advice?’



“‘To turn over a new leaf, you [[topoi/double|double]]-dyed scoundrel,’ shouted Ralph,

‘and beg your wife’s pardon, and be a good boy for the future.’



“‘My wife! what wife? I have no wife,’ replied Huntingdon, looking

innocently up from his glass, ‘or if I have, look you, gentlemen: I

value her so highly that any one among you, that can fancy her, may

have her and welcome: you may, by Jove, and my blessing into the

bargain!’



“I—hem—someone asked if he really meant what he said; upon which he

solemnly swore he did, and no mistake. What do you think of that, Mrs.

Huntingdon?” asked Mr. Hargrave, after a short pause, during which I

had felt he was keenly examining my half-averted face.



“I say,” replied I, calmly, “that what he prizes so lightly will not be

long in his possession.”



“You cannot mean that you will break your heart and die for the

detestable conduct of an infamous [[archetypes/villain|villain]] like that!”



“By no means: my heart is too thoroughly dried to be broken in a hurry,

and I mean to live as long as I can.”



“Will you leave him then?”



“Yes.”



“When: and how?” asked he, eagerly.



“_When_ I am ready, and _how_ I can manage it most effectually.”



“But your [[archetypes/child|child]]?”



“My [[archetypes/child|child]] goes with me.”



“He will not allow it.”



“I shall not ask him.”



“Ah, then, it is a secret flight you meditate! but with whom, Mrs.

Huntingdon?”



“With my son: and possibly, his [[characters/nurse|nurse]].”



“[[works/alone-(poe)|Alone]]—and unprotected! But where can you go? what can you do? He will

follow you and bring you back.”



“I have laid my plans too [[motifs/well|well]] for that. Let me once get clear of

Grassdale, and I shall consider myself safe.”



Mr. Hargrave advanced one step towards me, looked me in the face, and

drew in his breath to speak; but that look, that heightened colour,

that sudden sparkle of the eye, made my [[motifs/blood|blood]] rise in wrath: I abruptly

turned away, and, snatching up my brush, began to dash away at my

canvas with rather too much energy for the good of the picture.



“Mrs. Huntingdon,” said he with bitter solemnity, “you are cruel—cruel

to me—cruel to yourself.”



“Mr. Hargrave, remember your promise.”



“I _must_ speak: my heart will burst if I don’t! I have been silent

long enough, and you _must_ hear me!” cried he, boldly intercepting my

retreat to the door. “You tell me you owe no allegiance to your

husband; he openly declares himself weary of you, and calmly gives you

up to anybody that will take you; you are about to leave him; no one

will believe that you go alone; all the world will say, ‘She has left

him at last, and who can [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] at it? Few can blame her, fewer still

can pity him; but who is the companion of her flight?’ Thus you will

have no credit for your virtue (if you call it such): even your best

friends will not believe in it; because it is monstrous, and not to be

credited but by those who suffer, from the effects of it, such cruel

torments that they know it to be indeed reality. But what can you do in

the cold, rough world alone? you, a young and inexperienced woman,

delicately nurtured, and utterly—”



“In a word, you would advise me to stay where I am,” interrupted I.

“[[motifs/well|Well]], I’ll see about it.”



“By _all means_, leave him!” cried he earnestly; “but NOT alone! [[characters/helen|Helen]]!

let _me_ protect you!”



“Never! while heaven spares my reason,” replied I, snatching away the

hand he had presumed to seize and press between his own. But he was in

for it now; he had fairly broken the barrier: he was completely roused,

and determined to hazard all for victory.



“I must not be denied!” exclaimed he, vehemently; and seizing both my

hands, he held them very tight, but dropped upon his knee, and looked

up in my face with a half-imploring, half-imperious gaze. “You have no

reason now: you are flying in the face of heaven’s decrees. God has

designed me to be your comfort and protector—I feel it, I know it as

certainly as if a voice from heaven declared, ‘Ye twain shall be one

flesh’—and you spurn me from you—”



“Let me go, Mr. Hargrave!” said I, sternly. But he only tightened his

grasp.



“Let me go!” I repeated, quivering with indignation.



His face was almost opposite the [[motifs/window|window]] as he knelt. With a slight

start, I saw him glance towards it; and then a gleam of malicious

triumph lit up his countenance. Looking over my shoulder, I beheld a

[[archetypes/shadow|shadow]] just retiring round the corner.



“That is Grimsby,” said he deliberately. “He will report what he has

seen to Huntingdon and all the rest, with such embellishments as he

thinks proper. He has no [[motifs/love|love]] for you, Mrs. Huntingdon—no reverence for

your sex, no belief in virtue, no admiration for its image. He will

give such a version of this story as will leave no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] at all about

your character, in the minds of those who hear it. Your fair fame is

gone; and nothing that I or you can say can ever retrieve it. But give

me the power to protect you, and show me the [[archetypes/villain|villain]] that dares to

insult!”



“No one has ever dared to insult me as you are doing now!” said I, at

length releasing my hands, and recoiling from him.



“I do not insult you,” cried he: “I worship you. You are my angel, my

divinity! I lay my powers at your feet, and you must and shall accept

them!” he exclaimed, impetuously starting to his feet. “I _will_ be

your consoler and defender! and if your [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] upbraid you for it,

say I overcame you, and you could not choose but yield!”



I never saw a man go terribly excited. He precipitated himself towards

me. I snatched up my palette-knife and held it against him. This


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Nel frattempo, seduto in silenzio beveva il suo vino… o guardava con un sorriso dentro di sé.

Senza interruzioni né risposte, fino a quando Hattersley non gridò

“Ascolti bene, amico?”



“‘Sì, continua,’ disse lui.”



“‘No, l’ho già fatto’, rispose l’altro: ‘Voglio solo sapere se tu…’”

“Intendo seguire il mio consiglio.”



“Qual consiglio?”



“‘Per iniziare una nuova vita, tu mascalzone che ti sei tinto i capelli due volte,’ gridò Ralph,”

“Chiedi scusa a tua moglie e cerca di comportarti bene in futuro.”



“‘Mia moglie? Quale moglie? Non ho nessuna moglie,’ rispose Huntingdon, guardando…”

“Alzando innocentemente il bicchiere… o se l’ho fatto, guardate un po’, signori: io…”

La considero così preziosa che chiunque di voi, se riesce a immaginarla, può…

“Prendetela pure, e ben venga: potete farlo, per Giove e con la mia benedizione.”

“Offerta speciale!”



“Qualcuno gli ha chiesto se davvero intendesse quello che aveva detto; e lui…”

Giurò solennemente che era vero, senza alcun dubbio. Cosa ne pensate, signora?

“Huntingdon?”, chiese il signor Hargrave, dopo una breve pausa.

Aveva l'impressione che stesse esaminando attentamente il mio viso, parzialmente girato dall’altra parte.



“Dico io,” risposi con calma, “che ciò che lui valuta così poco non sarà…”

“Da molto tempo è in suo possesso.”



Non puoi davvero dire che spezzerai il tuo cuore e morirai per…

Un comportamento disgustoso da parte di un infame [[archetypes/villain|malvagio]] del genere!



"Nemmeno per idea: il mio cuore è ormai troppo arido per poter essere spezzato così facilmente."

“E intendo vivere il più a lungo possibile.”



“Allora lo lascerai andare?”



“Sì, davvero.”



“Quando? E come?”, chiese lui con impazienza.



"#Quando sarò pronto, e _come_ potrò farlo al meglio."



“Ma tuo figlio, ”



“Mio figlio viene con me.”



“Non lo permetterà mai.”



“Non glielo chiederò mai.”



“Allora, si tratta di un volo segreto che state pianificando. Ma con chi, signora?”

“Huntingdon?”



“Con mio figlio. E forse, anche con la sua [[characters/nurse|nutrice]].”



“Da solo, e senza protezione! Ma dove puoi andare? Cosa puoi fare? Lui, ”

“Ti seguirò e ti riporterò indietro.”



Ho preparato i miei piani in modo molto accurato per farlo. Lasciami prima liberarmi di.

“Grassdale… e allora mi considererò al sicuro.”



Mr. Hargrave fece un passo verso di me, mi guardò negli occhi e…

Trasse un respiro profondo per parlare… ma quel suo sguardo, quel colore intensificato sul viso…

Quel improvviso scintillio negli occhi fece ribollire la mia rabbia nel sangue; reagii bruscamente.

Rifiutato, afferrai la mia penna e iniziai a scrivere freneticamente…

Un telaio su cui si applicano troppi elementi, con un’energia che non è necessariamente vantaggiosa per il risultato finale dell’opera d’arte.



“Signora Huntingdon”, disse con amara solennità, “siete crudele… crudele”.

“Per me… crudele verso te stesso.”



"#Mr. Hargrave, ricorda la tua promessa."



“Devo parlare… altrimenti il mio cuore esploderà! Sono stata in silenzio troppo a lungo.”

“Basta che ascoltiate abbastanza a lungo, e _dovete_ assolutamente sentirmi!”, gridò, interrompendomi con decisione.

“Ritirati alla porta… E dimmi che non sei legato da alcuna lealtà verso di loro.”

Marito: dichiara apertamente di essere stanco di te e, con calma, ti…

“Chiunque sia disposto ad accettarti… stai per lasciarlo… nessuno…”

Credranno che tu te ne sia andata da sola; tutta la gente dirà: “Se n’è andata”.

Finalmente lo ha trovato. E chi può biasimarla per questo? Pochi possono farlo; ancora meno persone.

“Si può provare pietà per lui… ma chi sarà il compagno della sua fuga?” Così si dirà.

Non si può attribuire alcun merito alla propria virtù… anche la migliore di esse.

“Creditato… ma da coloro che ne soffrono gli effetti, una crudeltà del genere…”

Titolo:  
Tormenti di cui sanno con certezza che sono realtà… Ma cosa si può fare?

Il freddo, duro mondo, da sola? Tu, una donna giovane e inesperta.

Cultivato con cura estrema… e completamente…



“In altre parole, mi consigliereste di rimanere dove sono,” interruppi io.

“Beh, ne parlerò io.”



“Assolutamente, lasciatelo andare!” gridò con fervore; “ma NON da solo! [[characters/helen|Helen]]!”

“Lascia che ti protegga io!”



“Mai! finché il cielo non mi priva della ragione”, risposi, strappandoglielo di mano.

La mano che aveva osato afferrare e stringere tra le sue… Ma lui si trovava…

e deciso a rischiare tutto per la vittoria.

Le teneva strette molto forte, ma poi le lasciò cadere sulle ginocchia e guardò…

“Con uno sguardo a metà supplichevole, a metà imperioso… ‘Non hai alcun diritto’.”

Non sfidare i voleri del cielo. Dio ha…

Destinato ad essere il tuo conforto e il tuo protettore… Lo sento, lo so con certezza.

Certamente, come se una voce dal cielo dichiarasse: “Voi due diventerete uno”.

“Lasciatemi andare, signor Hargrave!”, dissi con fermezza. Ma lui si limitò a stringere ancora di più la presa su di me.

comprendere.



“Lasciami andare!” ripetei, tremando di indignazione.



Il suo viso era quasi di fronte alla [[motifs/window|finestra]] mentre si inginocchiava; con un leggero.

“#Inizio… Lo vidi lanciare un’occhiata verso di esso; poi un bagliore malizioso nei suoi occhi…”

Il trionfo illuminò il suo volto. Guardando oltre la mia spalla, vidi…

[[archetypes/shadow|ombra]] sta per ritirarsi, è proprio dietro l'angolo.



“Quello è Grimsby,” disse deliberatamente. “Riferirà ciò che ha visto.”

Credo sia giusto così. Lui non prova alcun [[motifs/love|amore]] per voi, signora Huntingdon, né il minimo rispetto.

Il tuo sesso, nessuna fede nella virtù, nessun ammiramento per la sua immagine… Lui lo farà.

Dai una versione di questa storia tale da non lasciare alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] al riguardo.

Il tuo carattere, nella mente di coloro che lo ascoltano… La tua nobile reputazione…

“Insulto!”

Divinità! Metto le mie forze ai tuoi piedi, e tu devi e dovrai accettarle.

Il tuo conforto e il tuo difensore. E se la tua [[concepts/conscience|coscienza]] ti rimprovera per questo,

“Me… Ho afferrato il mio coltello da paletta e l’ho puntato contro di lui.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_39--part_04" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 39 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 39" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/grave,motif/night,motif/rose,motif/well,motif/window,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/imagination,character/arthur"></span>


startled him: he stood and gazed at me in astonishment; I daresay I

looked as fierce and resolute as he. I moved to the bell, and put my

hand upon the cord. This tamed him still more. With a

half-authoritative, half-deprecating wave of the hand, he sought to

deter me from ringing.



“Stand off, then!” said I; he stepped back. “And listen to me. I don’t

like you,” I continued, as deliberately and emphatically as I could, to

give the greater efficacy to my words; “and if I were divorced from my

husband, or if he were dead, I would not marry you. There now! I [[concepts/hope|hope]]

you’re satisfied.”



His face grew blanched with anger.



“I _am_ satisfied,” he replied, with bitter emphasis, “that you are the

most cold-hearted, unnatural, ungrateful woman I ever yet beheld!”



“Ungrateful, sir?”



“Ungrateful.”



“No, Mr. Hargrave, I am not. For all the good you ever did me, or ever

wished to do, I most sincerely thank you: for all the evil you have

done me, and all you would have done, I pray God to pardon you, and

make you of a better mind.”



Here the door was thrown open, and Messrs. Huntingdon and Hattersley

appeared without. The latter remained in the hall, busy with his ramrod

and his gun; the former walked in, and stood with his back to the [[motifs/fire|fire]],

surveying Mr. Hargrave and me, particularly the former, with a smile of

insupportable meaning, accompanied as it was by the impudence of his

brazen brow, and the sly, malicious, twinkle of his eye.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], sir?” said Hargrave, interrogatively, and with the air of one

prepared to stand on the defensive.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], sir,” returned his host.



“We want to know if you are at liberty to join us in a go at the

pheasants, Walter,” interposed Hattersley from without. “Come! there

shall be nothing shot besides, except a puss or two; _I’ll_ vouch for

that.”



Walter did not answer, but walked to the [[motifs/window|window]] to collect his

faculties. [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] uttered a low whistle, and followed him with his

eyes. A slight flush of anger [[motifs/rose|rose]] to Hargrave’s cheek; but in a moment

he turned calmly round, and said carelessly:



“I came here to bid farewell to Mrs. Huntingdon, and tell her I must go

to-morrow.”



“Humph! You’re mighty sudden in your resolution. What takes you off so

soon, may I ask?”



“Business,” returned he, repelling the other’s incredulous sneer with a

glance of scornful defiance.



“Very good,” was the reply; and Hargrave walked away. Thereupon Mr.

Huntingdon, gathering his coat-laps under his arms, and setting his

shoulder against the mantel-piece, turned to me, and, addressing me in

a low voice, scarcely above his breath, poured forth a volley of the

vilest and grossest abuse it was possible for the [[concepts/imagination|imagination]] to

conceive or the tongue to utter. I did not attempt to interrupt him;

but my spirit kindled within me, and when he had done, I replied, “If

your accusation were true, Mr. Huntingdon, how _dare you_ blame me?”



“She’s hit it, by Jove!” cried Hattersley, rearing his gun against the

wall; and, stepping into the room, he took his precious friend by the

arm, and attempted to drag him away. “Come, my lad,” he muttered; “true

or false, _you’ve_ no right to blame her, you _know_, nor him either;

after what you said last [[motifs/night|night]]. So come along.”



There was something implied here that I could not endure.



“Dare you suspect me, Mr. Hattersley?” said I, almost beside myself

with fury.



“Nay, nay, I suspect nobody. It’s all right, it’s all right. So come

along, Huntingdon, you blackguard.”



“She can’t deny it!” cried the gentleman thus addressed, grinning in

mingled rage and triumph. “She can’t deny it if her life depended on

it!” and muttering some more abusive language, he walked into the hall,

and took up his hat and gun from the table.



“I scorn to justify myself to you!” said I. “But you,” turning to

Hattersley, “if you presume to have any doubts on the subject, ask Mr.

Hargrave.”



At this they simultaneously burst into a rude laugh that made my whole

frame tingle to the fingers’ ends.



“Where is he? I’ll ask him myself!” said I, advancing towards them.



Suppressing a new burst of merriment, Hattersley pointed to the outer

door. It was half open. His brother-in-law was standing on the front

without.



“Mr. Hargrave, will you please to step this way?” said I.



He turned and looked at me in [[motifs/grave|grave]] surprise.



“Step this way, if you please!” I repeated, in so determined a manner

that he could not, or did not choose to resist its authority. Somewhat

reluctantly he ascended the steps and advanced a pace or two into the

hall.



“And tell those gentlemen,” I continued—“these men, whether or not I

yielded to your solicitations.”



“I don’t understand you, Mrs. Huntingdon.”



“You _do_ understand me, sir; and I charge you, upon your [[concepts/honour|honour]] as a

gentleman (if you have any), to answer truly. Did I, or did I not?”



“No,” muttered he, turning away.



“Speak up, sir; they can’t hear you. Did I grant your request?



“You did not.”



“No, I’ll be sworn she didn’t,” said Hattersley, “or he’d never look so

black.”



“I’m willing to grant you the satisfaction of a gentleman, Huntingdon,”

said Mr. Hargrave, calmly addressing his host, but with a bitter sneer

upon his countenance.



“Go to the deuce!” replied the latter, with an impatient jerk of the

head. Hargrave withdrew with a look of cold disdain, saying,—“You know

where to find me, should you feel disposed to send a friend.”



Muttered oaths and curses were all the answer this intimation obtained.



“Now, Huntingdon, you see!” said Hattersley. “Clear as the day.”



“I don’t care _what_ he sees,” said I, “or what he imagines; but you,

Mr. Hattersley, when you hear my name belied and slandered, will you

defend it?”



“I will.”



I instantly departed and shut myself into the library. What could

possess me to make such a request of such a man I cannot tell; but

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_39--part_05" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 39 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 39" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/villain,motif/dawn,motif/love,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,motif/winter,concept/despair,concept/exile,concept/hope,concept/madness,character/arthur"></span>


drowning men catch at straws: they had driven me desperate between

them; I hardly knew what I said. There was no other to preserve my name

from being blackened and aspersed among this nest of boon companions,

and through them, perhaps, into the world; and beside my abandoned

wretch of a husband, the base, malignant Grimsby, and the false [[archetypes/villain|villain]]

Hargrave, this boorish ruffian, coarse and brutal as he was, shone like

a glow-worm in the dark, among its fellow worms.



What a scene was this! Could I ever have imagined that I should be

doomed to bear such insults under my own roof—to hear such things

spoken in my presence; nay, spoken _to_ me and _of_ me; and by those

who arrogated to themselves the name of gentlemen? And could I have

imagined that I should have been able to endure it as calmly, and to

repel their insults as firmly and as boldly as I had done? A hardness

such as this is taught by rough experience and [[concepts/despair|despair]] alone.



Such thoughts as these chased one another through my mind, as I paced

to and fro the room, and longed—oh, _how_ I longed—to take my [[archetypes/child|child]] and

leave them now, without an hour’s delay! But it could not be; there was

work before me: hard work, that must be done.



“Then let me do it,” said I, “and lose not a moment in vain repinings

and idle chafings against my fate, and those who influence it.”



And conquering my agitation with a powerful effort, I immediately

resumed my task, and laboured hard all day.



Mr. Hargrave did depart on the morrow; and I have never seen him since.

The others stayed on for two or three weeks longer; but I kept aloof

from them as much as possible, and still continued my labour, and have

continued it, with almost unabated ardour, to the present day. I soon

acquainted Rachel with my design, confiding all my motives and

intentions to her ear, and, much to my agreeable surprise, found little

difficulty in persuading her to enter into my views. She is a sober,

cautious woman, but she so hates her master, and so loves her mistress

and her nursling, that after several ejaculations, a few faint

objections, and many [[motifs/tears|tears]] and lamentations that I should be brought to

such a pass, she applauded my resolution and consented to aid me with

all her might: on one condition only: that she might share my [[concepts/exile|exile]]:

otherwise, she was utterly inexorable, regarding it as perfect [[concepts/madness|madness]]

for me and [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] to go alone. With touching generosity, she modestly

offered to aid me with her little hoard of savings, hoping I would

“excuse her for the liberty, but really, if I would do her the favour

to accept it as a loan, she would be very happy.” Of course I could not

think of such a thing; but now, thank heaven, I have gathered a little

hoard of my own, and my preparations are so far advanced that I am

looking forward to a speedy emancipation. Only let the stormy severity

of this [[motifs/winter|winter]] weather be somewhat abated, and then, some morning, Mr.

Huntingdon will come down to a solitary breakfast-table, and perhaps be

clamouring through the house for his invisible wife and [[archetypes/child|child]], when

they are some fifty miles on their way to the Western world, or it may

be more: for we shall leave him hours before the [[motifs/dawn|dawn]], and it is not

probable he will discover the loss of both until the day is far

advanced.



I am fully alive to the evils that may and must result upon the step I

am about to take; but I never waver in my resolution, because I never

forget my son. It was only this morning, while I pursued my usual

employment, he was sitting at my feet, quietly playing with the shreds

of canvas I had thrown upon the carpet; but his mind was otherwise

occupied, for, in a while, he looked up wistfully in my face, and

gravely asked,—“Mamma, why are you wicked?”



“Who told you I was wicked, [[motifs/love|love]]?”



“Rachel.”



“No, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], Rachel never said so, I am certain.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], then, it was papa,” replied he, thoughtfully. Then, after a

reflective pause, he added, “At least, I’ll tell you how it was I got

to know: when I’m with papa, if I say mamma wants me, or mamma says I’m

not to do something that he tells me to do, he always says, ‘Mamma be

damned,’ and Rachel says it’s only wicked people that are damned. So,

mamma, that’s why I think you must be wicked: and I wish you wouldn’t.”



“My dear [[archetypes/child|child]], I am not. Those are bad words, and wicked people often

say them of others better than themselves. Those words cannot make

people be damned, nor show that they deserve it. God will judge us by

our own thoughts and deeds, not by what others say about us. And when

you hear such words spoken, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]], remember never to repeat them: it

is wicked to say such things of others, not to have them said against

you.”



“Then it’s papa that’s wicked,” said he, ruefully.



“Papa is wrong to say such things, and you will be very wrong to

imitate him now that you know better.”



“What _is_ imitate?”



“To do as he does.”



“Does _he_ know better?”



“Perhaps he does; but that is nothing to you.”



“If he doesn’t, you ought to tell him, mamma.”



“I _have_ told him.”



The little moralist paused and pondered. I tried in vain to divert his

mind from the subject.



“I’m sorry papa’s wicked,” said he mournfully, at length, “for I don’t

want him to go to hell.” And so saying he burst into [[motifs/tears|tears]].



I consoled him with the [[concepts/hope|hope]] that perhaps his papa would alter and

become good before he died—; but is it not [[motifs/time|time]] to deliver him from

such a parent?


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

"Uomini che annegano si aggrappano a qualsiasi cosa: mi avevano ridotto alla disperazione..."

Non so quasi cosa ho detto… Non c’era nessun altro che potesse salvare il mio nome.

Tra compagni così preziosi…

E attraverso di loro, forse, nel mondo… E accanto al mio abbandonato…

Maledetto marito, quel vile e malvagio Grimsby, e quel falso [[archetypes/villain|antagonista]].

Hargrave: quel bruto rozzo e crudele, ma pur sempre…

Un lucciole nel buio, tra i suoi simili.



Che scena incredibile… Avrei mai potuto immaginare di trovarmi in una situazione del genere?

Condannato a subire simili insulti sotto il mio stesso tetto… ad ascoltare cose del genere

Detto davanti a me; anzi, detto a me e di me… e da quelle persone

Chi si è arrogato il nome di gentiluomini? E avrei potuto…

Immaginavo di essere in grado di sopportarlo con la stessa calma…

Rifiutare le loro offese con la stessa fermezza e coraggio con cui l’avevo fatto io… Una determinazione incrollabile.

Qualcosa del genere viene insegnato soltanto attraverso dure esperienze e [[concepts/despair|-disperazione]], da-solo.



Pensieri del genere si susseguivano nella mia mente mentre camminavo avanti e indietro…

Avanti e indietro nella stanza, desideravo ardentemente, oh, _quanto_ ardentemente desideravo prendere il mio [[archetypes/child|bambino]] e.

"Lasciali andare ora, senza un minuto di ritardo! Ma non era possibile; c’era..."

Il lavoro che ho davanti a me: un lavoro duro, che deve essere portato a termine.



“Allora lasciate che lo faccia io,” dissi, “e non perdiamo nemmeno un istante in vani rimpianti.”

“E inutili lamentele contro il mio destino, e coloro che ne influenzano lo svolgimento…”



Conquistando la mia agitazione con uno sforzo deciso, immediatamente…

Ripresi il mio compito e lavorai sodo per tutto il giorno.



Il signor Hargrave partì il giorno seguente; da allora non l’ho più visto.

Gli altri rimasero ancora due o tre settimane; ma io mi tenni alla larga.

Prendevo da loro tutto ciò che potevo, e continuavo comunque il mio lavoro.

Lo ha continuato, con un entusiasmo quasi inesauribile, fino ai giorni nostri. Presto…

Presentai il mio piano a Rachel, spiegandole tutti i miei motivi…

“Intentioni sussurrate alle sue orecchie… e, con mia grande sorpresa, quasi nessuna reazione.”

Difficoltà nel convincerla ad aderire alle mie opinioni… È una persona sobria, razionale…

Donna cauta… ma odia così tanto il suo padrone e ama così tanto la sua padrona…

E lei e il suo piccolo… dopo alcuni sforzi, qualche debole risultato…

Obiezioni, e molte [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] e lamenti riguardo al fatto che io dovessi essere portato via.

“Che bel gesto…”, esclamò, applaudendo la mia determinazione e acconsentendo ad aiutarmi.

Con tutte le sue forze, ma solo a una condizione: che potesse condividere il mio [[concepts/exile|esilio]].

Altrimenti, era assolutamente spietata, considerandolo un esempio perfetto di [[concepts/madness|pazzia]].

Per me e [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] per andare da soli. Con una generosità commovente, lei, con umiltà.

Mi offrì di aiutarmi con la sua piccola riserva di risparmi, nella speranza che io accettassi…

"Scusate la libertà, ma davvero… se volessi farle questo favore…"

“Accettarlo come prestito la renderebbe molto felice… Ovviamente, non potevo farlo.”

Mai avrei pensato a una cosa del genere; ma ora, grazie al cielo, ho finalmente raccolto qualcosa…

“Una riserva personale… e i miei preparativi sono ormai molto avanzati.”
