“Che destino e circostanze caratterizzano le loro dimore terrene?”



“Può darsi, può darsi!”, esclamò lei, con un improvviso impeto di gioia.

Entusiasmo. “Anch’io ci ho pensato, Gilbert, ma temevo di menzionarlo…”

Perché temevo che non avreste compreso le mie opinioni al riguardo

Soggetto. Lo [[concepts/fear|temo]] ancora adesso; temo che qualsiasi amico potrebbe dirci che siamo.

Entrambi ci inganniamo pensando di riuscire a mantenere un livello spirituale adeguato

Un rapporto senza [[concepts/hope|speranza]] né prospettive future, senza nulla.

Cultivare rimpianti vani e aspirazioni nocive, alimentando pensieri negativi…

“Deve essere lasciato morire di inedia, in modo severo e senza pietà.”



“Lasciate perdere i nostri ‘amici’… Se sono disposti a separare i nostri corpi, allora…”

“Basta! Per amor di Dio, che non distruggano le nostre anime!” gridai io.

Terrore che possa ritenere suo dovere negarci quest’ultima possibilità rimasta

Consolazione.



“Ma qui non è possibile che alcuna lettera venga scambiata tra di noi”, disse lei, “senza che…”

“Cibo fresco per scandali… E quando me ne sono andato, avevo intenzione che il mio nuovo…”

“L’ubicazione di quell’abitazione dovrebbe rimanere sconosciuta sia per te che per il resto del mondo… Non che io…”

Se avessi promesso di non venire a trovarmi, dovrei forse [[concepts/doubt|dubitare]] della tua parola, ma ho pensato che.

Se solo sapessi di non poter… saresti più in pace con te stesso.

Fallo, e probabilmente avrai meno difficoltà nel distaccarti da…

“Immagina solo la mia situazione… Ma ascolta.”

“Così disse, sorridendo e alzando un dito per fermare la mia risposta impaziente…”

“In sei mesi riceverete notizie da Frederick riguardo al mio esatto luogo di trovarmi; e…”

Se ancora desideri scrivermi e credi di poterlo fare…

Mantenere una corrispondenza con tutto il pensiero, con tutto lo spirito… come se fossero entità disincarnate.

“Anime o, almeno, amici senza passione… Scrivete, e io farò.”

“Risponderò a te.”



“Sei mesi!”



“Sì, per dare al tuo attuale entusiasmo il tempo di calmarsi e per verificare la [[concepts/truth|verità]], ”

La costanza dell’amore della tua [[motifs/soul|'anima]] per la mia. Ora, basta aver detto.

“Tra di noi… Perché non possiamo separarci subito?” esclamò lei, quasi impazzita.

Dopo un momento di pausa, lei si alzò improvvisamente dalla sedia, con.

Le mani strette con determinazione… Pensai che fosse mio dovere andare.

Senza indugio; mi avvicinai e allungai quasi la mano, come per afferrarlo.

“Lasciare, ”, lo afferrò in [[motifs/silence|silenzio]]. Ma questo pensiero di separazione definitiva.

Era troppo insopportabile: sembrava che strizzasse tutto il [[motifs/blood|sangue]] dal mio cuore.

E i miei piedi erano incollati al pavimento.



“E non dovremo mai più incontrarci?” mormorai, nell’angoscia della mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]].



“Ci rivedremo in cielo… Pensiamoci”, disse lei con quel tono…

Calma disperata; ma i suoi occhi brillavano follemente, e il suo viso…

Terribilmente pallido.



“Ma non come siamo ora”, non potei fare a meno di rispondere. “Questo mi dà poco…”

Consolazione nel pensare che presto ti rivedrò come uno spirito senza corpo…

O un essere alterato, con un corpo perfetto e splendido… ma non simile agli altri.

“Questo… e forse un cuore completamente distante da me.”



“No, Gilbert, in cielo esiste un amore perfetto!”



“Così perfetto, immagino, da superare qualsiasi distinzione…”

Titolo:  
Non proverà mai verso di me un’empatia maggiore di quella che prova verso chiunque altro tra questi dieci.

Migliaia e migliaia di angeli e l’innumerevole schiera di spiriti felici

“Intorno a noi.”



“Qualunque cosa io sia, tu sarai lo stesso… e quindi non è possibile che…”

Mi dispiace… E qualunque sia quel cambiamento, sappiamo che deve essere per il meglio.

"Migliore."



“Ma se devo cambiare così tanto da smettere di amarti con tutto il mio…”

Con tutto il mio cuore e la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]], e con un amore che va oltre ogni altra creatura, ti amerò.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_45--part_04" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 45 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 45" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/garden,motif/hill,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/pain,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/wind,concept/doubt,concept/faith,concept/hope,concept/melancholy,concept/nature,concept/suffering,character/arthur,character/bottom,character/helen"></span>


not be myself; and though, if ever I win heaven at all, I must, I know,

be infinitely better and happier than I am now, my earthly [[concepts/nature|nature]]

cannot rejoice in the anticipation of such beatitude, from which itself

and its chief joy must be excluded.”



“Is your [[motifs/love|love]] _all_ earthly, then?”



“No, but I am supposing we shall have no more intimate communion with

each other than with the rest.”



“If so, it will be because we [[motifs/love|love]] them more, and not each other less.

Increase of [[motifs/love|love]] brings increase of happiness, when it is mutual, and

pure as that will be.”



“But can _you_, [[characters/helen|Helen]], contemplate with delight this prospect of losing

me in a sea of glory?”



“I own I cannot; but we know not that it will be so;—and I do know that

to regret the exchange of earthly pleasures for the joys of heaven, is

as if the grovelling caterpillar should lament that it must one day

quit the nibbled leaf to soar aloft and flutter through the air, roving

at will from flower to flower, sipping sweet honey from their cups, or

basking in their sunny petals. If these little creatures knew how great

a change awaited them, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] they would regret it; but would not all

such sorrow be misplaced? And if that illustration will not move you,

here is another:—We are children now; we feel as children, and we

understand as children; and when we are told that men and women do not

play with toys, and that our companions will one day weary of the

trivial sports and occupations that interest them and us so deeply now,

we cannot help being saddened at the thoughts of such an alteration,

because we cannot conceive that as we grow up our own minds will become

so enlarged and elevated that we ourselves shall then regard as

trifling those objects and pursuits we now so fondly cherish, and that,

though our companions will no longer join us in those childish

pastimes, they will drink with us at other fountains of delight, and

mingle their souls with ours in higher aims and nobler occupations

beyond our present comprehension, but not less deeply relished or less

truly good for that, while yet both we and they remain essentially the

same individuals as before. But, Gilbert, can you really derive no

consolation from the thought that we may meet together where there is

no more [[motifs/pain|pain]] and sorrow, no more striving against sin, and struggling

of the spirit against the flesh; where both will behold the same

glorious truths, and drink exalted and supreme felicity from the same

fountain of light and goodness—that Being whom both will worship with

the same intensity of holy ardour—and where pure and happy creatures

both will [[motifs/love|love]] with the same divine affection? If you cannot, never

write to me!”



“[[characters/helen|Helen]], I can! if [[concepts/faith|faith]] would never fail.”



“Now, then,” exclaimed she, “while this [[concepts/hope|hope]] is strong within us—”



“We will part,” I cried. “You shall not have the [[motifs/pain|pain]] of another effort

to dismiss me. I will go at once; but—”



I did not put my request in words: she understood it instinctively, and

_this_ [[motifs/time|time]] she yielded too—or rather, there was nothing so deliberate

as requesting or yielding in the matter: there was a sudden impulse

that neither could resist. One moment I stood and looked into her face,

the next I held her to my heart, and we seemed to grow together in a

close embrace from which no physical or mental force could rend us. A

whispered “God bless you!” and “Go—go!” was all she said; but while she

spoke she held me so fast that, without violence, I could not have

obeyed her. At length, however, by some heroic effort, we tore

ourselves apart, and I rushed from the house.



I have a confused remembrance of seeing little [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] running up the

[[motifs/garden|garden]]-walk to meet me, and of bolting over the wall to avoid him—and

subsequently running down the steep fields, clearing the stone fences

and hedges as they came in my way, till I got completely out of sight

of the old hall and down to the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the [[motifs/hill|hill]]; and then of long

hours spent in bitter [[motifs/tears|tears]] and lamentations, and [[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] musings in

the lonely valley, with the eternal music in my ears, of the west [[motifs/wind|wind]]

rushing through the overshadowing trees, and the brook babbling and

gurgling along its stony bed; my eyes, for the most part, vacantly

fixed on the deep, chequered shades restlessly playing over the bright

sunny grass at my feet, where now and then a withered leaf or two would

come dancing to share the revelry; but my heart was away up the [[motifs/hill|hill]] in

that dark room where she was weeping desolate and alone—she whom I was

not to comfort, not to see again, till years or [[concepts/suffering|suffering]] had overcome

us both, and torn our spirits from their perishing abodes of clay.



There was little business done that day, you may be sure. The farm was

abandoned to the labourers, and the labourers were left to their own

devices. But one duty must be attended to; I had not forgotten my

assault upon Frederick Lawrence; and I must see him to apologise for

the unhappy deed. I would fain have put it off till the morrow; but

what if he should denounce me to his sister in the meantime? No, no! I

must ask his pardon to-day, and entreat him to be lenient in his

accusation, if the revelation must be made. I deferred it, however,

till the evening, when my spirits were more composed, and when—oh,

wonderful perversity of human [[concepts/nature|nature]]!—some faint germs of indefinite

hopes were beginning to rise in my mind; not that I intended to cherish

them, after all that had been said on the subject, but there they must

lie for a while, uncrushed though not encouraged, till I had learnt to

live without them.



Arrived at Woodford, the young squire’s abode, I found no little

difficulty in obtaining admission to his presence. The servant that

opened the door told me his master was very ill, and seemed to think it


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Non potrò essere me stesso… E anche se, un giorno, riuscissi davvero ad entrare in paradiso, so che dovrei comunque cambiare.

Essere infinitamente meglio e più felice di quanto non lo sia ora, la mia natura terrena.

Non si può gioire all’idea di una tale beatitudine, che per sua natura…

“E la sua principale gioia deve essere esclusa.”



“Allora, il tuo [[motifs/love|amore]] è soltanto terreno?”



"No, ma presumo che non avremo più alcun tipo di intima comunicazione..."

“Ognuno di loro si relaziona solo con gli altri, non con il resto del mondo.”



“Se è così, sarà perché li [[motifs/love|amiamo]] di più, e non meno l’uno dell’altro.”

L'aumento dell'''[[motifs/love|amore]]''' porta a un aumento della felicità, soprattutto quando è reciproco.

“Puro come sarà.”



“Ma tu, [[characters/helen|Helen]], riesci davvero a considerare con gioia l’idea di perdere, ”

“Mi trovo in un mare di gloria?”



“Ammetto di non poterlo fare; ma non sappiamo se sarà davvero così… E io so per certo che…”

Pentirsi di aver scambiato i piaceri terreni con le gioie del cielo

Come se la larva che striscia per terra dovesse lamentarsi del fatto che un giorno dovrà trasformarsi…

Lascia quella foglia che stai mordicchiando e vola in alto, planando nell’aria libera…

Da un fiore all’altro, a piacimento, assaporando il dolce miele che racchiudono… o forse altro ancora.

Godersi al sole tra i loro petali luminosi… Se solo queste piccole creature potessero sapere quanto sia meraviglioso…

Un cambiamento li aspettava; non c'era alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] che se ne sarebbero pentiti. Ma forse tutti quanti.

Una tristezza così profonda… eppure inutile? E se nemmeno questa descrizione riesce a commuovervi…

Ecco un altro esempio: ora siamo bambini; ci sentiamo come bambini…

Capire come fanno i bambini… E quando ci viene detto che uomini e donne non fanno la stessa cosa…

Gioca con i giocattoli… e un giorno anche i nostri compagni ne avranno abbastanza

Sport e attività banali che oggi ci interessano profondamente, sia a noi che a loro.

Non possiamo fare a meno di sentirci tristi al pensiero di un tale cambiamento.

Perché non possiamo immaginare che, crescendo, i nostri pensieri cambieranno

Tanto ampliato e elevato che allora anche noi lo considereremo così…

“Disprezzare quegli oggetti e quelle attività che oggi teniamo tanto in considerazione…”

“Sebbene i nostri compagni non ci accompagnino più in quelle azioni infantili…”

Passatempi… beranno con noi anche presso altre fonti di gioia.

Unire le loro anime alle nostre per obiettivi più elevati e occupazioni più nobile.

Al di là della nostra attuale comprensione, ma non per questo meno apprezzato…

“Veramente adatto a quello scopo… eppure sia noi che loro rimaniamo essenzialmente gli stessi.”

Gli stessi individui di prima… Ma, Gilbert, davvero non riesci a dedurre nulla?

Consolazione nel pensiero che potremo incontrarci lì dove c’è…

Nessun altro [[motifs/pain|dolore]] né tristezza, nessuna più lotta contro il peccato e le difficoltà.

Lo spirito contro la carne: dove entrambi vedranno lo stesso

Verità gloriose: bevi una felicità elevata e suprema proprio da esse

Fontana di luce e bontà: quell’Essere che entrambi adoreranno…

La stessa intensità di ardore sacro… e lì, dove esistono creature pure e felici…

Entrambi ameranno con la stessa affetto divino? Se non puoi, allora mai.

Scrivimi!



“[[characters/helen|Helen]], posso farcela! se solo la [[concepts/faith|fede]] non dovesse mai mancare.”



“Allora,” esclamò lei, “finché questa [[concepts/hope|speranza]] è ancora forte in noi, ”



“Ci separeremo,” gridai. “Non dovrà più sopportare il [[motifs/pain|dolore]] di un altro tentativo.”

“Per scacciarmi via… Me ne andrò subito, ma…”



Non ho espresso la mia richiesta a parole: lei l’ha compresa istintivamente.

_Questa volta_ lei cedette anche lei, o meglio, non ci fu nulla di deliberato in quel comportamento.

Un impulso improvviso

“Uno sguardo che nessuno poteva resistere… In quel momento mi alzai e la fissai negli occhi.”

Il momento successivo la strinsi al mio cuore, e sembrò che crescessimo insieme…

Un abbraccio stretto dal quale nessuna forza, fisica o mentale, potrebbe separarci.

“Sussurrò ‘Dio ti benedica!’ e ‘Vai… vai!’, ma mentre lo faceva…”

“Mi teneva così stretto che, senza alcuna forza, non avrei potuto liberarmi…”

Obbedì alle sue istruzioni. Tuttavia, dopo molti sforzi, riuscimmo infine a farlo.

Ci siamo separati, e io sono corso via dalla casa.



Ho un ricordo confuso di aver visto il piccolo [[characters/arthur|Arthur]] correre su.

Camminare nel [[motifs/garden|giardino]] per incontrarmi, oppure scavalcare il muro per evitarlo, e poi.

In seguito, correndo giù per i ripidi campi, superando le recinzioni di pietra…

“E gli ostacoli che mi si paravano davanti, finché non sono completamente scomparso dalla loro vista…”

Dalla vecchia sala, giù fino alla [[characters/bottom|base]] della [[motifs/hill|collina]]; e poi ancora per un lungo tratto.

Ore trascorse tra amare [[motifs/tears|lacrime]] e lamenti, e pensieri [[concepts/melancholy|malinconici]].

La valle desolata, con la musica eterna del vento occidentale nelle mie orecchie.

Attraverso gli alberi ombrosi, e il ruscello che mormora…

“Gorgogliando lungo il suo letto di pietre… i miei occhi, per lo più, fissi nel vuoto.”

Fissi nelle profonde ombre a scacchi, che si muovono inquiete sulla luce brillante…

“Erba soleggiata ai miei piedi, dove di tanto in tanto giaceva una o due foglie appassite…”

Come se danzassi per condividere la festa. Ma il mio cuore era lassù, sulla [[motifs/hill|collina]], in.

Quella stanza buia, dove lei piangeva disperata e sola. Lei, di cui io ero.

Non per consolare, non per rivederlo di nuovo, finché gli anni o la [[concepts/suffering|sofferenza]] non lo avessero superato.

Usare entrambi, e riportare i nostri spiriti dalle loro dimore di fango in cui stanno per perire.



“Quel giorno non ci furono molte attività da svolgere, potete esserne certi… La fattoria…”

Abbandonati ai lavoratori, e i lavoratori furono lasciati a se stessi.

Dispositivi… Ma c’è un dovere che devo assolvere: non avevo dimenticato il mio…

Attacco contro Frederick Lawrence; devo incontrarlo per scusarmi

L'atto infelice… Avrei voluto rimandarlo al domani, ma…

“E se nel frattempo dovesse denunciarmi a sua sorella? No, no!”

Devo chiedergli scusa oggi stesso e supplicarlo di essere clemente…

Accusa… se proprio deve essere rivelata. Tuttavia, l’ho rimandata.

Fino alla sera, quando il mio spirito si fu calmato un po’… e quando… oh…

Che meravigliosa perversione della natura umana. Alcuni deboli germi di qualcosa di indefinito.

Nelle mie mente iniziavano ad affiorare delle speranze… anche se non avevo intenzione di tenerle a cuore.

“Loro, dopo tutto ciò che era stato detto sull’argomento… ma dovevano pur esserci.”

Titolo:  
Restai disteso per un po’, senza essere incoraggiato ma nemmeno oppresso, finché non imparai…

Vivere senza di loro.



Arrivato a Woodford, la residenza del giovane signore, scoprii che non era affatto…

Difficoltà nell’ottenere l’ammissione alla sua presenza… Il servitore che…

Ha aperto la porta e mi ha detto che il suo padrone era molto malato… e sembrava davvero crederlo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_45--part_05" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 45 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 45" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/blood,motif/fire,motif/time,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/truth"></span>


doubtful whether he would be able to see me. I was not going to be

baulked, however. I waited calmly in the hall to be announced, but

inwardly determined to take no denial. The message was such as I

expected—a polite intimation that Mr. Lawrence could see no one; he was

feverish, and must not be disturbed.



“I shall not disturb him long,” said I; “but I must see him for a

moment: it is on business of importance that I wish to speak to him.”



“I’ll tell him, sir,” said the man. And I advanced further into the

hall and followed him nearly to the door of the apartment where his

master was—for it seemed he was not in bed. The answer returned was

that Mr. Lawrence hoped I would be so good as to leave a message or a

note with the servant, as he could attend to no business at present.



“He may as [[motifs/well|well]] see me as you,” said I; and, stepping past the

astonished footman, I boldly rapped at the door, entered, and closed it

behind me. The room was spacious and handsomely furnished—very

comfortably, too, for a bachelor. A clear, red [[motifs/fire|fire]] was burning in the

polished grate: a superannuated greyhound, given up to idleness and

good living, lay basking before it on the thick, soft rug, on one

corner of which, beside the sofa, sat a smart young springer, looking

wistfully up in its master’s face—perhaps asking permission to share

his couch, or, it might be, only soliciting a caress from his hand or a

kind word from his lips. The invalid himself looked very interesting as

he lay reclining there, in his elegant dressing-gown, with a silk

handkerchief bound across his temples. His usually pale face was

flushed and feverish; his eyes were half closed, until he became

sensible of my presence—and then he opened them wide enough: one hand

was thrown listlessly over the back of the sofa, and held a small

volume, with which, apparently, he had been vainly attempting to

beguile the weary hours. He dropped it, however, in his start of

indignant surprise as I advanced into the room and stood before him on

the rug. He raised himself on his pillows, and gazed upon me with equal

degrees of nervous horror, anger, and amazement depicted on his

countenance.



“Mr. Markham, I scarcely expected this!” he said; and the [[motifs/blood|blood]] left

his cheek as he spoke.



“I know you didn’t,” answered I; “but be quiet a minute, and I’ll tell

you what I came for.” Unthinkingly, I advanced a step or two nearer. He

winced at my approach, with an expression of aversion and instinctive

physical [[concepts/fear|fear]] anything but conciliatory to my feelings. I stepped back,

however.



“Make your story a short one,” said he, putting his hand on the small

silver bell that stood on the table beside him, “or I shall be obliged

to call for assistance. I am in no state to bear your brutalities now,

or your presence either.” And in [[concepts/truth|truth]] the moisture started from his

pores and stood on his pale forehead like dew.



Such a reception was hardly calculated to diminish the difficulties of

my unenviable task. It must be performed however, in some fashion; and

so I plunged into it at once, and floundered through it as I could.



“The [[concepts/truth|truth]] is, Lawrence,” said I, “I have not acted quite correctly

towards you of late—especially on this last occasion; and I’m come

to—in short, to express my regret for what has been done, and to beg

your pardon. If you don’t choose to grant it,” I added hastily, not

liking the aspect of his face, “it’s no matter; only _I’ve_ done _my_

duty—that’s all.”



“It’s easily done,” replied he, with a faint smile bordering on a

sneer: “to abuse your friend and knock him on the head without any

assignable cause, and then tell him the deed was not quite correct, but

it’s no matter whether he pardons it or not.”



“I forgot to tell you that it was in consequence of a

mistake,”—muttered I. “I should have made a very handsome apology, but

you provoked me so confoundedly with your—. [[motifs/well|Well]], I suppose it’s my

fault. The fact is, I didn’t know that you were Mrs. Graham’s brother,

and I saw and heard some things respecting your conduct towards her

which were calculated to awaken unpleasant suspicions, that, allow me

to say, a little candour and confidence on your part might have

removed; and, at last, I chanced to overhear a part of a conversation

between you and her that made me think I had a right to hate you.”



“And how came you to know that I was her brother?” asked he, in some

anxiety.



“She told me herself. She told me all. _She_ knew I might be trusted.

But you needn’t disturb yourself about _that_, Mr. Lawrence, for I’ve

seen the last of her!”



“The last! Is she gone, then?”



“No; but she has bid adieu to me, and I have promised never to go near

that house again while she inhabits it.” I could have groaned aloud at

the bitter thoughts awakened by this turn in the discourse. But I only

clenched my hands and stamped my foot upon the rug. My companion,

however, was evidently relieved.



“You have done right,” he said, in a tone of unqualified approbation,

while his face brightened into almost a sunny expression. “And as for

the mistake, I am sorry for both our sakes that it should have

occurred. Perhaps you can forgive my want of candour, and remember, as

some partial mitigation of the offence, how little encouragement to

friendly confidence you have given me of late.”



“Yes, yes—I remember it all: nobody can blame me more than I blame

myself in my own heart; at any rate, nobody can regret more sincerely

than I do the result of my _brutality_, as you rightly term it.”



“Never mind that,” said he, faintly smiling; “let us forget all

unpleasant words on both sides, as [[motifs/well|well]] as deeds, and consign to

oblivion everything that we have cause to regret. Have you any

objection to take my hand, or you’d rather not?” It trembled through

weakness as he held it out, and dropped before I had [[motifs/time|time]] to catch it


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Dubito che riuscisse a vedermi… Comunque, non avevo intenzione di andare.”

Ma fui ignorato. Aspettai tranquillamente nell’atrio che venissi chiamato, ma…

“Deciso interiormente a non accettare alcuna negazione… Il messaggio era proprio quello.”

Aspettato… un modo educato per indicare che il signor Lawrence non voleva ricevere nessuno.

Febbrile, e non deve essere disturbato.



“Non lo disturberò a lungo,” dissi; “ma devo assolutamente vederlo.”

“Per una questione di grande importanza, desidero parlare con lui.”



“Glielo dirò, signore,” disse l’uomo. E io proseguii oltre…

Hall lo seguì quasi fino alla porta dell’appartamento dove abitava…

“Il maestro… perché sembrava che non fosse a letto.” La risposta ricevuta fu…

Che il signor Lawrence sperasse che fossi così gentile da lasciare un messaggio o qualcosa del genere…

Nota al servitore, poiché in quel momento non era in grado di occuparsi di nulla.



“Potrebbe benissimo considerarmi come te,” dissi; e, passandogli accanto.

“Con un servitore sorpreso alle mie spalle, bussai coraggiosamente alla porta, entrai e la chiusi.”

Dietro di me… La stanza era spaziosa e arredata con gusto… molto bella.

Anche in modo confortevole, per un scapolo. Un chiaro fuoco rosso ardeva nel.

Polito e lucido… ma ormai inutile: un levriero anziano, abbandonato alla pigrizia…

Buona vita… sdraiarsi e rilassarsi su quel tappeto spesso e morbido…

Angolo in cui, accanto al divano, sedeva un grazioso giovane cane di razza Springer…

Sollevato con malinconia davanti al suo padrone… forse chiedendo il permesso di condividerlo.

Il suo divano… o forse, semplicemente, il desiderio di ricevere una carezza dalla sua mano…

Una parola gentile uscita dalle sue labbra… L’invalido stesso aveva un aspetto davvero interessante…

Giaceva disteso lì, nel suo elegante pigiama di seta…

Un fazzoletto legato intorno alle tempie… Il suo viso solitamente pallido…

Arrossito e febbrile; gli occhi semichiusi, fino a quando…

“Consapevole della mia presenza… e poi le aprì abbastanza per far passare una mano.”

Fu gettato con noncuranza sullo schienale del divano e tenuto in mano… un piccolo oggetto.

Titolo:  
Il volume con cui, apparentemente, aveva tentato invano di…

Distrai le ore noiose… Ma lo lasciò cadere all’inizio del suo movimento.

Sorpresa indignata mentre entrai nella stanza e mi fermai davanti a lui

“Il tappeto… Si sollevò sui cuscini e mi fissò con lo stesso sguardo.”

Gradi di orrore nervoso, rabbia e stupore riflessi nel suo volto

espressione del volto.



“Signor Markham, non me l’aspettavo affatto!” disse; e il [[motifs/blood|sangue]] gli lasciò.

Gli si arrossò la guancia mentre parlava.



“So che non l’hai fatto”, risposi; “ma aspetta un attimo e te lo spiegherò”.

“Sei quello per cui sono venuto,” dissi, avvicinandomi senza pensarci due volte di un paio di passi. Lui…

Si ritrasse al mio avvicinamento, con un’espressione di disgusto e istintiva repulsione.

La paura fisica non faceva altro che peggiorare i miei sentimenti. Mi sono allontanato.

tuttavia.



“Racconta una storia breve”, disse, posando la mano sulla piccola…

“La campanella d’argento posata sul tavolo accanto a lui… altrimenti sarò costretto…”

Chiedo aiuto… Non sono più in grado di sopportare le vostre crudeltà.

“O nemmeno la tua presenza, ” E, in [[concepts/truth|verità]], l’umidità iniziò a uscire dal suo.

Gocce di sudore apparvero sulla sua pallida fronte, simili a rugiada.



Un’accoglienza del genere certamente non aiutava ad alleviare le difficoltà…

Il mio compito poco invidiabile… Deve comunque essere eseguito, in qualche modo o altro.

Quindi mi ci immersi subito, cercando di farcela nel modo migliore possibile.



“La [[concepts/truth|verità]] è questa, Lawrence,” dissi, “non ho agito del tutto correttamente.”

“Verso di te ultimamente… soprattutto in questa ultima occasione; ed eccomi qui.”

In breve, voglio esprimere il mio rammarico per quanto è accaduto e chiedere scusa.

“Scusi… Se non decidesi di concederlo,” aggiunsi in fretta.

“Mi piace l’aspetto del suo viso… Non importa; è solo che _io_ ho fatto _la mia parte_.”

Dovere… e basta.



“È facile da fare,” rispose lui, con un debole sorriso che sembrava sfiorare…

"Sdegno: abusare di un amico e colpirlo in testa senza alcuna ragione..."

Cause assegnabile… e poi dirgli che l’atto non era del tutto corretto… ma…

“Non importa se lo perdoni o meno.”



Dimenticai di dirti che tutto ciò è avvenuto a causa di…

“Un errore…”, mormorai. “Avrei dovuto scusarmi in modo molto appropriato…”

Mi hai provocato in modo così confuso con le tue. Beh, immagino che sia colpa mia.

Colpa mia… La verità è che non sapevo che foste il fratello della signora Graham.

E vidi e udii alcune cose riguardo al tuo comportamento verso di lei

Titolo:  
Calcolati apposta per suscitare sospetti sgradevoli… che, permettetemi di dire…

In altre parole, un po’ più di franchezza e fiducia da parte tua avrebbero potuto aiutare…

Ascoltato per caso…

“Qualcosa tra te e lei mi ha fatto credere di avere il diritto di odiarti.”



“E come facesti a sapere che ero suo fratello?”, chiese lui, con un certo…

ansia.



“Me lo ha detto lei stessa. Mi ha raccontato tutto. _Lei_ sapeva che si poteva fidare di me.”

“Ma non c’è bisogno che si preoccupi per quella questione, signor Lawrence, perché io ho già…”

“L’ultima volta che l’abbiamo vista…”



“L’ultima… Quindi se n’è andata?”



“No; ma lei mi ha detto addio, e io ho promesso di non avvicinarmi mai più a lei.”

Quella casa, di nuovo, mentre lei vi abita. Avrei potuto lamentarmi ad alta voce.

I pensieri amari risvegliati da questo cambiamento nel discorso… Ma io solo…

“Strinsi i pugni e calpestai il tappeto con il piede… Il mio compagno…”

Tuttavia, era evidentemente sollevato.



“Hai fatto bene”, disse, con un tono di approvazione senza riserve.

Mentre il suo viso si illuminava di un’espressione quasi radiosa… “E per quanto riguarda…”

Il errore… Mi dispiace per entrambi che sia successo.

Occorse… Forse potrete perdonare la mia mancanza di franchezza, e ricordate…

Una parziale attenuazione della colpa… quanto scarso incoraggiamento questo rappresenti.

“La fiducia che mi hai dimostrato in questi ultimi tempi…”



“Sì, sì… Me lo ricordo tutto: nessuno può incolparmi di più di quanto io stesso mi incolpi.”

“Me stesso nel mio cuore… In ogni caso, nessuno può pentirsi con maggiore sincerità.”

“Più di chiunque altro, so quali siano le conseguenze della mia ‘brutalità’, come la definite voi con ragione.”



“Lasciamo perdere,” disse lui, sorridendo debolmente; “dimentichiamoci tutto.”

Parole spiacevoli da entrambe le parti, tanto quanto azioni negative, e, lasciar perdere.

Oblio di tutto ciò per cui abbiamo motivo di rimpiangere… Ne hai qualche esempio?

“Obiezioni ad prendere la mia mano… o preferisci di no?” Tremava mentre lo diceva.

Mentre lo teneva in mano, mostrò segni di debolezza e lo lasciò cadere prima che io avessi il tempo di afferrarlo.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_45--part_06" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 45 (part 6)" data-chapter="Chapter 45" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/home,motif/time,concept/courage,concept/fear,concept/madness,concept/temptation,concept/truth"></span>


and give it a hearty squeeze, which he had not the strength to return.



“How dry and burning your hand is, Lawrence,” said I. “You are really

ill, and I have made you worse by all this talk.”



“Oh, it is nothing; only a cold got by the rain.”



“My doing, too.”



“Never mind that. But tell me, did you mention this affair to my

sister?”



“To confess the [[concepts/truth|truth]], I had not the [[concepts/courage|courage]] to do so; but when you

tell her, will you just say that I deeply regret it, and—?”



“Oh, never [[concepts/fear|fear]]! I shall say nothing against you, as long as you keep

your good resolution of remaining aloof from her. She has not heard of

my illness, then, that you are aware of?”



“I think not.”



“I’m glad of that, for I have been all this [[motifs/time|time]] tormenting myself with

the [[concepts/fear|fear]] that somebody would tell her I was dying, or desperately ill,

and she would be either distressing herself on account of her inability

to hear from me or do me any good, or perhaps committing the [[concepts/madness|madness]] of

coming to see me. I must contrive to let her know something about it,

if I can,” continued he, reflectively, “or she will be hearing some

such story. Many would be glad to tell her such news, just to see how

she would take it; and then she might expose herself to fresh scandal.”



“I wish I had told her,” said I. “If it were not for my promise, I

would tell her now.”



“By no means! I am not dreaming of that;—but if I were to write a short

note, now, not mentioning you, Markham, but just giving a slight

account of my illness, by way of excuse for my not coming to see her,

and to put her on her guard against any exaggerated reports she may

hear,—and address it in a disguised hand—would you do me the favour to

slip it into the post-office as you pass? for I dare not trust any of

the servants in such a case.”



Most willingly I consented, and immediately brought him his desk. There

was little need to disguise his hand, for the poor fellow seemed to

have considerable difficulty in writing at all, so as to be legible.

When the note was done, I thought it [[motifs/time|time]] to retire, and took leave,

after asking if there was anything in the world I could do for him,

little or great, in the way of alleviating his sufferings, and

repairing the injury I had done.



“No,” said he; “you have already done much towards it; you have done

more for me than the most skilful physician could do: for you have

relieved my mind of two great burdens—anxiety on my sister’s account,

and deep regret upon your own: for I do believe these two sources of

torment have had more effect in working me up into a fever than

anything else; and I am persuaded I shall soon recover now. There is

one more thing you can do for me, and that is, come and see me now and

then—for you see I am very lonely here, and I promise your entrance

shall not be disputed again.”



I engaged to do so, and departed with a cordial pressure of the hand. I

posted the letter on my way [[motifs/home|home]], most manfully resisting the

[[concepts/temptation|temptation]] of dropping in a word from myself at the same [[motifs/time|time]].


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

E lo strinse con forza, ma non aveva la forza sufficiente per restituirlo.



“Che mano asciutta e bruciante hai, Lawrence… Davvero.”

“Malato… e ho peggiorato le cose parlando così tanto.”



“Ah, niente di grave… solo un raffreddore preso a causa della pioggia.”



“Anche colpa mia.”



“Lascia perdere quella questione… Ma dimmi: hai menzionato questa faccenda a mio…”

“Sorella?”



“Per confessare la [[concepts/truth|verità]], non ho avuto il [[concepts/courage|coraggio]] di farlo; ma quando tu, ”

"Dille che mi dispiace profondamente, e…?"



“Oh, mai [[concepts/fear|temere]]! Non dirò nulla contro di te, purché tu mantenga, ”

La tua ferma decisione di mantenere le distanze da lei… Lei non ne sa nulla.

“La mia malattia… di cui siete a conoscenza, quindi?”



“No, penso di no.”



“Sono felice di questo, perché per tutto questo [[motifs/time|tempo]] mi sono tormentato con, ”

La [[concepts/fear|paura]] che qualcuno le dicesse che stavo morendo, o che fossi gravemente malato.

E lei si sarebbe angosciata per la propria incapacità…

Per ricevere notizie da me o per farmi qualche favore, oppure forse commettendo l’[[concepts/madness|pazzia]] di.

“Qualcuno sta venendo a trovarmi… Devo trovare un modo per farle sapere.”

“Se riesco…”, continuò riflettendo, “altrimenti lei sentirà qualcosa…”

Una storia del genere… Molti sarebbero felici di raccontarle notizie del genere, solo per vedere come reagisce.

“Lo accetterebbe… e poi potrebbe esporsi a nuovi scandali.”



“Vorrei averglielo detto”, dissi. “Se non fosse stato per la mia promessa…”

“Glielo direi adesso.”



"Assolutamente no! Non sto nemmeno pensando a una cosa del genere… Ma se dovesse capitarmi di scrivere qualcosa di breve…"

Not Menacing, But Just a Little...

Descrizione della mia malattia, come scusa per non essere andato a trovarla.

E avvertirla di fare attenzione a eventuali notizie esagerate che potrebbero arrivare…

Ascolta… e affrontalo con cautela… Mi faresti questo favore?

Mettitelo dentro l’ufficio postale mentre passi… Perché non oso fidarmi di nessuno.

“I servitori, in tal caso…”



Con grande piacere acconsentii e subito gli portai la sua scrivania. Lì.

Non c’era quasi bisogno di nascondere la sua mano, perché quel povero ragazzo sembrava…

Hanno notevoli difficoltà a scrivere, al punto che il testo risultante non è leggibile.

Quando la nota fu completata, pensai che fosse arrivato il momento di ritirarmi, quindi presi congedo.

Dopo aver chiesto se ci fosse qualcosa al mondo che potessi fare per lui…

Qualunque cosa sia stata fatta, per alleviare le sue sofferenze…

Riparare il danno che avevo causato.



“No“, disse lui; “hai già fatto molto al riguardo; hai compiuto un ottimo lavoro“.

“Per me è più efficace di quanto possa fare il medico più abile… perché tu hai…”

Ha sollevato il peso di due grandi preoccupazioni: l’ansia per mia sorella.

Profondo rimorso per te stesso… perché credo davvero che queste due fonti…

Il tormento ha avuto più effetto nel farmi venire la febbre di…

Qualcos’altro… e sono convinto che presto mi riprenderò del tutto. C’è…

“Un’altra cosa che puoi fare per me… è venire a trovarmi subito.”

“Allora… perché vedete, sono molto solo qui, e vi prometto che potrete entrare.”

“Non dovrà essere più discusso.”



Promisi di farlo e me ne andai, dopo aver stretto calorosamente la sua mano.

Ho messo la lettera in viaggio verso casa, resistendo con grande forza alla tentazione.

La tentazione di aggiungere una parola di mia parte nello stesso momento.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_46--part_01" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 46 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 46" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/blood,motif/desire,motif/home,motif/night,motif/rose,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/doubt,concept/fear,concept/reconciliation,character/helen"></span>


CHAPTER XLVI





I felt strongly tempted, at times, to enlighten my mother and sister on

the real character and circumstances of the persecuted tenant of

Wildfell Hall, and at first I greatly regretted having omitted to ask

that lady’s permission to do so; but, on due reflection, I considered

that if it were known to them, it could not long remain a secret to the

Millwards and Wilsons, and such was my present appreciation of Eliza

Millward’s disposition, that, if once she got a clue to the story, I

should [[concepts/fear|fear]] she would soon find means to enlighten Mr. Huntingdon upon

the place of his wife’s retreat. I would therefore wait patiently till

these weary six months were over, and then, when the fugitive had found

another [[motifs/home|home]], and I was permitted to write to her, I would beg to be

allowed to clear her name from these vile calumnies: at present I must

content myself with simply asserting that I knew them to be false, and

would prove it some day, to the shame of those who slandered her. I

don’t think anybody believed me, but everybody soon learned to avoid

insinuating a word against her, or even mentioning her name in my

presence. They thought I was so madly infatuated by the seductions of

that unhappy lady that I was determined to support her in the very face

of reason; and meantime I grow insupportably morose and misanthropical

from the idea that every one I met was harbouring unworthy thoughts of

the supposed Mrs. Graham, and would express them if he dared. My poor

mother was quite distressed about me; but I couldn’t help it—at least I

thought I could not, though sometimes I felt a pang of remorse for my

undutiful conduct to her, and made an effort to amend, attended with

some partial success; and indeed I was generally more humanised in my

demeanour to her than to any one else, Mr. Lawrence excepted. [[motifs/rose|Rose]] and

Fergus usually shunned my presence; and it was [[motifs/well|well]] they did, for I was

not fit company for them, nor they for me, under the present

circumstances.



Mrs. Huntingdon did not leave Wildfell Hall till above two months after

our farewell interview. During that [[motifs/time|time]] she never appeared at church,

and I never went near the house: I only knew she was still there by her

brother’s brief answers to my many and varied inquiries respecting her.

I was a very constant and attentive visitor to him throughout the whole

period of his illness and convalescence; not only from the interest I

took in his recovery, and my [[motifs/desire|desire]] to cheer him up and make the utmost

possible amends for my former “brutality,” but from my growing

attachment to himself, and the increasing pleasure I found in his

society—partly from his increased cordiality to me, but chiefly on

account of his close connection, both in [[motifs/blood|blood]] and in affection, with

my adored [[characters/helen|Helen]]. I loved him for it better than I liked to express: and

I took a secret delight in pressing those slender white fingers, so

marvellously like her own, considering he was not a woman, and in

watching the passing changes in his fair, pale features, and observing

the intonations of his voice, detecting resemblances which I wondered

had never struck me before. He provoked me at times, indeed, by his

evident reluctance to talk to me about his sister, though I did not

question the friendliness of his motives in wishing to discourage my

remembrance of her.



His recovery was not quite so rapid as he had expected it to be; he was

not able to mount his pony till a fortnight after the date of our

[[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]]; and the first use he made of his returning strength was

to ride over by [[motifs/night|night]] to Wildfell Hall, to see his sister. It was a

hazardous enterprise both for him and for her, but he thought it

necessary to consult with her on the subject of her projected

departure, if not to calm her apprehensions respecting his health, and

the worst result was a slight relapse of his illness, for no one knew

of the visit but the inmates of the old Hall, except myself; and I

believe it had not been his intention to mention it to me, for when I

came to see him the next day, and observed he was not so [[motifs/well|well]] as he

ought to have been, he merely said he had caught cold by being out too

late in the evening.



“You’ll _never_ be able to see your sister, if you don’t take care of

yourself,” said I, a little provoked at the circumstance on her

account, instead of commiserating him.



“I’ve seen her already,” said he, quietly.



“You’ve seen her!” cried I, in astonishment.



“Yes.” And then he told me what considerations had impelled him to make

the venture, and with what precautions he had made it.



“And how was she?” I eagerly asked.



“As usual,” was the brief though sad reply.



“As usual—that is, far from happy and far from strong.”



“She is not positively ill,” returned he; “and she will recover her

spirits in a while, I have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]]—but so many trials have been almost

too much for her. How threatening those clouds look,” continued he,

turning towards the [[motifs/window|window]]. “We shall have thunder-showers before

[[motifs/night|night]], I imagine, and they are just in the midst of stacking my corn.

Have you got yours all in yet?”



“No. And, Lawrence, did she—did your sister mention me?”



“She asked if I had seen you lately.”



“And what else did she say?”



“I cannot tell you all she said,” replied he, with a slight smile; “for

we talked a good deal, though my stay was but short; but our

conversation was chiefly on the subject of her intended departure,

which I begged her to delay till I was better able to assist her in her

search after another [[motifs/home|home]].”



“But did she say no more about me?”



“She did not say much about you, Markham. I should not have encouraged

her to do so, had she been inclined; but happily she was not: she only

asked a few questions concerning you, and seemed satisfied with my


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Avevo spesso la forte tentazione di illuminare mia madre e mia sorella su…

circostanze.



La signora Huntingdon lasciò Wildfell Hall soltanto dopo oltre due mesi

Il nostro ultimo colloquio di addio. Durante quel periodo, lei non si presentò mai in chiesa.

Il piacere segreto di premere quelle sottili dita bianche…

Meravigliosamente simile a lei stessa… considerando che non era una donna.

Le inflessioni della sua voce… rilevavo somiglianze che mi lasciavano perplesso.

Mettere in dubbio la cordialità delle sue intenzioni nel voler scoraggiarmi

Il ricordo di lei.



La sua guarigione non fu così rapida come aveva previsto; lui…

[[concepts/reconciliation|riconciliazione]]; e la prima volta che utilizzò le sue forze ritrovate fu.

Un’impresa pericolosa sia per lui che per lei, ma lui pensò che…

Necessario consultarla riguardo al tema del suo progetto futuro

Se non per tranquillizzarla riguardo alle sue preoccupazioni per la sua salute…

Il peggior risultato fu un lieve ritorno della sua malattia, poiché nessuno lo sapeva.

Della visita, ma gli interni dell’antica Hall, tranne me… e io.

Non credo che avesse intenzione di menzionarmelo… perché quando io…

Andò a trovarlo il giorno dopo e notò che non stava affatto così [[motifs/well|bene]] come prima.

Avrebbe dovuto esserlo… Ma ha semplicemente detto di essersi raffreddato per essere stato troppo tempo all’aperto.

tardi nella serata.



“Non riuscirai mai più a vedere tua sorella, se non ti prendi cura di…”

“Te ne occuperai tu stessa,” dissi, un po’ infastidita dalla situazione in cui mi trovavo.

Rispondere al suo messaggio, invece di compiangerlo.



“L’ho già vista,” disse lui, in silenzio.



“L’hai vista!” esclamai, stupito.



“Sì.” E poi mi spiegò quali considerazioni lo avevano spinto a prendere quella decisione.

L’impresa, e le precauzioni che aveva preso per realizzarla.



“E come era?” chiesi con impazienza.



“Come al solito”, fu la breve ma triste risposta.



“Come al solito… cioè, lontano dall’essere felice e lontano dall’essere forte.”

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_46--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 46 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 46" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/desire,motif/home,motif/love,motif/tears,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/fear,concept/imagination,concept/revenge,concept/truth,concept/union"></span>


brief answers, wherein she showed herself wiser than her friend; and I

may tell you, too, that she seemed to be far more anxious lest you

should think too much of her, than lest you should forget her.”



“She was right.”



“But I [[concepts/fear|fear]] _your_ anxiety is quite the other way respecting her.”



“No, it is not: I wish her to be happy; but I don’t wish her to forget

me altogether. She knows it is impossible that I should forget _her;_

and she is right to wish me not to remember her too [[motifs/well|well]]. I should not

[[motifs/desire|desire]] her to regret me _too_ deeply; but I can scarcely imagine she

will make herself very unhappy about me, because I know I am not worthy

of it, except in my appreciation of her.”



“You are neither of you worthy of a broken heart,—nor of all the sighs,

and [[motifs/tears|tears]], and sorrowful thoughts that have been, and I [[concepts/fear|fear]] will be,

wasted upon you both; but, at present, each has a more exalted opinion

of the other than, I [[concepts/fear|fear]], he or she deserves; and my sister’s feelings

are naturally full as keen as yours, and I believe _more_ constant; but

she has the good sense and fortitude to strive against them in this

particular; and I trust she will not rest till she has entirely weaned

her thoughts—” he hesitated.



“From me,” said I.



“And I wish you would make the like exertions,” continued he.



“Did she _tell_ you that that was her intention?”



“No; the question was not broached between us: there was no necessity

for it, for I had no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] that such was her determination.”



“To forget me?”



“Yes, Markham! Why not?”



“Oh, [[motifs/well|well]]!” was my only audible reply; but I internally answered,—“No,

Lawrence, you’re wrong there: she is _not_ determined to forget me. It

would be _wrong_ to forget one so deeply and fondly devoted to her, who

can so thoroughly appreciate her excellencies, and sympathise with all

her thoughts, as I can do, and it would be wrong in me to forget so

excellent and divine a piece of God’s creation as she, when I have once

so truly loved and known her.” But I said no more to him on that

subject. I instantly started a new topic of conversation, and soon took

leave of my companion, with a feeling of less cordiality towards him

than usual. Perhaps I had no right to be annoyed at him, but I was so

nevertheless.



In little more than a week after this I met him returning from a visit

to the Wilsons’; and I now resolved to do _him_ a good turn, though at

the expense of his feelings, and perhaps at the risk of incurring that

displeasure which is so commonly the reward of those who give

disagreeable information, or tender their advice unasked. In this,

believe me, I was actuated by no motives of [[concepts/revenge|revenge]] for the occasional

annoyances I had lately sustained from him,—nor yet by any feeling of

malevolent enmity towards Miss Wilson, but purely by the fact that I

could not endure that such a woman should be Mrs. Huntingdon’s sister,

and that, as [[motifs/well|well]] for his own sake as for hers, I could not bear to

think of his being deceived into a [[concepts/union|union]] with one so unworthy of him,

and so utterly unfitted to be the partner of his quiet [[motifs/home|home]], and the

companion of his life. He had had uncomfortable suspicions on that head

himself, I imagined; but such was his inexperience, and such were the

lady’s powers of attraction, and her skill in bringing them to bear

upon his young [[concepts/imagination|imagination]], that they had not disturbed him long; and I

believe the only effectual causes of the vacillating indecision that

had preserved him hitherto from making an actual declaration of [[motifs/love|love]],

was the consideration of her connections, and especially of her mother,

whom he could not abide. Had they lived at a distance, he might have

surmounted the objection, but within two or three miles of Woodford it

was really no light matter.



“You’ve been to call on the Wilsons, Lawrence,” said I, as I walked

beside his pony.



“Yes,” replied he, slightly averting his face: “I thought it but civil

to take the first opportunity of returning their kind attentions, since

they have been so very particular and constant in their inquiries

throughout the whole course of my illness.”



“It’s all Miss Wilson’s doing.”



“And if it is,” returned he, with a very perceptible blush, “is that

any reason why I should not make a suitable acknowledgment?”



“It is a reason why you should not make the acknowledgment she looks

for.”



“Let us drop that subject if you please,” said he, in evident

displeasure.



“No, Lawrence, with your leave we’ll continue it a while longer; and

I’ll tell you something, now we’re about it, which you may believe or

not as you choose—only please to remember that it is not my custom to

speak falsely, and that in this case I can have no motive for

misrepresenting the [[concepts/truth|truth]]—”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], Markham, what now?”



“_Miss Wilson hates your sister._ It may be natural enough that, in her

ignorance of the relationship, she should feel some degree of enmity

against her, but no good or amiable woman would be capable of evincing

that bitter, cold-blooded, designing malice towards a fancied rival

that I have observed in her.”



“Markham!”



“Yes—and it is my belief that Eliza Millward and she, if not the very

originators of the slanderous reports that have been propagated, were

designedly the encouragers and chief disseminators of them. She was not

desirous to mix up _your_ name in the matter, of course, but her

delight was, and still is, to blacken your sister’s character to the

utmost of her power, without risking too greatly the exposure of her

own malevolence!”



“I cannot believe it,” interrupted my companion, his face burning with

indignation.



“[[motifs/well|Well]], as I cannot prove it, I must content myself with asserting that

it is so to the best of my belief; but as you would not willingly marry

Miss Wilson if it _were_ so, you will do [[motifs/well|well]] to be cautious, till you

have proved it to be otherwise.”

“Then you have no right to make such an assertion respecting her.” He

“Wait a moment, Lawrence, and let me explain myself; and don’t be so

very—I don’t know what to call it—_inaccessible_ as you are.—I know

what you think of Jane Wilson; and I believe I know how far you are

mistaken in your opinion: you think she is singularly charming,

elegant, sensible, and refined: you are not aware that she is selfish,

cold-hearted, ambitious, artful, shallow-minded—”



“Enough, Markham—enough!”



“No; let me finish:—you don’t know that, if you married her, your [[motifs/home|home]]

would be rayless and comfortless; and it would break your heart at last

to find yourself united to one so wholly incapable of sharing your

tastes, feelings, and ideas—so utterly destitute of sensibility, good

feeling, and true nobility of [[motifs/soul|soul]].”



“Have you done?” asked my companion quietly.



“Yes;—I know you hate me for my impertinence, but I don’t care if it

only conduces to preserve you from that fatal mistake.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]]!” returned he, with a rather wintry smile—“I’m glad you have

overcome or forgotten your own afflictions so far as to be able to

study so deeply the affairs of others, and trouble your head so

unnecessarily about the fancied or possible calamities of their future

life.”



We parted—somewhat coldly again: but still we did not cease to be

friends; and my [[motifs/well|well]]-meant warning, though it might have been more

judiciously delivered, as [[motifs/well|well]] as more thankfully received, was not

wholly unproductive of the desired effect: his visit to the Wilsons was

not repeated, and though, in our subsequent interviews, he never

mentioned her name to me, nor I to him,—I have reason to believe he

pondered my words in his mind, eagerly though covertly sought

information respecting the fair lady from other quarters, secretly

compared my character of her with what he had himself observed and what

he heard from others, and finally came to the conclusion that, all

things considered, she had much better remain Miss Wilson of Ryecote

Farm than be transmuted into Mrs. Lawrence of Woodford Hall. I believe,

too, that he soon learned to contemplate with secret amazement his

former predilection, and to congratulate himself on the lucky escape he

had made; but he never confessed it to me, or hinted one word of

acknowledgment for the part I had had in his deliverance, but this was

not surprising to any one that knew him as I did.



As for Jane Wilson, she, of course, was disappointed and embittered by

the sudden cold neglect and ultimate desertion of her former admirer.

Had I done wrong to blight her cherished hopes? I think not; and

certainly my [[concepts/conscience|conscience]] has never accused me, from that day to this, of

any evil design in the matter.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_47--part_01" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 47 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 47" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,motif/fire,motif/home,motif/horse,motif/rose,motif/time,motif/well,concept/fear,concept/hope,concept/reconciliation"></span>


CHAPTER XLVII





One morning, about the beginning of November, while I was inditing some

business letters, shortly after breakfast, Eliza Millward came to call

upon my sister. [[motifs/rose|Rose]] had neither the discrimination nor the virulence

to regard the little demon as I did, and they still preserved their

former intimacy. At the moment of her arrival, however, there was no

one in the room but Fergus and myself, my mother and sister being both

of them absent, “on household cares intent”; but _I_ was not going to

lay myself out for her amusement, whoever else might so incline: I

merely honoured her with a careless salutation and a few words of

course, and then went on with my writing, leaving my brother to be more

polite if he chose. But she wanted to tease me.



“What a pleasure it is to find you at [[motifs/home|home]], Mr. Markham!” said she,

with a disingenuously malicious smile. “I so seldom see you now, for

you never come to the vicarage. Papa, is quite offended, I can tell

you,” she added playfully, looking into my face with an impertinent

laugh, as she seated herself, half beside and half before my desk, off

the corner of the table.



“I have had a good deal to do of late,” said I, without looking up from

my letter.



“Have you, indeed! Somebody said you had been strangely neglecting your

business these last few months.”



“Somebody said wrong, for, these last two months especially, I have

been particularly plodding and diligent.”



“Ah! [[motifs/well|well]], there’s nothing like active employment, I suppose, to

console the afflicted;—and, excuse me, Mr. Markham, but you look so

very far from [[motifs/well|well]], and have been, by all accounts, so moody and

thoughtful of late,—I could almost think you have some secret care

preying on your spirits. _Formerly_,” said she timidly, “I could have

ventured to ask you what it was, and what I could do to comfort you: I

dare not do it now.”



“You’re very kind, Miss Eliza. When I think you can do anything to

comfort me, I’ll make bold to tell you.”



“Pray do!—I suppose I mayn’t guess what it is that troubles you?”



“There’s no necessity, for I’ll tell you plainly. The thing that

troubles me the most at present is a young lady sitting at my elbow,

and preventing me from finishing my letter, and, thereafter, repairing

to my daily business.”



Before she could reply to this ungallant speech, [[motifs/rose|Rose]] entered the room;

and Miss Eliza rising to greet her, they both seated themselves near

the [[motifs/fire|fire]], where that idle lad Fergus was standing, leaning his shoulder

against the corner of the chimney-piece, with his legs crossed and his

hands in his breeches-pockets.



“Now, [[motifs/rose|Rose]], I’ll tell you a piece of news—I [[concepts/hope|hope]] you have not heard it

before: for good, bad, or indifferent, one always likes to be the first

to tell. It’s about that sad Mrs. Graham—”



“Hush-sh-sh!” whispered Fergus, in a tone of solemn import. “‘We never

mention her; her name is never heard.’” And glancing up, I caught him

with his eye askance on me, and his finger pointed to his forehead;

then, winking at the young lady with a doleful shake of the head, he

whispered—“A monomania—but don’t mention it—all right but that.”



“I should be sorry to injure any one’s feelings,” returned she,

speaking below her breath. “Another [[motifs/time|time]], perhaps.”



“Speak out, Miss Eliza!” said I, not deigning to notice the other’s

buffooneries: “you needn’t [[concepts/fear|fear]] to say anything in my presence.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]],” answered she, “perhaps you know already that Mrs. Graham’s

husband is not really dead, and that she had run away from him?” I

started, and felt my face glow; but I bent it over my letter, and went

on folding it up as she proceeded. “But perhaps you did _not_ know that

she is now gone back to him again, and that a perfect [[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]]

has taken place between them? Only think,” she continued, turning to

the confounded [[motifs/rose|Rose]], “what a [[archetypes/fool|fool]] the man must be!”



“And who gave you this piece of intelligence, Miss Eliza?” said I,

interrupting my sister’s exclamations.



“I had it from a very authentic source.”



“From whom, may I ask?”



“From one of the servants at Woodford.”



“Oh! I was not aware that you were on such intimate terms with Mr.

Lawrence’s household.”



“It was not from the man himself that I heard it, but he told it in

confidence to our maid Sarah, and Sarah told it to me.”



“In confidence, I suppose? And you tell it in confidence to us? But _I_

can tell _you_ that it is but a lame story after all, and scarcely

one-half of it true.”



While I spoke I completed the sealing and direction of my letters, with

a somewhat unsteady hand, in spite of all my efforts to retain

composure, and in spite of my firm conviction that the story _was_ a

lame one—that the supposed Mrs. Graham, most certainly, had not

_voluntarily_ gone back to her husband, or dreamt of a [[concepts/reconciliation|reconciliation]].

Most likely she was gone away, and the tale-bearing servant, not

knowing what was become of her, had _conjectured_ that such was the

case, and our fair visitor had detailed it as a certainty, delighted

with such an opportunity of tormenting me. But it was possible—barely

possible—that some one might have betrayed her, and she had been taken

away by force. Determined to know the worst, I hastily pocketed my two

letters, and muttered something about being too late for the post, left

the room, rushed into the yard, and vociferously called for my [[motifs/horse|horse]].

No one being there, I dragged him out of the stable myself, strapped

the saddle on to his back and the bridle on to his head, mounted, and

speedily galloped away to Woodford. I found its owner pensively

strolling in the grounds.



“Is your sister gone?” were my first words as I grasped his hand,

instead of the usual inquiry after his health.



“Yes, she’s gone,” was his answer, so calmly spoken that my terror was

at once removed.

CAPITOLO XLVII





Una mattina, all’inizio di novembre, mentre stavo scrivendo qualcosa…

Lettere d’affari: poco dopo colazione, Eliza Millward venne a far visita.

Su mia sorella. [[motifs/rose|Rose]] non possedeva né la capacità di discriminare, né la crudeltà necessarie per farlo.

Considerare quel piccolo demone come facevo io… eppure loro continuarono a conservarlo.

Antica intimità… Ma al momento del suo arrivo, non c’era nulla di tutto ciò.

“Uno nella stanza… ma solo Fergus e io; mia madre e mia sorella non c’erano.”

Di loro assenti, “immersi nelle cure domestiche”; ma io non intendevo andare.

Mi metto a disposizione della sua divertimento, così come di chiunque altro ne abbia voglia… Io.

Le ha rivolto soltanto un saluto superficiale e alcune parole di circostanza…

Certo, ecco la traduzione in italiano del titolo: “Naturalmente, continuai con il mio lavoro di scrittura, lasciando che mio fratello si occupasse del resto.”

Poteva essere gentile, se avesse voluto. Ma voleva solo prendermi in giro.

Con un sorriso falsamente malizioso: “Ora ti vedo così di rado…”

Non vieni mai alla canonica… Papà è davvero offeso, lo si capisce.

“Tu”, aggiunse scherzando, guardandomi dritto negli occhi con un tono un po’ irriverente…

Ride, mentre si sedeva, metà accanto e metà davanti alla mia scrivania…

l'angolo del tavolo.

La mia lettera.

“Affari… negli ultimi mesi.”



“Qualcuno ha detto il contrario, perché proprio in questi ultimi due mesi… ho…”

“Si è dimostrato particolarmente meticoloso e diligente.”



“Ah! Beh, suppongo che non ci sia nulla di meglio del lavoro attivo, ”

Consolare chi è afflitto… E scusi, signor Markham, ma lei sembra davvero molto stanco.

Lontano dall’essere in buone condizioni, e, a quanto si dice, molto malinconico.

Di recente sei stato molto pensieroso… Sembra quasi che tu abbia qualche preoccupazione nascosta.

“Consumendo la tua anima… In passato”, disse lei timidamente, “forse avrei potuto…”

Ho osato chiederti di cosa si trattasse e cosa potessi fare per consolarti…

“Non oso farlo adesso.”



“È molto gentile da parte sua, signorina Eliza… Quando penso che lei sia in grado di fare qualsiasi cosa…”

“Consolami… e sarò coraggioso abbastanza da dirtelo.”



“Per favore, fatelo! Immagino di non riuscire a indovinare cosa ti preoccupi…”



“Non c’è alcuna necessità, ve lo dico chiaramente… La cosa che…”

Quello che mi preoccupa di più in questo momento è una giovane signora seduta al mio fianco…

Impedendomi di completare la mia lettera e, successivamente, di sistemarla…

“Alle mie occupazioni quotidiane.”



Prima che potesse rispondere a quel discorso scortese, [[motifs/rose|Rose]] entrò nella stanza.

E la signorina Eliza si alza per salutarla; entrambe si siedono vicine.

Il [[motifs/fire|fuoco]], dove quel ragazzo indolente, Fergus, stava in piedi appoggiandosi alla spalla.

Appoggiato contro l’angolo del camino, con le gambe incrociate…

Le mani nelle tasche dei suoi calzoni.



“Ora, [[motifs/rose|Rose]], ti dirò una notizia. Spero che tu non l’abbia già sentita.”

Prima di tutto… sempre vogliamo essere i primi

“Per raccontare… Si tratta di quella triste signora Graham…”



“Zitto-zitto-zitto!”, sussurrò Fergus con un tono solenne e grave. “‘Noi mai…’”

“Mai si menziona il suo nome; non viene mai pronunciato.” E alzando lo sguardo, lo vidi…

Con lo sguardo obliquo rivolto verso di me e il dito puntato alla fronte…

“Allora, facendo l’occhiolino alla giovane signorina e scuotendo tristemente la testa…”

“Una monomania… ma non ne parliamo, d’accordo?”



“Mi dispiacerebbe molto se dovessi ferire i sentimenti di qualcuno”, rispose lei.

Parlando a bassa voce: “Forse, un’altra [[motifs/time|volta]], ”



“Parliate apertamente, signorina Eliza!”, dissi io, senza degnarmi di prestare attenzione all’altro.

Ora è tornata da lui di nuovo, ed è stata una perfetta [[concepts/reconciliation|riconciliazione]].

Interrompendo le esclamazioni di mia sorella.



L'ho avuto da una fonte molto autentica.



“Da chi, posso chiedere?”



“Da uno dei servitori di Woodford.”



“Oh! Non sapevo che foste in rapporti così stretti con il signor, ”

“La famiglia di Lawrence”.

Una storia davvero mediocre…

Mentre parlavo, completai la sigillatura e l’indirizzamento delle mie lettere.

Una mano piuttosto incerta, nonostante tutti i miei sforzi per mantenerla ferma…

Composizione… e nonostante la mia ferma convinzione che quella storia _fosse_ davvero così…

Si era volontariamente riunita con suo marito, o sognava una [[concepts/reconciliation|riconciliazione]].

Sapendo cosa le fosse accaduto, aveva ipotizzato che fosse andata proprio così.

Caso certo… e la nostra gentile ospite lo aveva descritto come una certezza, con grande entusiasmo.

Con un’opportunità del genere per tormentarmi… Ma era possibile… Appena.

Possibile… che qualcuno l’abbia tradita e che lei sia stata portata via.

Via con la forza. Deciso a scoprire il peggio, infilai rapidamente in tasca i miei due…

Lettere… e mormorò qualcosa riguardo al fatto che fosse troppo tardi per la consegna postale… se ne andò.

Entrò nella stanza di corsa, uscì nel cortile e chiamò ad alta voce il mio [[motifs/horse|cavallo]].

"In sella e con la briglia in testa, montato a cavallo..."

Si allontanò al galoppo verso Woodford… Il suo proprietario sembrava assorto nei suoi pensieri.

Passeggiando nei giardini.



“Tua sorella se n’è andata?” furono le mie prime parole mentre gli stringevo la mano.

Invece dell’abituale domanda sul suo stato di salute.



“Sì, se n’è andata,” rispose lui con tale calma che il mio terrore aumentò ancora di più.

<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_47--part_02" data-title="The Tenant of Wildfell Hall — Chapter 47 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 47" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,motif/death,motif/garden,motif/grave,motif/horse,motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/time,motif/window,histref/reformation,character/arthur,character/helen,character/helen_huntingdon,character/nurse"></span>


“I suppose I mayn’t know where she is?” said I, as I dismounted, and

relinquished my [[motifs/horse|horse]] to the gardener, who, being the only servant

within call, had been summoned by his master, from his employment of

raking up the dead [[motifs/leaves|leaves]] on the lawn, to take him to the stables.



My companion gravely took my arm, and leading me away to the [[motifs/garden|garden]],

thus answered my question,—“She is at Grassdale Manor, in ——shire.”



“Where?” cried I, with a convulsive start.



“At Grassdale Manor.”



“How was it?” I gasped. “Who betrayed her?”



“She went of her own accord.”



“Impossible, Lawrence! She _could_ not be so frantic!” exclaimed I,

vehemently grasping his arm, as if to force him to unsay those hateful

words.



“She did,” persisted he in the same [[motifs/grave|grave]], collected manner as before;

“and not without reason,” he continued, gently disengaging himself from

my grasp. “Mr. Huntingdon is ill.”



“And so she went to [[characters/nurse|nurse]] him?”



“Yes.”



“[[archetypes/fool|Fool]]!” I could not help exclaiming, and Lawrence looked up with a

rather reproachful glance. “Is he dying, then?”



“I think not, Markham.”



“And how many more nurses has he? How many ladies are there besides to

take care of him?”



“None; he was alone, or she would not have gone.”



“Oh, confound it! This is intolerable!”



“What is? That he should be alone?”



I attempted no reply, for I was not sure that this circumstance did not

partly conduce to my distraction. I therefore continued to pace the

walk in silent anguish, with my hand pressed to my forehead; then

suddenly pausing and turning to my companion, I impatiently exclaimed,

“Why did she take this infatuated step? What fiend persuaded her to

it?”



“Nothing persuaded her but her own sense of duty.”



“Humbug!”



“I was half inclined to say so myself, Markham, at first. I assure you

it was not by my advice that she went, for I detest that man as

fervently as you can do,—except, indeed, that his [[historical-references/reformation|reformation]] would

give me much greater pleasure than his [[motifs/death|death]]; but all I did was to

inform her of the circumstance of his illness (the consequence of a

fall from his [[motifs/horse|horse]] in hunting), and to tell her that that unhappy

person, Miss Myers, had left him some [[motifs/time|time]] ago.”



“It was ill done! Now, when he finds the convenience of her presence,

he will make all manner of lying speeches and false, fair promises for

the future, and she will believe him, and then her condition will be

ten times worse and ten times more irremediable than before.”



“There does not appear to be much ground for such apprehensions at

present,” said he, producing a letter from his pocket. “From the

account I received this morning, I should say—”



It was _her_ writing! By an irresistible impulse I held out my hand,

and the words, “Let me see it,” involuntarily passed my lips. He was

evidently reluctant to grant the request, but while he hesitated I

snatched it from his hand. Recollecting myself, however, the minute

after, I offered to restore it.



“Here, take it,” said I, “if you don’t want me to read it.”



“No,” replied he, “you may read it if you like.”



I read it, and so may you.



Grassdale, Nov. 4th.





DEAR FREDERICK,—I know you will be anxious to hear from me, and I will

tell you all I can. Mr. Huntingdon is very ill, but not dying, or in

any immediate danger; and he is rather better at present than he was

when I came. I found the house in sad confusion: Mrs. Greaves, Benson,

every decent servant had left, and those that were come to supply their

places were a negligent, disorderly set, to say no worse—I must change

them again, if I stay. A professional [[characters/nurse|nurse]], a grim, hard old woman,

had been hired to attend the wretched invalid. He suffers much, and has

no fortitude to bear him through. The immediate injuries he sustained

from the accident, however, were not very severe, and would, as the

doctor says, have been but trifling to a man of temperate habits, but

with _him_ it is very different. On the [[motifs/night|night]] of my arrival, when I

first entered his room, he was lying in a kind of half delirium. He did

not notice me till I spoke, and then he mistook me for another.



“Is it you, Alice, come again?” he murmured. “What did you leave me

for?”



“It is I, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]—it is [[characters/helen|Helen]], your wife,” I replied.



“My wife!” said he, with a start. “For heaven’s sake, don’t mention

her—I have none. Devil take her,” he cried, a moment after, “and you,

too! What did you do it for?”



I said no more; but observing that he kept gazing towards the foot of

the bed, I went and sat there, placing the light so as to shine full

upon me, for I thought he might be dying, and I wanted him to know me.

For a long [[motifs/time|time]] he lay silently looking upon me, first with a vacant

stare, then with a fixed gaze of strange growing intensity. At last he

startled me by suddenly raising himself on his elbow and demanding in a

horrified whisper, with his eyes still fixed upon me, “Who is it?”



“It is [[characters/helen-huntingdon|Helen Huntingdon]],” said I, quietly rising at the same [[motifs/time|time]], and

removing to a less conspicuous position.



“I must be going mad,” cried he, “or something—delirious, perhaps; but

leave me, whoever you are. I can’t bear that white face, and those

eyes. For God’s sake go, and send me somebody else that doesn’t look

like that!”



I went at once, and sent the hired [[characters/nurse|nurse]]; but next morning I ventured

to enter his chamber again, and, taking the [[characters/nurse|nurse]]’s place by his

bedside, I watched him and waited on him for several hours, showing

myself as little as possible, and only speaking when necessary, and

then not above my breath. At first he addressed me as the [[characters/nurse|nurse]], but,

on my crossing the room to draw up the [[motifs/window|window]]-blinds, in obedience to

his directions, he said, “No, it isn’t [[characters/nurse|nurse]]; it’s Alice. Stay with me,

Cammino nella silenziosa angoscia, con la mano premuta sulla fronte… Poi.

"Niente riuscì a convincerla se non il suo senso del dovere."

Grassdale, 4 novembre.





Caro Frederick, so so che sarai ansioso di ricevere mie notizie, e io…

“Sei tu, Alice… sei tornata di nuovo?”, mormorò. “Cosa mi hai lasciato…”

“Sono io, [[characters/arthur|Arthur]]. È [[characters/helen|Helen]], tua moglie,” risposi.



“Mia moglie!”, esclamò, sobbalzando. “Per l’amor del cielo, non parlarne…”

“Lei… non ne ho nessuna. Che il diavolo se la prenda”, gridò dopo un momento, “e tu…”

“Anche tu? E per quale motivo l’hai fatto?”



Non dissi più nulla; ma notando che continuava a fissare la base…

Sul letto, mi sono seduto e ho posizionato la lampada in modo che il suo chiaro si diffondesse ovunque.

spostandolo in una posizione meno evidente.

Andai subito e mandai la tata assunta; ma il giorno dopo mi azzardai.

do! That old hag will be the [[motifs/death|death]] of me.”
